News.title: Drummer, 56, dies mid-performance after collapsing over kit onstage at rock festival in front of horrified fans
News.content:
A DRUMMER has tragically died onstage after collapsing as he and his band performed for a packed out festival crowd.

Malaysian drummer, Raja Azreen Raja Talib fell unconscious while on stage after performing only two songs with his rock band Meditasi.



During the second song of their set, frontman Bakaruddin Daud – also known as Burn – noticed the 56-year-old drummer slump over on his drum kit.

Burn said Raja’s body “was already cold“, when he spoke with Malaysian newspaper Berita Harian.



He said: “I rushed towards him, but I could feel that he was gone,

“I called and patted [him], but there was no response.”

He added that Raja showed no signs of being ill before he went on stage at the Teruntum Rock Festival in Malaysia.

Burn later revealed that the late drummer had recently been diagnosed with diabetes.



After Raja collapsed, he was rushed to Tengku Ampuan Afzan Hospital and given respiratory assistance.

Unfortunately, he was pronounced dead due to heart complications.

Burn said that he was “deeply affected” by Raja’s death, as they had known each other for decades.

Burn handled all of the funeral arrangements, according to Raja’s brother, Azman.

Azman shared that the drummer was hospitalised in June due to heart issues.



He said: “He was hospitalised twice; the first stay lasted two to three weeks before he was admitted again.

“It is possible that extreme fatigue took a toll [on his heart],

He added that Raja “went straight” from a BMX competition to performing at the music festival.

Raja was very passionate about sport and had continued to compete in events after his health had improved.

Meditasi, which means Meditation in Malay, was active in the 1980s and 1990s and disbanded before reuniting in 2015.



The band has more than 46,000 monthly listeners on Spotify.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

As for the future of the band, Burn told the newspaper that he and Meditasi’s guitarist, Rosli Ahmad, have not yet discussed it.

He confirmed, however, that the group will continue to perform as they believe Raja Azreen would have wished.

News.title: Four kids found in deplorable conditions left with ‘unnatural’ walk after being ‘confined to tractor trailer for YEARS’
News.content:
'CURLED UP SIDE BY SIDE' Four kids found in deplorable conditions left with ‘unnatural’ walk after being ‘confined to tractor trailer for YEARS’

FOUR children were allegedly confined to the cab of a tractor-trailer for nearly seven years – leaving them with an “unnatural” walk, cops say.

The kids were reportedly forced to sleep curled up together in a tiny bunk and were deprived of schooling, medical care and even regular access to showers and a bathroom.



Florida couple Keisha Epps, 51, and her fiancé Tamra Marshon Stewart, 37, have now been charged with child neglect over the alleged horror conditions.

The children had reportedly been living inside the truck’s cab with the couple since December 2019 as Epps worked as a truck driver on a route between Miami and Atlanta.



They were allegedly kept inside the vehicle “for the majority of their days,” according to court documents.

Investigators claim the confinement had taken such a toll that a detective noticed the children were “walking with an unnatural gait from being confined to the cab.”

The four kids allegedly shared a single bunk where they had to lie “curled up side by side because they could not fit.”

They also claimed they were not given enough time to shower, use the restroom or exercise outside the truck.

And the children told interviewers at a child advocacy center they “have not been allowed to attend school for approximately five years,” Fox News reported.



Investigators said the youngsters were “fed poorly” and allegedly received no medical or dental care – even when they were injured.

One child recalled suffering a serious burn from cooked noodles while living in the truck.

“There was a lot of blood,” she told investigators.

The child claimed neither Epps nor Stewart sought medical treatment for the injury, which allegedly left her with a “permanent scar”.

More disturbing allegations emerged when the children were interviewed by investigators.



They reportedly claimed they witnessed sexual abuse and confronted Stewart about it.

Stewart then allegedly “beat them by punching them in their heads,” according to the reports.

The identity of the alleged sexual abuse victim was unclear in the heavily redacted court documents.

The children also claimed they told Epps about the alleged abuse and that she had witnessed it herself.

Investigators allege Epps called one of the children “derogatory names and continued to leave them alone with” Stewart.



One of the four children was also reportedly discovered to have an untreated sexually transmitted infection.

The reports do not disclose the children’s ages, sexes, relationships to one another or their relationships to Epps and Stewart.

Stewart allegedly watched the youngsters while Epps was driving, sleeping or showering.

Epps and Stewart were both arrested on August 6 following the investigation by the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office.

Each has been charged with four counts of child neglect – one for each child.



Investigators alleged their actions amounted to a “committed, willful failure or omission to provide a child with the care, supervision, and services necessary to maintain the child’s physical and mental health, including but not limited to, food, nutrition, clothing, shelter, supervision, medicine and medical services that a prudent person would consider essential to the wellbeing of the child.”

Each child neglect count is a third-degree felony carrying a possible sentence of up to five years behind bars, as well as up to five years of probation and a fine of up to $5,000.

Court documents also state that “capital sexual battery charges” against Stewart will be filed in Florida’s 9th Judicial District by the Statewide Prosecutor.

Under Florida law, a person convicted of sexual battery against a child younger than 12 can face life in prison without parole or the death penalty.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Epps and Stewart remain behind bars in the Duval County Jail awaiting trial.



Epps’ bond was set at $400,012, while Stewart was being held without bond.

News.title: Housewife, 51, battered woman and hurled protein shake at her after row at flower-arranging class
News.content:
WAR OF THE ROSES Housewife, 51, battered woman and hurled protein shake at her after row at flower-arranging class

A HOUSEWIFE battered a woman and hurled a protein shake at her after a row erupted at a flower-arranging class.

Lorraine Jae punched fellow student Tracey Musker after her coursework was criticised by their tutor.



The 51-year-old also hurled a drink over the victim and grabbed her coat during the lesson at St Helens College in Merseyside.

Tracey was left with bruises and a cut to her chin and a mark on her lip following the attack.



Jae has now pleaded guilty to assault by beating and was ordered to pay £200 in compensation.

She was also fined £300 plus £205 in costs and a victim surcharge at Liverpool Magistrates’ Court.



The attack took place on December 11 last year when the pair were getting feedback about their floristry diploma coursework.

Jae flew into a rage when she received criticism from the tutor about her Christmas wreath.

Tracey attempted to calm the situation but was told by Jae to “shut the f**k up”.

Tony Carey, prosecuting, added: “Miss Musker told the defendant not to speak to her in that manner and not to speak to her again and the defendant then began picking up her belongings.



”But as the defendant went to collect her coat from behind the victim she directed further verbal abuse at Miss Musker.

”Miss Musker laughed it off but whilst the victim was still sitting at her desk the defendant ran over to her and punched her in the face.

”When Miss Musker stood up the defendant picked up a full protein drink from the victim’s desk and threw it at her.”



The court was told another student intervened as Jae, who was later suspended from the course, ran out the classroom.

Helen Clarke, mitigating, said the assault was a “heat of the moment” reaction.

She continued: “[Jae] had been studying the course for some time, it had not been the best experience and she had some problems along the way.

”Nevertheless she persevered hoping to achieve a qualification as she was unable to continue other work she had been doing for many years.

“She thought this would be a new start but clearly it did not happen in that way.



“Clearly this happened out of character and she has learnt her lesson.. I can say from speaking to her she is sorry for what happened. She is apologetic to Miss Musker.”

News.title: When does Autumn officially start? Meteorological and astronomical autumn explained – and when the clocks go back
News.content:
AS the summer sun gradually starts to fade and welcome chills creep into the evening air, people across the UK are reaching for their jackets.

But when does summer actually end and autumn begin?



If you’re trying to figure out when autumn officially begins, the answer depends on who you ask.

Meteorologists have a fixed date on the calendar, while astronomers follow the movement of the Earth and stars.



When does autumn start?

Autumn can have two start dates depending on whether you follow climate records or the night sky.

There is no single “correct” answer as to which system you want to define the start of autumn by.

Read more on summer Rays of hope When the next UK heatwave could be: Met Office forecast for hot weather return



Meteorological autumn always starts on September 1 and finishes on November 30.

Astronomical autumn starts on the Autumnal Equinox – which in 2026 lands on September 23, and finishes on December 21.

What is Meteorological autumn?

Meteorologists split the year into four equal seasons made up of three full calendar months each.

This system relies on annual temperature trends rather than astronomical events.



Under this definition, the calendar splits into four clean, three-month blocks.

Spring covers March, April, and May, followed by summer across June, July, and August.

Autumn takes over for September, October, and November, before winter closes out the year through December, January, and February.

By fixing these dates to months, weather forecasters and climate scientists can easily compare rainfall, temperature stats, and weather patterns.

What is Astronomical autumn?

Astronomical autumn is governed by the Earth’s orbit around the Sun.



It officially kicks off on the Autumnal Equinox – the exact moment when the Earth’s equator lines up directly with the centre of the Sun.

On the day of the equinox, day and night are almost equal in length across the globe.

Once this moment passes, the Northern Hemisphere tilts further away from the Sun.

That is when the days start shrinking, the nights draw in, and the temperatures drop.

Because the Earth takes roughly 365.25 days to complete a full orbit around the Sun, the astronomical date shifts slightly each year.



But it almost always lands between September 21 and 24.

When do the clocks change?

Autumn also brings the end of British Summer Time (BST).

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The clocks go back one hour on the last Sunday of October – in 2026, that’s Sunday, October 25 – returning the UK to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).

While we lose an hour of evening daylight, the trade-off is an extra hour of sleep on Sunday morning and slightly brighter starts to the day.

News.title: ‘Wonderful’ pensioner, 75, killed during ‘burglary’ is pictured as family pay tribute after man arrested over ‘murder’
News.content:
'BURGLARY MURDER' ‘Wonderful’ pensioner, 75, killed during ‘burglary’ is pictured as family pay tribute after man arrested over ‘murder’

A “WONDERFUL” pensioner who was killed in an alleged burglary has been identified, as a 46-year-old man is arrested on suspicion of murder.

Police were called to reports of an aggravated burglary in Finsbury Park, London, on Tuesday, August 11.

A woman, identified as Rose Smith, 75, was found at the scene and rushed to hospital by paramedics for treatment.

An 81-year-old man was also treated at the scene before being taken to hospital, cops previously said.





Tragically, Rose passed away the following day – her grieving family are being supported by specially trained officers.

A 46-year-old man has since been arrested on suspicion of murder and aggravated burglary in connection with the incident.

Paying tribute, Rose’s heartbroken family said: “This is the most devastating loss our family could ever have imagined.

“Rose was a truly wonderful, outgoing woman who was loved by so many people.

“She loved bingo, going to cafés with her friends and, above all, spending time with her family.

“She treasured the time she spent with her children, grandchildren and great-grandchild.

“She was the life and soul of every party. She had a wonderful personality, a big heart and a way of bringing laughter and happiness wherever she went.

“We want people to remember Rose for the person she truly was — loving, fun, kind, sociable and full of life.”



Detective Chief Inspector Ben Massink, who is leading the investigation, said: “Our thoughts remain with Rose’s family and friends, they continue to be supported by specialist officers during this difficult time and have been informed of this update in our investigation.

“While we have made an arrest, I know this incident has caused significant concern in the local community.

“An increased police presence has remained in Tollington Park and I am grateful to those who supported our appeal for more information.

“We thank those who have already come forward to provide witness accounts and continue to appeal for anyone with information or doorbell footage to come forward. No detail is too small.”

News.title: Two men arrested for ‘manslaughter’ as body of missing soldier, 22, found after ‘car ramming’ & disturbance at pub
News.content:
TWO men have been arrested on suspicion of manslaughter after a body was found in a river during a frantic search for a missing soldier.

Liam Potts, 22, was last seen at 12.20am last Saturday heading into Wylam from Wylam Bridge in Northumberland after a night out with friends.



His disappearance sparked extensive searches with specialist officers from Northumbria Police’s Marine Unit making the tragic find in the River Tyne on Tuesday.

Cops are scrambling for answers as they probe whether reports of a “disturbance” at a nearby pub and a car crash led to the soldier entering the water.



A man and woman, both in their 20s, were seriously injured after a car was thought to have struck a group of pedestrians on Wylam Bridge.

The woman was discharged from hospital as the man remains there for further treatment.



Officers said Liam was on the bridge at the time but he wasn’t in the vehicle, and it’s not believed he was injured in the collision.

The force confirmed the soldier entered the water within minutes of the crash.



Liam was last seen wearing black joggers, black Nike trainers and a black T-shirt with white text and a diamond logo on the back, and a gold chain, as cops released a CCTV image.

Two men, aged 22 and 23, were initially arrested in connection to the reports and have now been rearrested on suspicion of manslaughter as they remain in police custody.

Detective Inspector Rachael Rutherford said: “Our thoughts remain with Liam’s family during this difficult time.

“The facts remain the same that Liam was on the bridge at the time of the collision, but he was not an occupant of the vehicle and was not struck by the vehicle.

“Enquiries have revealed that Liam, for reasons yet to be established, entered the water within minutes of the collision.



“We have therefore made the further re-arrests as we are looking to establish whether there is any link between the collision and Liam entering the water.”

She added: “We know there has been a lot of confusion and speculation in the community. It’s clear that Liam was a very popular young man.

“We are committed to finding answers for Liam’s family and we will continue to provide updates on our investigation.



“We would remind people to avoid speculation both online and in our communities as this could impact the ongoing investigation.

“We would continue to ask that people respect the family’s privacy at this tragic time.”

Liam was a soldier who served with the Coldstream Guards, and his unit was believed to be on leave at the time of his disappearance.

He completed his training at Catterick Garrison, North Yorkshire, and also played a role in the funeral procession of Queen Elizabeth in 2022.

Liam’s family paid a heartwarming tribute to him and said: “To our Liam. You may no longer be here beside us, but your presence will never be forgotten.



“Your family, friends and colleagues have all said the same thing, ‘once you met Pottsy, you could never forget him.’ You really were the heart and soul of any room.

“We are going to miss your smile, your laugh, and the little things that made you who you are. Though time may pass, the love we have for you will never fade.

“You will always be remembered, and forever loved. Rest peacefully, knowing that your memory lives on in all those whose lives you touched.”

Anyone with information that could help Northumbria Police with their investigation is urged to get in contact.

A spokesperson for the force said: “Liam was reported missing on Saturday, August 15, following a night out with friends.



“Sadly, his body was found on Tuesday, August 18, in the River Tyne a short distance away from Wylam Bridge.

“Prior to Liam’s disappearance, officers received a report of a disturbance at The Boathouse and a subsequent collision on Wylam Bridge involving a vehicle and a group of pedestrians.

“A man and woman – each aged in their 20s – both sustained serious injuries in the collision which were not life-threatening.

“The woman has since been discharged, whilst the man remains in hospital for further treatment.

“It remains the case that Liam was not an occupant of the vehicle nor was he struck by it and was last seen leaving the bridge on foot towards Wylam.



“At the time Liam’s body was found, officers did not believe there to be any third-party involvement in his disappearance.

“However, following further enquiries, officers are looking to establish whether the circumstances of the disturbance and subsequent collision on Wylam bridge have directly led to Liam entering the water.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The Force’s Major Investigation Team (MIT) are now leading the investigation and today (Saturday) have re-arrested two men, aged 22 and 23, on suspicion of manslaughter.

“They are currently in police custody.”

News.title: Wild moment mass brawl erupts in stands as fan leaps down rows to stomp on man’s stomach & punches are thrown
News.content:
THIS is the wild moment a mass brawl erupts at a baseball game with dozens of fans punching one another in the face.

Shocking footage shows one man leaping down several rows and landing feet-first on a man’s stomach in the Chicago stands.



“There’s a kid!” shouted one terrified fan while others fled the scene or whipped out their phones to record the dramatic fisticuffs.

It is unclear what exactly sparked the stadium skirmish amongst the White Sox fans, whose team beat the New York Mets 2-1 on Sunday.



One man was thrown to the ground – before he dramatically jumped down two rows to stomp on a guy below him.

The attacked fan then grabbed the aggressor by the shirt and flung him down another row of seats.

Another pair repeatedly swung fists at each other while a man in a red baseball cap prowled up and down, picking fights with multiple people.

And a third assailant found himself shirtless in the heat of the brawl.

Security guards stormed onto the scene, wielding hand cuffs, but people continued to battle across the stands.

Some even swarmed to the melee with evident glee as bystanders filmed the encounter from multiple angles.



One clip was sarcastically captioned “Happy Sunday!”

Team rivalries were not to blame as White Sox supporters appeared determined to attack each another.

People viewing the clip online said the fighting looked “absolutely insane” with others slamming the fans as “degenerates”.



It comes just days after another huge fight broke out at a Chicago White Sox game on Monday.

News.title: I worked as Michael Jackson & Bella Hadid’s bodyguard – terrifying taxi tactics that deluded fans used to get to stars
News.content:
BUSY BODY I worked as Michael Jackson & Bella Hadid’s bodyguard – terrifying taxi tactics that deluded fans used to get to stars

MICHAEL Jackson’s former bodyguard has revealed the surprisingly gruelling reality of a model’s working day, and the reason he decided to quit on the spot.

Simon Newton, 45, who lives in Eastbourne, bodyguarding followed a career in the army, with stints in Iraq and Afghanistan; then in private security, which included defending oil tankers against Somali pirates.



His high-profile clients include Bella Hadid, Kendall Jenner, Kate Moss, Michael Jackson, Rita Ora, Halsey and Dizzee Rascal, who he “really enjoyed” working with, and still speaks to.

Kendall was the first model he looked after, but it was Bella he worked with most frequently.



“You can do long days – really long days. You can start at five or six in the morning and you won’t go to bed until midnight,” Simon told The Sun.



“If the girls are on the catwalk, you could be dressing first thing in the morning, going to where the show is to do the walkthrough and rehearsal. Then you go back again for the show.



“Then if there’s a dinner or something in the evening with the show, they might go, you might get back to the hotel at 12, one in the morning and you might be back at nine again the next day.

“You just eat when you can… It had to be fairly quick. You can’t be sitting there waiting for a big steak dinner and all of a sudden you’re going.”

Despite the long days, for Simon the job was nothing compared to life in a warzone.

“I’d lived and worked in Afghanistan and Iraq collectively for about seven years. There’s a lot of things that most people should never be subjected to seeing really,” said Simon.

“One minute you’re in Afghanistan, the next day you land in a Gatwick and you’re walking through the terminal with everyone else, like no one’s got a clue where you’ve just been or what you’ve just been doing.”



Simon’s first ever celeb client was the King of Pop, Michael Jackson, himself.

“I was working in Afghanistan and actually on leave back at home for a month. It wasn’t until I got to the airport I found out who it was,” Simon said.

“I didn’t put much thought into it, to be honest, before the job started.”



He soon realised the lengths obsessive fans would go to see their idol.

“We were getting a lot of people following us around,” he said. “I realised there were five or six black taxis, all on a meter, that were just running the whole day, which fans were paying for to follow him.

“People booked the same hotel so they could be in the lobby, because otherwise it was shut off to people outside.

“There were people coming over from China and they were following him wherever he was going after he was finished with us.

“But it was quite an expensive hotel, so the money these fans must have been spending… that’s when it dawned on me how die-hard these people are.”



Though the mobs were ecstatic, they were rarely in genuine danger.

“There were a few people we were told to look out for. They weren’t well people. It wasn’t like they were trying to harm Jackson, but they weren’t well people,” Simon said.

“There was a guy who used to dress as Jesus all the time and follow him around the world. Again, where they got their money from and how they had time to do it, I’ve got no idea.”

That was in 2006. Since then, Jackson passed away, and faced further allegations that he sexually abused young boys, which are denied by his estate and family.



Working as his bodyguard around London, Simon was only beside him for a few weeks.

“I found him very young for his age, the way he would talk and interact,” Simon said. “But then when he was on stage and singing, he was very professional.”

After guarding Michael, Simon spent five years working as a Close Protection Officer in the Middle East before picking up more bodyguarding jobs in London.

Being papped next to so many icons of the fashion industry has its perks, and by the end of the last decade Simon was being interviewed in Vogue himself.

Since then, he’s started his own fashion brand and has moved into acting, appearing in the new Rise of the Footsoldier film out this month.



When he works with artists, they are provided with a rider – a list given to the venue detailing what drinks, food, and other demands are required in the dressing room. But in reality, most of it gets chucked away.

“You could take it all with you, if you wanted. There might be Champagne in there. There might be chocolate and fruit, maybe sandwiches in the fridge,” said Simon.

“But sometimes we’d go in there, bust open a bottle of water, and the rest of it would get chucked.”

Simon is well versed on the downsides of fame – and his thoughts might make you rethink applying to the next series of Love Island.

“It’s not what people think, if you actually realise what it brings. You need money as well, because you can’t do the same things as what everybody else does,” he said.



“You can’t just get a bus or a train, it’s too much of a nightmare.

“You can’t just leave your house anymore. There’s always some sort of restriction to doing what you and I would take for granted.”

As well as celebs, he’s looked after “some of the richest people in the world” – names you’ve never heard of, who have fortunes of up to £30 billion.

“Celebrities by and large haven’t got a lot of money compared to these people. It’s a different way of living when you’ve got billions. It did make me realise it ruins your life.”

“A lot of them don’t have family,” he said. If you’ve got that money when you’re single, how do you ever trust a woman, or vice versa?



“You might cross paths with someone who genuinely is interested in you, but you’re always going to think that that might not be the case.”

After years working as a bodyguard, Simon was ready for a new challenge – acting.

He’d had a taste of it already, playing a US Special Forces soldier in Matt Damon’s film Green Zone. Then in 2016, he acted as Dave Bautista’s body double in the film Final Score, which came out in 2018.

He said: “I basically woke up one morning and thought I don’t want to be a bodyguard anymore.

“I always had a lot of work, but you could be in another country the next morning and I was just getting pushed from pillar to post, and I’d done everything I wanted to do in the industry.



“I still own a private security company today off the back of it. So I still make a bit of money through that job.”

Having never worked with actors personally, Simon didn’t have a “little black book” of agents to call. But he’s enjoyed breaking into the industry, and experiencing fame from the other side.

“That’s the thing about acting, I get to go and see better parts of the world. Now I get looked after,” he said.

“When you’re a bodyguard, you’re the only one on the team. You don’t get a day off. If no one’s working on Sunday, you still are, because you’re looking after whoever you’re looking after.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“When you’re an actor, everything’s sorted out for me, everything’s paid for.”

News.title: Social media firms should remove dangerous driving videos, minister says
News.content:
On Saturday, PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 near Middlesbrough.

All five of the Passat's occupants - Saddington, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.

A video posted on the TikTok account believed to belong to Saddington in March 2025 showed him and four other young people involved in what appears to be a police pursuit. The video has since been deleted.

BBC Verify analysed the 94 second-long clip, which showed the car driving on footpaths and parkland in Ormesby, Middlesbrough, with Saddington a rear-seat passenger.

Another video posted by the same account, also since deleted, appears to show a joyride where a passenger is smoking, with the speedometer showing 100mph.

Then, later in the video, a different car is set on fire. The passengers in this video are not identifiable.

Cleveland Police and Crime Commissioner Matt Storey said: "Without being able to say whether that was anything like involved in this case, it's absolutely idiotic for anybody to be doing anything other than being completely 100% focused on the road when they're behind the wheel of a vehicle."

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that someone filming themselves or others driving dangerously is "absolutely ridiculous, and of course nobody should be doing that".

"It is a worrying situation if that's becoming more prevalent because it is incredibly dangerous", he added.

News.title: 'It's not Alton Towers' - rows break out over queuing at Wales' highest mountain
News.content:
Visitors to Wales' highest mountain are being urged to respect others by not skipping queues to reach the top following rows among climbers.

Recent hot weather means there have been bumper summer crowds at Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, where people have reportedly waited more than one hour to reach the 1,085m (3,560ft)-high summit.

Social media videos have shown arguments among queue-jumpers and those patiently waiting their turn to touch the metal plate that marks the top.

A recent video showed Marc Screeton, from Manchester, being heckled as he bypassed the line, saying: "Imagine queuing on a mountain? No chance."

But others have said queuing is necessary for safety reasons.

News.title: Australian shark attack victim grateful for 'second chance at life'
News.content:
An Australian woman bitten by a shark at a popular Sydney beach earlier this year says she has been given a "second chance at life" and will be making the most of it.

Leah Stewart, 34, was mauled by a shark during a morning swim at Coogee Beach in June, suffering multiple bites to her arms and legs, amid a spate of attacks in Australia.

The mother-of-one was placed in an induced coma and had several surgeries, including having one of her arms amputated.

In an online post on Monday, she thanked her supporters who have raised more than AU$550,000 (US$394,000; Â£289,000) for her, saying her recovery has been "incredibly difficult" but she is making "remarkable" progress.

"After what has been an incredibly difficult few months, I'm so happy that I've progressed enough to build some independence, and I can finally see some light after all of this," Stewart wrote, in her first comments since the attack.

"I want you to know that I feel like I've been given a second chance at life, and I'm not going to waste it."

Stewart said she had been "overwhelmed" by the support from family, friends and "even strangers", adding that the "you've inspired me to get better, not bitter".

An online fundraiser for her would now be closed, she wrote, with the money raised giving her the chance to recover at home as well as "options for further medical treatment down the road".

"I still have a long way to go, but my recovery has been remarkable, and a huge part of that is because of the absolute army of love, support, prayers and encouragement surrounding my family and I from all over the world."

In an interview with Nine Network's 60 Minutes, due to be aired this weekend, Stewart described seeing the shark's "horrific" face.

"I'll never forget its face - it was a monster," she says.

"It was holding onto my leg and I just thought of (my daughter) August, and I thought, 'she's not going to have a mum. She's gonna grow up without a mum'."

Fighting back tears, she goes on: "I couldn't handle that, I didn't want her to not have a mum. I just thought, I've got to fight it, do everything I can to be here."

There have been a spate of shark attacks in Australia this year, with four attacks over a two-day period in January, including one on a 12-year-old boy who later died from his injuries.

In May, a man was killed by a shark in Queensland while spearfishing and in Western Australia, a father-of-two died after he was attacked by a 4m (13ft) shark.

News.title: Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies aged 61 one year after son's death
News.content:
A former Race Across the World contestant has died, a year after her son and co-star's death in a car crash.

Jo Gardiner, 61, died "following a long and courageous battle with cancer", her family said.

Gardiner, a physiotherapist from Manchester, travelled across South America with her son Sam in the second series of the BBC show, which aired in 2020.

Her family said she was "one of a kind" who "lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves".

News.title: Why is it so hard to find an NHS dentist? Find out how many have closed where you live
News.content:
Sykes says that none of his friends in his graduating class in dentistry still works in the NHS. "My friends have gone private, retired or teach - any pathway to avoid NHS dentistry."

Shiv Pabary, chair of the British Dental Association's General Dental Practice Committee, says the situation is "the direct result of choices made by successive governments". He warns that unless ministers "fix and fund NHS dentistry", more dentists could choose to reduce their NHS work or leave the service altogether.

Overall dentist practice numbers have risen in England over the last decade.

"This is not a shortage of dentistry but a shortage of NHS dentistry," says Dayan. "Practices will need to be incentivised back into NHS work in the places where the NHS footprint has thinned most."

While most parts of England recorded declines in practices offering NHS dental care, the reductions were smallest in North West London, the Black Country and North East London.

North East London was the only area to see any increase during the period, recording one additional practice offering NHS treatment compared with a decade ago.

Every other region of England saw the number of NHS dental practices fall.

Looking at the number of practices doing NHS work is not the same as looking at exactly how much health service capacity there is - practices can vary in size. But if you look at other measures such as the amount of treatment being done, the numbers are still down, although not as steep as the fall in practice numbers.

The government says that it is changing the dental contract and training more dentists in the areas most in need. The government says it will also make it a requirement for newly qualified dentists to practice in the NHS for a minimum period of at least three years.

Campaign group 38 degrees calls the current dental crisis "shameful", with people being "forced to pay money they can't afford or suffer with the pain, shame, and further complications that come from being denied vital NHS healthcare".

News.title: UK's rarest bird of prey rears new chicks in secret location
News.content:
The UK's rarest bird of prey has successfully nested for the second year running in the same secret location, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) has reported.

A male Montagu's harrier, known as "AU" by conservationists, bred with two different females, rearing six chicks across two nests on English farmland.

Montagu's harriers were put on a "red list" of birds most at risk in the UK in 2021. Numbers have declined from a high of nine successful nests in 2011, to no evidence of successful breeding between 2020 and 2024.

An RSPB spokesperson said: "We are doing our absolute utmost to save this iconic species in the UK and are delighted with six flying juveniles this year."

Four chicks hatched in the same secret location last year.

The charity said careful monitoring, in partnership with the farmers on whose land the birds nested, meant the nests were protected by fences to exclude ground predators such as foxes.

The single male Montagu's harrier has also been working very hard to keep his two nests of hungry chicks fed.

The BBC was given exclusive access to the nest and was able to witness some of the spectacular feeding behaviour of the raptors: the male drops prey in mid-air and the female rolls upside down to catch it in her talons.

News.title: Doctors said I was too young to have endometriosis at 13 - I had to take morphine to cope
News.content:
But the most frustrating thing for Grace, and why she contacted BBC Your Voice, is because she does not feel medical experts recognise that teenagers and adolescents can suffer from endometriosis.

Grace's GP did not diagnose her condition and nor did the first consultant she saw privately.

She says: "Even a specialist didn't believe me. And if a specialist won't listen to me, who will?" It was not until the family pushed for a second private opinion that she got a positive diagnosis.

Endometriosis, which occurs when tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows outside it, can cause debilitating symptoms, such as pelvic pain, heavy periods and fatigue. About 10% of women are affected by it, according to NHS data.

This week BBC presenter Emma Barnett revealed she had to have a hysterectomy for her endometriosis - which she said she never wanted to have.

It can develop at any age once periods begin - and it is a common misconception that only older women suffer from the condition, says the charity Endometriosis UK,

Faye Farthing, a spokesperson for the charity, says the government, NHS and health practitioners need to improve menstrual health education for young people "if we are to ensure the next generation are not robbed of the future they deserve".

The charity says it can take a long time to diagnose endometriosis - an average of nine years in older women.

And in the early stages, for example with teenagers, it often doesn't show up on an ultrasound scan. However, new tests are being developed which will help spot the condition earlier.

Getting pregnant can be more difficult - even aged 14, Grace says she has been warned it is likely to affect her fertility. She's been advised she may not be able to have children after the age of 30 because of damage to her reproductive organs.

She feels rushed: "I have to have kids within the next 15 years, otherwise I might not be able to."

News.title: How to get £2,000 to play computer games at university
News.content:
As parents across the country prepare to wave their children off to university, conversations about family finances and the cost of living are growing ever more frequent - and fervent.

Yet every year, millions of pounds worth of scholarships and bursary funding goes unclaimed by students - with many unaware the extra help exists.

So roll up the next generation of gamers, who this year can apply for as esports scholarship from the University of Roehampton - with more than 100 handed out so far.

But can the students balance their studies and their esports? And is the scholarship set to catch on?

Esports, meaning electronic sports, is the name for competitive video gaming.

It is different from standard video gaming as esports includes spectators, much like traditional sports.

Gamers compete against one another in high-stakes tournaments for cash prizes and trophies.

News.title: Pubs and hotels could see business rates reformed after review
News.content:
A review is being launched into the way business rates are calculated for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, and could lead to a reform of the system.

The Treasury says business rates expert Jerry Schurder will lead the review into rate valuations and report back in March 2027, with the government calling for the views of landlords, hoteliers and business owners to feed in to the process.

Last month, Andy Burnham announced a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, to come into effect in April.

Pub groups have argued they face disproportionately higher rates bills, but other businesses have called for a wider reform of the rates system.

According to the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA), 161 pubs closed in the first three months of this year across England, Scotland and Wales, equating to the loss of around 2,400 jobs.

Rising business rates are cited as one issue facing the sector, although there have also been complaints that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made staff costs more expensive.

James Murray, financial secretary to the Treasury, said the new review would look at "a rethink of valuations - so that we can build a fairer system for the future".

Emma McClarkin, chief executive of the BBPA, said: "For years pubs have paid a disproportionately higher business rates bill which has ground down their ability to keep the doors open, so this review is sorely needed and hugely welcome."

The BBPA says pubs are valued differently for rates than retail venues. Instead of being based just on floor area, they are judged by a measure called Fair Maintainable Trade (FMT) - which means when a pub's turnover increases, so does its rates bill.

Jonathan Lawson, the chief executive of Butcombe Group, which has 120 pubs across the south and south west of England, told the BBC's Today programme that the use of FMT meant pubs were effectively being "punished for success", while large online retailers that operate out of warehouses were not subject to revenue-based rates calculations.

Their rates, he said, "are calculated based on what is deemed to be the market rent for that area, and takes very little on board in terms of revenue driven through that site".

"You can have a very large site paying a relatively low level of business rates versus a relatively small pub... paying a very high level of business rates."

Schurder is a former business rates policy lead at advisory firm Newmark UK, and his review will feed into the next rates revaluation in 2029.

Northern Ireland and Scotland set their own valuations, while Wales presently chooses to align its methodology with England. As the same approach is used across England and Wales, the review will be looking for responses from both nations.

Schurder's appointment was welcomed by Craig Beaumont of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) who said he would bring "crucial heavyweight business rates expertise into the Treasury".

However, Beaumont said the government needed to address the wider business rates system and exempt more smaller firms by increasing the rates relief threshold for small businesses.

Jonny Haseldine from the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) also said the review of valuations should be wider.

"The full reform of business rates, promised by the government at the last election, is urgently needed. This continued piecemeal approach to reform is the wrong approach," he said.

While the BCC said hospitality was the sector most worried about rates, Haseldine warned firms in every sector were struggling with the "complex and outdated" system.

Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the review was "far too late for a sector this Labour government has already done its best to kill off".

"Tax hikes on business premises and jobs, alongside job-destroying regulation in the Employment Rights Act, have left many hospitality businesses on the brink," he said.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said reform of business rates was "long overdue", but also called for an emergency VAT cut and a reverse to jobs tax changes "which have hammered hospitality in particular".

News.title: 'It took 30 years to talk about my teacher raping me'
News.content:
It wasn't until 2022 when she had grief counselling that she confronted what had happened.

The following year she made a formal complaint to police.

"I am a mum now and my children are the age that I was then - and that cannot happen to them," she said.

She said finding the courage to contact police was difficult and it "took me a few days just to pluck up the courage".

Det Con Andrew Jones, from West Midlands Police's Major Crime Team, said: "I would like to express my gratitude to the brave woman who came forward to report what Allen had done to her as a child.

"She has been so brave throughout the investigation and court process."

Allen was sentenced at Birmingham Crown Court in July.

His defence argued the offence was committed during a difficult period in his life while he was experiencing anxiety.

But, during his sentencing remarks, His Honour Judge Paul Farrer KC, said he did not accept Allen's judgement was impaired at the time and said he had abused a position of trust.

That his offending remained undiscovered for more than three decades meant he was able to enjoy life in the community, the court heard.

It was noted the defendant was now in poor health, had diabetes, glaucoma and impaired hearing, had previously had a heart attack and might be experiencing the onset of Parkinson's disease.

The woman said it was not the sentencing but the guilty verdict that had been most important to her.

"I felt heard, I felt people have listened and they believe me," she added. "It is really validating and it raises your self-esteem a little bit, it means a lot."

News.title: Rain to return this week with chance of thunderstorms and flooding
News.content:
The weather is set to turn more unsettled this week as rain returns with a chance of thunderstorms and localised flooding.

Some places could see a return to showery conditions by Tuesday, but it is from Wednesday onwards that more widespread and persistent rain will arrive from the south.

The wet weather will be welcome for parched regions of the UK, but a lot more will be needed before drought conditions start to ease.

As well as the rain, temperatures will also be on the rise once more, as warmer air moving in could push midweek highs close to 27C (81F) in places.

News.title: Girl gets tumour diagnosis 12 hours after eye test
News.content:
A mum said she "fell apart" after finding out her four-year-old daughter had a brain tumour, just 12 hours after an eye test.

Katie, 41, said her daughter Phoebe, now five, started to be sick and was getting severe headaches in February, but was told "it was just migraines" by a GP.

Following an eye test in May, Katie was called by the optician who told her to take her daughter straight to A&E at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge. Just hours later, she was diagnosed with a brain tumour.

"I fell apart and just sobbed and sobbed," said the mum from St Neots, Cambridgeshire. Thankfully, Phoebe's tumour was not cancerous and she is now under the care of specialists.

Katie said: "I felt like we were probably wasting the hospital's time because Phoebe was running around playing like normal but, looking back, she was probably the sickest kid there.

"I kept thinking, how am I going to tell her dad and the other children?

"I kept asking if Phoebe would survive but the doctors said they were unable to answer that at that time, which is the worst thing in the world as a parent."

News.title: Reform says it will prioritise British-born young workers for social housing
News.content:
Reform previously announced it would evict foreign nationals from social housing - a plan criticised by housing charity Shelter which said building more homes is the solution, rather than "changing the order of the queue" and "stoking division".

Tice will set out how Reform intends to pay for the 50,000 affordable homes during Monday's news conference, the party added.

"It is time for us to prioritise young British workers, and that is what our policy is about," Tice said on Sunday.

"I have spent my entire career in property development, as a private citizen I have led companies which delivered thousands of new homes. In government I will break down the barriers to getting generation rent onto the housing ladder."

He added it is "time to get Britain building" and give "our young people the homes they deserve".

UK or Irish nationals made up 88.5% of main social home householders in 2024/25, according to the English Housing Survey.

That means around 11.5% of main householders, the perÂ­son in whose name the social home is renÂ­ted, were non-UK or Irish nationÂ­als.

For its part, Reform estimates 540,000 social homes are currently occupied by foreign nationals.

Labour rubbished Reform's plans and insisted social housing is already "tightly controlled".

"Illegal migrants, asylum seekers and migrants on student or work visas are not eligible for social housing," the Labour spokesperson said.

Labour said the Reform plan would target long-term UK residents that have contributed to our country but are not British citizens, including NHS staff.

"It would leave more families at risk of homelessness and drive up use of temporary accommodation at the taxpayers' expense. It would also mean renegotiations with the EU, resulting in years of wrangling."

The Conservative Party, which also said it would revoke the right of foreign nationals to social housing, accused Reform of "trying to catch up" with its policies.

The Tories have said their plan, which would allow Irish citizens and some EU nationals to remain in social housing, would free up around 230,000 homes.

Sir James Cleverly, shadow housing secretary, added: "The Conservatives have already set out comprehensive plans to ensure British nationals are at the front of the queue for social housing. Now Reform are trying to catch up.

"We also believe in a home owning society and that those who work hard should be able to buy their own home, without unnecessary barriers standing in their way."

Liberal Democrat spokesperson Gideon Amos said that Reform's plan was a "cruel gimmick".

Green MP SiÃ¢n Berry said her party would tackle housing issues by ending Right to Buy, building and buying hundreds of thousands of new council homes, and introducing rent controls.

She added: "Another blatantly racist and cruel policy from Reform, adding to a host of plans to create a two-tier Britain â one for those born in the UK and one for everyone else."

News.title: CrossCountry to run full train service after power outage causes major disruption
News.content:
Train operator CrossCountry says it expects to run a full service on Monday after cancelling nearly all of its UK services the day before following a power cut at its control centre.

The outage in Birmingham at the weekend brought disruption from Glasgow to Penzance.

Major routes were affected between Birmingham and Manchester, which pass through Stoke-on-Trent, Coventry and Wolverhampton. Journeys from Leeds to York and Cheltenham to Cardiff were also caught in the travel chaos, leaving passengers frustrated.

On Monday morning, CrossCountry reported a handful of service cancellations, although these were put down to trains departing late and staff shortages.

Customers are advised to check their journey before travelling.

The operator on Sunday thanked passengers for their patience and understanding during the disruption.

Tickets purchased for travel on CrossCountry services on Sunday will be valid for travel on CrossCountry services until Wednesday, the company has said.

News.title: Wicker Man director's sons complete their late father's film trilogy
News.content:
Robin Hardy always envisaged his iconic 1973 folk horror film The Wicker Man as the first part of a trilogy.

The Wicker Tree, released in 2011, brought him closer to that ambition, but his death in 2016 at the age of 86 left the project incomplete.

Now his sons, Justin and Dominic, have been able to complete their father's trilogy, after finding a script for the final film.

Wrath of the Gods has its premiere at the FrightFest horror festival in London, external on Friday, a family dream made possible thanks to the surprise discovery of some long-lost family archive.

"The person who bought Justin's old family home said they'd discovered six sacks of letters, scripts and other material pertaining to Robin Hardy and The Wicker Man in the attic," says Dominic, an art historian at the University of Quebec in Montreal.

"Justin's first instinct was to burn them, but we couldn't ignore this original source material. Although we left it unopened for six months or more."

News.title: Newcastle and Liverpool united in tribute to legend Keegan
News.content:
Kevin Keegan's family were in attendance as Newcastle United and Liverpool supporters came together to pay tribute to the former England captain.

Keegan, who played for both clubs, before going on to manage Newcastle, died at the age of 75 last month following a battle with cancer.

As the teams met for the first time since his death, in their Premier League season opener at St James' Park on Sunday, members of Keegan's family were present in the directors' box.

A number of Keegan's former players from this memorable first spell in charge of Newcastle, between 1992 and 1997, were also at the game.

President Donald Trump’s insistence that his $600 million White House ballroom is justified because of the security upgrades it will bring is undermined by the fact that the complex already has a secret bunker, according to former officials.

The Washington Post cites three ex-officials who point to the existence of the nuclear-proof underground base as a basis for rejecting Trump’s case for proceeding with his pet project.

The bunker was commissioned in response to the 9/11 attacks and completed during Barack Obama’s tenure to keep the commander-in-chief safe.

It is reportedly situated 60 feet below street level, is accessible by private elevator, stores a month’s supply of food, has its own air supply system and is intended to shield its inhabitants from a range of threats, including the blast of a weapon of mass destruction.

It was itself constructed as a successor to the existing Presidential Emergency Operations Center in the basement of the East Wing, which was built to protect Franklin D Roosevelt in the Second World War and served to safeguard first lady Laura Bush and vice president Dick Cheney when al-Qaeda struck 25 years ago.

open image in gallery The existence of a secret bunker beneath the White House undermines the case for President Donald Trump’s $600 million ballroom in place of the East Wing, ex-officials have argued ( Reuters )

The unnamed former officials told The Post the arguments put forward for the bunker during the War on Terror are similar to those being made by the Trump administration now to explain the need for the new ballroom, raising questions about whether the latter is really essential.

“The East Wing Modernization Project is inextricably tied to the security of the president, the White House grounds and the certain security infrastructure assets,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle countered in a statement to the Post.

“Recent events such as the foiled attack on the historic UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House proves exactly why the East Wing Modernization Project is severely needed for large scale events, which include drone proof structures and drone ports among other critical security enhancements.”

The Independent has reached out to the White House for further comment.

The fate of the construction project currently sits with the U.S. Supreme Court. Chief Justice John Roberts issued an order Friday allowing work to continue while his bench considers an emergency appeal arguing that it must be halted unless congressional approval is granted.

open image in gallery Work is currently continuing on the project but its future ultimately rests with the Supreme Court ( Reuters )

Both a U.S. district judge and a federal appeals panel have found that the support of a majority of lawmakers in the House of Representatives and Senate is required before the undertaking can proceed but did make an exception for the planned subterranean military complex.

White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller said in an August filing that the proposed complex “serves continuity-of-government interests by ensuring that the president and senior national security staff are able to operate from a protected facility during any attack on the nation’s capital.”

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has similarly claimed: “Securing this reinforced subterranean node guarantees uninterrupted command and control in place.”

Driscoll called it “a nondiscretionary prerequisite to ensure the president can maintain continuity of government, uninterrupted operations, and effectively exercise National Command Authority during an attack or global crisis.”

open image in gallery Trump has enthusiastically promoted his ballroom project since its inception ( AFP/Getty )

Lawyers for the White House told the Supreme Court earlier this month the complex is 65 percent complete and that a 250-strong construction crew was working on it 20 hours per day, seven days a week to get it done.

Trump himself has meanwhile claimed that opposition to the project is “disloyal” and attacked the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the organization tasked by Congress with preserving D.C. institutions and landmarks, for challenging the ballroom in court, suggesting their lawsuit risked compromising national security.

“I said the problem with the suit – I told them this – is that we have many military things in this ballroom, and ideally, they shouldn’t be revealed,” he complained in the Oval Office last week.

“But now they are revealed, so the world knows about it.”

Richard E Grant has revealed that he “edited” friends out of his life after they avoided him following the death of his wife, Joan Washington.

Washington — a renowned dialect coach — died in 2021, aged 74, eight months after being diagnosed with lung cancer. She and Grant, 69, had been married for 35 years and shared one daughter, Olivia, 37.

In the past, Grant has described how friends would avoid him following Washington’s death to avoid an awkward conversation.

In a new interview with The Times, Grant said he would never forgive those who kept their distance during that time.

“I’m very unequivocal, black and white, all or nothing,” he said.

open image in gallery British actor Richard E Grant has revealed he ‘edited’ friends out of his life after they avoided him following his wife’s death ( AFP/Getty )

open image in gallery Grant’s wife, Joan Washington (right), died in 2021, less than a year after being diagnosed with lung cancer ( AFP/Getty )

“I’ve tried to go for the grey areas but it’s not succeeded for very long. There are people that have been edited out of my life and I will never see them again. If I had done that to them, I wouldn’t be able to look them in the face.”

“No, portcullis down,” he added. “Goodbye.”

Grant went on to share that he still writes to Washington every night before bed and that the idea of finding companionship again was incomprehensible. “I know it happens but I’ve not had any twinkles of that yet,” he said.

It’s not the first time that Grant has been ruthless about cutting friends out of his life.

Earlier this year, the Withnail and I actor revealed he cut off a friend of 29 years after he was accidentally CC’d on an email filled with “brutal” comments about him.

During a February episode of the Mad, Sad, & Bad podcast, Grant described the person as someone who he “thought was one of the five best friends in my life.”

“She sent an email from Africa to a mutual friend in Australia who'd asked for my email address, and, because my name was in the body of the email, I got inadvertently sent this email.”

Grant explained that the message “arrived on a day when I had heard for a third time that a film that I’d written and was about to direct, the finances had collapsed. And I was doing the final episode of Frasier,” which aired in May 2004.

He said that the email contained “such toxicity” that he immediately decided to cut off the friendship.

“And I thought, ‘That's not a real friend anymore.’ And I was absolutely devastated,” Grant said. “So I copied and pasted that and then sent it back. And I said, ‘29 years of friendship?’”

Asked what the offensive comments were about, Grant replied: “It was of my script that I had written, which was entirely autobiographical.” Grant’s 2005 comedy Wah-Wah was loosely based on his own life. “And she had read this script.”

He said that years later, his daughter, now 37, had questioned whether the friendship was really genuine in the first place.

“Our daughter was very smart, because she was 16, so exactly 20 years ago. She said to me, ‘In your heart of hearts, haven’t you always known this about that person?’”

Grant added that the turn of events was “just brutal.”

“Because that person knows you in the most formative part of your life, when you're still dreaming of getting regular work out there as an actor,” Grant said. “Nevermind the other things that have happened to me since. So when you’re betrayed like that, there’s no going back for me.”

Iran warned that U.S. sanctions set to be announced would not bring peace to the region.

Meanwhile, Israeli and Syrian officials met less than a week after Israeli strikes in Syria.

The Palestinian American whose home in the West Bank was besieged by Israeli settlers earlier this month said he still worried they could attack his home after Israel's military withdraws.

Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Monday. Full coverage can be found here.

Iran threatens response ahead of US sanctions announcement

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson on Monday warned that Tehran would respond harshly to expanded U.S. sanctions, including measures against countries it sees as cooperating with Washington.

“Any escalation of this situation will undoubtedly bring about consequences,” Esmail Baghaei said. “Our hands are not tied.”

The prospect of expanded sanctions and Iran’s threat to respond come after weeks of impasse, with the United States having not yet dislodged Iran’s grip on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian attacks and threats have severely hampered traffic through the waterway, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil passed before the war started nearly six months ago.

Iran has maintained its demands for reopening the strait — including lifting the U.S. naval blockade, withdrawing U.S. forces from the region and reparations for damages it sustained throughout the war. It has held separate talks with neighboring Oman on jointly managing the waterway regardless of whether a new deal is brokered with the U.S.

Sanctions have historically raised the prices of basic goods in Iran, but after years withstanding them, Iran’s economy has adapted through finding new trading partners and building domestic industries.

Ahead of the expected announcement, the country's currency hit a record low on Monday, with traders anticipating higher prices if tighter sanctions further restrict Iran’s export capacity.

Israeli and Syrian officials meet following an Israeli airstrike

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani met over the weekend with a high-level Israeli delegation in Jordan to try to defuse tensions after Israel last week struck an air base in northern Syria, Syrian state news agency SANA reported Monday.

The U.S.-mediated discussions on Sunday focused on restarting negotiations for a future security agreement between the two countries, SANA said.

Israel struck the Abu Duhur air base in Idlib province last week, saying that it aimed to stop Turkey — which has been supporting the new Syrian government’s efforts to rebuild its armed forces after 14 years of civil war — from establishing a presence there.

Syrian officials asserted during the talks the right to develop an army and freely forge alliances with any country, the agency said.

They also called for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from a buffer zone in southern Syria that they have occupied since December 2024 and reiterated Syria’s stance that the Golan Heights — which Israel captured in the 1967 Mideast war and later annexed — is Syrian territory.

Israeli officials didn't immediately comment on the meeting as of Monday.

Palestinian American says he can't freely leave his home in the West Bank

The Palestinian American homeowner whose residence was besieged earlier this month by Israeli settlers said on Monday that he remained unable to move freely in the West Bank village of Qusra. Loui Ridi traveled from Ohio to the Israeli-occupied West Bank to join his relatives defending his home from Israeli settlers a week ago.

Palestinians whose homes have been besieged can only now move about following prior authorization from the Israeli military, which declared the area a closed zone to restore order in Qusra and converted a nearby home into a makeshift drone base.

Ridi said settlers returned throughout the week to the hill above his house, while he and his relatives had spent hours coordinating movement to purchase essential supplies like food and water.

Since Israeli settlers surrounded Ridi’s home more than two weeks ago, preventing occupants from leaving, Israeli soldiers have encouraged them to leave, but Israel’s police have not announced any arrests.

The siege — and Israel’s response — has sparked condemnation from Israeli rights groups and foreign officials, including U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who called the violence terrorism.

Palestinians consider the Israeli-occupied West Bank, home to some 3 million Palestinians and 560,000 Israeli settlers, the heart of any future state and have condemned Israel's expansion in the territory. It has seen a dramatic spike in violence carried out by Israeli settlers against Palestinians this year.

Apple’s major new iPhone redesign has been revealed in more detail – including its one downside.

This September, Apple is set to introduce its first ever iPhone Ultra, multiple rumours have suggested. It will be Apple’s first ever foldable device, with a screen that can bend in half.

It will be the first major new form factor for the iPhone for years. And there has been much speculation about how Apple will embrace the folding phone form factor – which has proven popular for rivals such as Samsung, but which has also come with some problems.

Now, a new report from reliable leaker Mark Gurman at Bloomberg offers new details on how that device will actually work. The new insight comes from several people who have used the device in early testing, he reported.

Users say that the folding phone fits well in the pocket when it is shut, that the hinge that allows it to fold has proven durable, and that Apple’s software design for the bigger screen works well. They borrow from the iPad to allow apps and the operating system to be useable on a larger screen, he reported.

The larger screen – rumoured to be 5.5-inches – also works well as a camera viewfinder, he reported. But some early users expressed dissatisfaction with the camera itself, which doesn’t include the telephoto lens that is found on the iPhone Pro models, he said.

However, overall he said that the new device could be enough to bring the “Apple magic” back after years of iterative new designs.

The new device could be Apple’s most expensive iPhone ever made, by some distance. Rumours suggest that it could cost more than $2,000, or the same in pounds, in part because of the new design but also because of increased costs that have already dramatically driven up the price of some Apple products and may do the same to the rest of the iPhone line-up.

The same supply problems could also mean that other phones in the line-up are hard to buy, as Apple is unable to make enough to satisfy demand, previous reports have suggested.

The iPhone Ultra is expected to be revealed by Apple at an event in early September. It will come alongside updates to its iPhone Pro series – but not a new iPhone 18, which may not arrive until the autumn, reports have suggested.

Apple could also use the event to introduce its updated new AirPods, which include a camera for the first time. Files found in a recent Apple update have finally revealed how those long-rumoured but largely mysterious cameras might actually work.

A cross-party group of Japanese lawmakers headed to Beijing on Monday seeking to mend strained ties following Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s comment on Taiwan that angered China and led to tensions that have spilled over into the economy.

The group, which includes Gaku Hashimoto, a lawmaker of Takaichi's governing Liberal Democratic Party and a former health and welfare vice minister, and a lawmaker each from the Komeito and Centrist Reform Alliance opposition parties, will meet with Chinese Communist Party officials during a visit through Thursday.

“Communication has been severed in all areas and we are beginning to see their impact in many areas,” Shinichi Isa, a spokesperson for the CRA party, told reporters before leaving Tokyo's Haneda airport. “I hope we can somehow find a clue to restart a dialogue.”

Soon after taking office, Takaichi said a Chinese attack on Taiwan could constitute “a survival-threatening situation” for Japan that would justify the use of force, enraging Beijing.

Isa, who has served as a diplomat at the Japanese Embassy in China, wrote on X earlier this month that bilateral ties have sunk to their worst since the 1972 normalization of relations. He wrote that officials had always remained in communication even during previous lows: “Now all channels between officials and ministries have been cut off.”

The situation is not in the national interest of either side, Isa said at the time, and the Chinese side accepted a request from Japanese lawmakers for a “window for dialogue.”

China's Foreign Ministry last Friday noted “some people of insight from both Japan's ruling and opposition parties” are concerned about the state of China-Japan relations and hoping to make efforts to push them back on track. “We urge those running the Japanese government to take these voices seriously ... and take concrete actions to create the necessary conditions for normal exchanges between the two countries.”

Takaichi's remark crossed what China considers a red line in its relations with other countries about Taiwan, which is a self-governing island that Beijing claims as its territory.

Takaichi has not retracted her comment, but when marking Japan's World War II surrender on Aug. 15, she prayed remotely instead of visiting the controversial Yasukuni Shrine, seen by China and South Korea as lacking remorse for Japan's wartime militarism and atrocities.

An executive order signed this month that scales back the U.S. childhood vaccination schedule was driven by President Donald Trump's frustration that his administration was not moving fast enough to tackle what he views as a probable contributor to autism, according to administration officials.

Privately, five current and former officials acknowledge that the directive does not fundamentally transform U.S. immunization policy on its own. They note it will neither fulfill Trump’s demands nor fully satisfy the "Make America Healthy Again" political base aligned with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Instead, Kennedy and his supporters are prioritizing a series of agency studies the health secretary initiated last year.

open image in gallery Donald Trump spread misinformation about vaccines and autism at an event on Monday where he unveiled an order changing the federal vaccine schedule ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

Those projects examine what they contend are the inherent dangers of immunizations, including a potential link to autism—concerns that medical experts and scientists emphasize have been thoroughly disproven by extensive research involving millions of children over many years.

"No one wants to see this get done with an executive order. Robert F. Kennedy Jr. knows ​that will not be a lasting change if it’s not backed up by credible science," said Del Bigtree, a longtime ally of Kennedy and chief executive officer of Informed Consent Action Network, an organization that has consistently raised questions regarding vaccine safety.

"This is only the beginning of a process that had to happen."

open image in gallery Kennedy Jr. and Trump shake hands during a campaign rally at Desert Diamond Arena on August 23, 2024 in Glendale, Arizona ( Getty )

Neither the White House nor the Department of Health and Human Services offered specific details on what prompted the order.

However, White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement that Trump was taking action on behalf of "countless parents (who) have had their questions and concerns ​about America’s childhood vaccine schedule ignored if not outright mocked."

HHS spokeswoman Grace Davis Jamison confirmed the department's ongoing research projects. "We are pursuing dozens of studies and analyses using some of the nation’s largest ​health datasets to uncover the root causes of America’s chronic disease epidemic," Jamison said in a statement.

open image in gallery Priscilla Luna holds her 3 year-old daughter Avery Dahl, while she gets the MMR vaccine from Raynard Covarrubio at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025 in Lubbock, Texas. ( Getty Images )

Leading medical associations caution that Trump’s order will sow further confusion and increase vaccine hesitancy among American families, ultimately leaving more children exposed to preventable illnesses.

Public health advocates worry that Kennedy’s push for safety reviews is designed to reach a predetermined conclusion that inoculations pose greater hazards than the diseases they are designed to prevent.

Trump’s directive mandates lowering the recommended federal childhood immunization schedule from 17 shots down to 11.

open image in gallery Leading medical groups say the Trump order will increase confusion and vaccine hesitancy among U.S. families and expose more children to preventable diseases ( Getty )

It also calls for unbundling the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three separate doses—an adjustment pharmaceutical manufacturers say could take years to accomplish—and instructs the Justice Department to challenge state-level vaccination mandates for school entry.

Kennedy previously introduced a similarly reduced immunization schedule in January, bypassing standard government procedures for altering vaccine policy.

In March, a federal judge enjoined those changes, ruling that health regulators had acted unlawfully in advancing the health secretary’s agenda. The administration remains bound by that court ruling as it pursues an appeal.

open image in gallery Executive Assistant to the President Natalie Harp stands in the Oval Office Trump signs an executive order calling for childhood vaccine shots to be spaced out into separate visits on August 10 ( Getty )

Kennedy, who has spent decades promoting anti-vaccine views, promised a sweeping overhaul upon becoming Trump’s top health official. Shortly after assuming office in early 2025, he announced that his department would investigate the factors behind rising U.S. autism rates and re-evaluate the safety of childhood inoculations.

Yet Kennedy’s self-imposed timelines for providing answers on autism—initially set for September of that year and later moved to March 2026—passed without any new findings. In recent months, Trump has repeatedly pressed Kennedy to fulfill his commitments on autism during Oval Office discussions and frequent phone conversations.

That pressure mounted even as the president’s political advisers cautioned the health secretary early this year against speaking publicly about vaccines in the lead-up to November’s midterm elections, advice Kennedy adhered to.

open image in gallery Officials say RFK Jr's vaccine studies are expected to take months, if not longer ( AFP/Getty )

Nevertheless, current and former officials say Trump remained fixated on decreasing the number of inoculations American children receive. Officials added that Trump and Kennedy have held extensive discussions about identifying potential treatments and a "cure" for autism.

These private tensions boiled over during a televised cabinet meeting at Camp David on July 31. Trump asked Kennedy: "How are you doing on the autism research?" Kennedy ​replied: "We will have an answer ⁠for you."

That public exchange clearly signaled to White House and health department aides that swift action was required, according to three senior administration officials. One official noted that Trump's executive order on vaccines was hastily put together over the summer.

open image in gallery Trump also ordered the Justice Department to challenge state school vaccination requirements ( Getty )

Since the cabinet meeting, there has been a notable "tide shift" in discussions surrounding vaccines, according to one official, who noted that "Trump and Kennedy are more synced up than they have been all year."

The research projects overseen by Kennedy are assessing whether the MMR vaccine induces unintended alterations in the immune system—a theory rejected by scientists—as well as potential links between childhood immunizations and autism diagnoses, possible connections to autoimmune conditions, and the effects of thimerosal, a compound removed from childhood vaccines more than two decades ago.

Much of this analytical work relies on federal health databases that medical experts warn can easily be misused or misinterpreted if not analyzed correctly. The investigations are expected to require months or longer to complete, further fueling Trump’s ongoing frustration, according to two officials.
