Sports.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from opening weekend of the season
Sports.content:
1 Wright laments Martinelli treatment

Arsenal’s treatment of Gabriel Martinelli has been questioned by Ian Wright after the Brazil forward was left out of their squad for Friday’s opening game against Coventry. Martinelli turned down a move to Galatasaray last week after Arsenal had agreed a fee with the Turkish club and the former striker Wright revealed on Sky Sports after the Coventry game that no one at the club has spoken to the 25-year-old to discuss his future. “I know they might want him out, and a lot of people might say: ‘Yeah, it’s time for him to move him on.’ But there’s ways of doing that and it should suit him as well, how he wants to leave,” said Wright. “He’s done enough with this squad to be treated with a little bit more respect than he’s being treated with at the moment.” Ed Aarons

2 Has Watkins tarnished legacy?

It was only one game after 278 for Aston Villa, accumulated over the previous six seasons – a period in which Ollie Watkins has scored 108 goals and made himself one of the most popular players in the club’s Premier League history. But the rules are the rules. Nobody can refuse to play and emerge without a mark against their character. This is the charge against Watkins, brought in none-too-subtle fashion by Unai Emery after Villa’s 4-0 defeat at Brighton – a match that Watkins missed as he considers an approach from Al-Hilal. We do not yet have Watkins’s side of the story. Or that of his agent. But given Emery had no other available No 9, it feels pretty clear the manager did not choose to omit Watkins. Villa claim they are not close to any agreement with Al-Hilal, having rejected more than one offer from them. Perish the thought that this could drag on. Villa have one more game before the window shuts – against Arsenal at home next Monday night. David Hytner

View image in fullscreen Unai Emery did nothing to deny that Ollie Watkins had refused to play for Villa in their sobering defeat. Photograph: Glyn Kirk/AFP/Getty Images

3 United falter as No 9 options look thin

Michael Carrick was limited in his options during Manchester United’s opener because Benjamin Sesko was unable to feature at any point in pre-season but Matheus Cunha was completely ineffective as a false 9. Hull’s back three enjoyed a very quiet lunchtime as they returned to the Premier League. Cunha did not embrace the physical battle and went missing, leaving United with barely any presence in the final third as they failed to threaten their opponents. Sesko was brought on to change the dynamic but was equally ineffectual, while his fellow striker Joshua Zirkzee was left on the bench, implying how little trust the coaches have in him. Carrick needs to get Sesko up to speed and sell Zirkzee soon, freeing up funds to find a better alternative if United are to compete this season, especially with the false 9 tactic looking flawed. Will Unwin

4 Tigers delight in Tzolakis’s debut

Manchester United were impressively unthreatening in their approach to losing at Hull. There was the odd half-baked attempt at scoring or putting a cross into a dangerous area but nothing that made the highlights reel. This was unfortunate for the Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, who had an impressive, if somewhat uncomplicated, debut between the sticks. United should have made a greater effort to test the £20m signing from Olympiakos. What duties the Greek international was forced to do were carried out with ease, instilling confidence in the defence in front of him. If he continues to look so calm and assured, Tzolakis could prove himself one of the smartest signings of the season. “We bought him and we spent some money there,” Sergej Jakirovic said. “He’s a national-team player of Greece, an Olympiakos player. If you’re following Greek football, Olympiakos, it’s a huge stress, huge pressure there, and he’s used to it. For him, I think this is like a cup of tea.” WU

5 Cherki’s crucial cameo after disquiet

Rayan Cherki wrested the three points in a cameo that consisted of the corner for Marc Guéhi’s equaliser and the cute pass for Josko Gvardiol’s winner. Enzo Maresca gave an insight into the Frenchman’s disquiet at not starting. “Rayan is quite a nice and clear boy, if he is not happy he wants to show it. If he’s next to me and he’s not happy, you all realise that he is not happy because he is doing anything just to show that he is not happy. I know that he was not happy today but at the end I had to take a decision,” said the manager. Jamie Jackson

6 Sangaré shines against big spenders

At a time when some Premier League are willing to spend more than £100m on midfielders there is unlikely to be a better bargain than Mamadou Sangaré. Brentford’s new signing was excellent for Lens last season and was outstanding on his debut against Tottenham. Sangaré dominated midfield, even with Spurs able to field upwards of £175m worth of talent in Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes, and his performance raised the question of why the league’s bigger clubs are not willing to look further afield for signings. Brentford, after all, paid only £39m for Sangaré. Yet it seems inevitable there will be clubs willing to pay double the price if he has a good first season in England. Jacob Steinberg

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

7 Isak struggles on return to Newcastle

As gut-wrenching as it must have been for Newcastle fans to see their side concede a stoppage-time penalty to Liverpool, at least they can take comfort that it wasn’t Alexander Isak that scored the Reds’ dramatic equaliser from 12 yards. The former Newcastle striker had a torrid time on his return to St James’ Park – booed at every touch, crunched by Lewis Hall in the tackle and sending his only real chance of note into orbit – but he would surely have fancied taking his revenge with the last kick of the game before Dominik Szoboszlai converted the 99th-minute spot-kick. Worryingly, Isak is lacking the fluency that convinced Liverpool to spend £125m last summer and with Hugo Ekitiké still sidelined with a long-term injury, Andoni Iraola doesn’t have a natural replacement at No 9. If Liverpool are to be successful this season, Isak has to turn it on. Michael Butler

View image in fullscreen Alexander Isak watches the ball during his return to Tyneside. Photograph: Molly Darlington/Getty Images

8 Ipswich combat set pieces with O’Shea

A defensive tactical shift from the Ipswich Town manager, Gary O’Neil, demonstrated the changing nature of the Premier League. O’Neil, an astute reader of the game, chose to play the tall centre-back Dara O’Shea at right-back to counter the threat of set pieces that have become so prevalent, in Ipswich’s surprise win against Sunderland. “Aerially the Premier League is such a test now, from long throws and set pieces,” O’Neil said. “To have three centre-half types in your back four helps us from set pieces, size-wise.” In the first season since Pep Guardiola departed, the top flight is already shifting away from his neat, passing football to a different beast. Sam Cunningham

9 Dewsbury-Hall on path to complete midfielder

David Moyes felt his young Everton team might have been uncomfortable chasing the game against Crystal Palace and were therefore indebted to Jordan Pickford’s save from Eddie Nketiah, plus Jean-Philippe Mateta’s finishing, for not having to do so. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall’s guidance was instrumental too. The performance of both teams altered once the midfielder imposed himself, while his superb strike beyond Dean Henderson underlined the quality of a player who will be crucial to Everton’s aspirations. “I want to be better than last season,” said Dewsbury-Hall, who delivered eight goals and four assists in his first Premier League campaign at Everton. “That’s not just goals and assists, it’s my overall play. A couple of years ago I probably wasn’t getting goals and assists but was influential in play. I want to mix that together and when you do that that’s when you become a complete midfielder. I know I have the ability to do it so fingers crossed I do.” Andy Hunter

10 Farke hopes Leeds can cement status

Optimism abounds at Leeds. An encouraging opening-day victory at Nottingham Forest gave credence to the idea that Daniel Farke’s side are capable of cementing their place in the league. Last season, survival was the aim but after investing about £80m to sign James Trafford, Tarik Muharemovic and Nico Elvedi, plus Harry Wilson on a free, they are seeking to build on a 14th-placed finish. Leeds and Forest, who meet again in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday, have both been linked with a move for Chelsea’s Liam Delap; a striker to share the load with Dominic Calvert-Lewin would surely elevate Farke’s side. “If we want to establish ourselves and after a few years perhaps speak about something else, then we need to add individual quality,” Farke said. “The last time this club was able to have two solid seasons at this level, you will perhaps find it in black-and-white photos.” Ben Fisher

Sports.title: Chelsea change course with Alonso primed to banish the chaos of youth
Sports.content:
It is a necessary reset. Although it would be pushing it to say that Chelsea have switched from development centre to retirement home, even after the signings of Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck, there has been a clear shift in strategy this summer. Some grownups are in the room at last and, for Xabi Alonso, the hope is that bringing in more experience will help a squad still packed with youngsters show more composure when adversity strikes.

Discipline was a problem for Chelsea last season: they had 11 red cards in all competitions and a lot of the wounds were self-inflicted. Chelsea were impetuous, on the receiving end of too many bookings for dissent and prone to collapsing at the first sign of trouble. No wonder Alonso, who was the epitome of calm during his playing career, has focused on maintaining “emotional control” before opening his tenure as manager with Monday’s trip to Fulham.

It will be a test of Chelsea’s mentality. Craven Cottage has been the setting for some spectacular implosions during the BlueCo era, the path to two 2-1 victories for Fulham over their neighbours smoothed by João Félix earning a red card on his Chelsea debut in 2023 and by Marc Cucurella getting himself sent off after 22 minutes last season.

Chelsea need to change, and hiring Alonso was a tacit admission that their approach required fine-tuning. Internally there was a recognition that the club had undervalued the importance of aura when it came to hiring coaches.

They blundered with Graham Potter and Liam Rosenior, neither of whom were capable of standing the heat. Alonso is a different breed. The 44-year-old burnished his reputation by leading Bayer Leverkusen to the Bundesliga title in 2024 and he wowed Chelsea during his discussions over the role, so much so that they broke with the past by naming him manager rather than head coach.

Now the players can look to the dugout and see an authority figure. Alonso has not seized absolute power – he is still part of a wider structure, collaborating with an extensive recruitment team – but there is no doubt that his arrival has lent credibility to a project that was in danger of falling apart when the Rosenior experiment ended.

View image in fullscreen Liam Rosenior struggled at Stamford Bridge, lasting less than four months. Photograph: Javier García/Shutterstock

Of course, it remains to be seen if success in Germany means Alonso can dominate in England. Leverkusen was special but Real Madrid left him with a scar. Then again, the Bernabéu is not exactly where managers go to develop. It makes Álvaro Arbeloa, who stepped in at Madrid after Alonso’s sacking last season, a similar unknown after replacing Marco Silva at Fulham.

Yet there is optimism around Chelsea. Can they mount a title challenge for the first time in a decade? There is a lot of ground to make up after finishing 10th last season. Weaknesses linger, particularly in goal, and a push for the top four looks likelier.

However, no European football could be a blessing, giving Alonso more time in training. He looks tactically flexible. Chelsea switched between a back four and a back three during pre-season. Cucurella has joined Madrid but Marco Palestra, signed from Atalanta for £43m, and Pep Chavarría, a £16.3m arrival from Rayo Vallecano, could play as wingbacks.

The recruitment looks purposeful. After years of buying promising youngsters Chelsea have targeted ready-made players. Maxence Lacroix, the 26-year-old France centre-back, is a sensible signing from Crystal Palace. Morgan Rogers, signed from Aston Villa for £117m, can play in a range of positions in attacking midfield and could form an exciting partnership with a rested Cole Palmer, who has a point to prove after missing out on England’s World Cup squad.

There is talent here. There always has been, though. The flaw has more been around mindset. It is a footballing norm to have wise heads around to protect young players. Chelsea went too far in the opposite direction and it is one of the first areas Alonso has addressed.

Perhaps he has heard the tale of one of his predecessors having to deal with a player prioritising a haircut over a team meeting. Either way it did not feel on brand when Chelsea made an unsuccessful attempt to sign the 33-year-old Granit Xhaka from Sunderland in June. Yet it underlined their desire for more leadership and the box was ticked when Welbeck, 35, joined from Brighton in a cut-price deal and Henderson, 36, was brought in on a free transfer from Brentford.

View image in fullscreen New signing Danny Welbeck offers experience, maturity and a reliable source of goals. Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty Images

They could be canny moves. Perhaps there is an element of overkill, a sense of Chelsea taking their new direction too far, but Welbeck and Henderson still have something to offer. Welbeck scored 13 league goals for Brighton last season and will provide cover for João Pedro up front, while Henderson did not look out of place for Brentford and, according to Jude Bellingham, is someone coaching staff will always go to when there are problems to resolve.

Alonso needs order. There are still rumblings of instability off the pitch, with Todd Boehly and Mark Walter looking to sell their stakes in the club to the majority shareholder, Clearlake Capital. Quiet is rare. Chelsea need to shift a host of players before the transfer window shuts and questions hover over Enzo Fernández, who favours a reunion with Enzo Maresca at Manchester City.

There has been a lot of noise around Fernández. The midfielder has made no secret of his desire to leave but speaking out so much when Chelsea were wounded underlined the decline in standards. Alonso needs leaders. He needs trust. He still has to prove the hype is justified but his attempts to change Chelsea’s mentality is an encouraging first step.

Sports.title: Ceferin brands Infantino’s failed World Cup plan as ‘even worse than the Super League’
Sports.content:
The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, has described Gianni Infantino’s doomed attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup as “even worse than the Super League plan” and warned his embattled Fifa counterpart that he will face an opponent if he runs for re-election next March.

Ceferin has led Uefa’s firm collective stance against the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, which was shelved amid widespread opposition at the start of August. Uefa are pushing for Infantino to quit, also drawing on support from Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation, and are yet to drop a threat to boycott Fifa competitions while talks are under way with Concacaf to set up a combined Nations League tournament.

In an interview with the podcast The Rest is Politics: Leading, Ceferin denounced Infantino’s project as more damaging than the breakaway Super League that was shelved in 2021 after large-scale protests. “I think this plan is even worse than the Super League plan,” he said. “In the first case, super-important clubs wanted to do their own league, which is wrong and would destroy football. But in this case, football would be literally sold.

“I’m absolutely sure that the [FFE] plan is dead. For me, the most important thing is that we stopped another try to sell the sport. It’s hard to imagine what kind of people would sell the sport that belongs to everyone.”

Earlier this month it was reported that Infantino had held talks about running the Super League under Fifa branding. Ceferin is confident that any revival of that plan would be decades away. “It might happen in 20 years, you never know, but for now we cooperate with everyone in a great way. I’m sure it cannot happen in the next 10 years,” he said.

Infantino spent much of the weekend courting support from Concacaf members at a meeting in the Dominican Republic, infuriating many of those present. Ceferin, who revealed the pair had not been in contact since the FFE scandal broke, believes the Fifa president’s path to survival is narrowing.

“I didn’t speak with him, he didn’t contact me since this happened,” he said. “But there are two options. One option is that he realises that he doesn’t have the support, and that’s not only political support of the ones who vote, but the political support of the football community, the political support of fans, the political support of the players, former players, coaches.

“And the second option [is] that he goes to the elections in March, but in that case, I think he will have a candidate against him. I don’t know yet who.” The Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, has been tipped as a potential opponent for Infantino if he chooses to run in Rabat.

Ceferin has proponents of his own but ruled out making his own bid for the Fifa presidency. “My credibility is much, much, much higher if I’m not interested in the position,” he said. The Slovenian is expected to run unopposed for a fourth term at the helm of Uefa, with the election due next April.

Asked whether Infantino had become too close to Donald Trump, with whom he forged a close relationship before the recent World Cup, Ceferin said: “To be honest, I think you are naive if you think that a politician like that, or any politician, is your good friend. The moment you are a problem, you stop being a friend of a politician.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

That friendship came under the spotlight last month when Trump said he had called Infantino to ask for a review of the red card given to the US striker Folarin Balogun, whose ban for the last-16 tie against Belgium was later suspended. “That was more than shocking,” Ceferin said. “We have rules and if you don’t respect your own rules, then the game doesn’t make any sense. That’s shocking and, trust me, almost everybody was shocked. Just not everybody dared to speak.”

Meanwhile, in a fresh show of European opposition to Infantino, the six Nordic football associations issued a statement saying they had “lost confidence in the Fifa president and have serious concerns about the governance and high-level decision making of the organisation”. They asked for binding assurances that Fifa will never again “open its governance or competitions to private ownership” and called for a full third-party review into the FFE scheme.

Earlier in August the Norwegian Football Federation was the first member association to call directly for Infantino to step down.

Infantino travelled straight from the Dominican Republic to Paris on Sunday, attending the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup. Television footage showed him exchanging greetings with the president of France, Emmanuel Macron.

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Alvarez set for Arsenal after being booed at Atlético?
Sports.content:
Booing Julián Alvarez during Atlético Madrid’s draw with Villarreal on Sunday has seemingly convinced the Argentinian forward to consider joining Arsenal in the window. The former Manchester City man has been kept out of the reaches of Barcelona, who may not have the funds to complete the signing, whereas the Gunners have plenty of cash to splash.

Alejandro Balde was left out of the Barcelona squad as they roared past Elche, as the Catalan club open the door for a move to Manchester United. A new left-back should solve all of the problems at Old Trafford, that’s for sure.

Jarrod Bowen has committed his future to West Ham, despite them being relegated and starting the Championship season in desperate fashion. Despite all that, perhaps he will be tempted by a £50m bid from Crystal Palace after a welcome to the Championship to forget? The Eagles were blunt at Everton over the weekend and could be about to initiate panic stations by splashing out quite severely for the Hammers skipper.

Losing 4-0 at Brighton is not going to do much for morale but it will make a team take drastic action in the market. Aston Villa have lined up Joel Ordóñez to solve all of their problems for the remainder of the season, if Club Brugge are willing to sell the centre-back.

There is only one way to bounce back from losing at Ipswich and that is to chase a £34m Barcelona player. Sunderland have tracked Marc Casadó throughout the summer and could be about to pounce for the 22-year-old, who has also been linked with most of the Premier League in recent weeks.

It is difficult to decipher if Cruzeiro’s Jonathan Jesus would sign for Strasbourg or Chelsea, but the talk in Brazil is that ownership group BlueCo want the 22-year-old centre-back. Real Betis, Valencia and Benfica are equally keen, adding a bit of jeopardy to the chase.

With Chelsea always looking to move on a few players, they will be ecstatic to hear that Napoli are contemplating a move for the striker Marc Guiu. Whether the Italians are up for splurging £25m on the Spaniard remains to be seen because the Serie A club currently believe the Blues’ valuation is a touch on the high side.

As alluded to, it was a fantastic start to the season for Hull on Saturday when they gave Manchester United a bit of a shooing. To help build on that, they have agreed a £15.4m deal to sign forward Mohamed-Ali Cho from Nice.

Sports.title: ‘Call his agent’: Emery feels Watkins should explain absence from Villa’s rout by Brighton
Sports.content:
Unai Emery did nothing to deny that Ollie Watkins had refused to play for Aston Villa in their sobering 4-0 defeat by Brighton at the Amex on Sunday. The head coach had a selection crisis up front with Brian Madjo and Tammy Abraham injured. However, he did not include Watkins in the matchday squad as the England striker considers a move to Al-Hilal in Saudi Arabia.

Emery was forced to rely on the attacking midfielder Emiliano Buendía as an emergency striker and his team disappeared without trace on the south coast. They were 4-0 down after 31 minutes and had their new signing João Gomes sent off on his debut in the 40th minute. Gomes kicked up and out at the Brighton striker Georginio Rutter after being dispossessed by him.

Al-Hilal have made a number of bids for Watkins, all of which have been rejected. It is understood the 30-year-old is open to the move and Emery talked on Friday like a manager who was realistic about the sale happening. Villa would plainly like to replace Watkins should he depart as they approach the end of another difficult summer window. They have already sold Ezri Konsa, Morgan Rogers, Lucas Digne and Youri Tielemans, while they are expected to move on Emiliano Martínez.

Emery was asked why he had not picked Watkins against Brighton. “This question is for him,” he said. “I can answer only with my silence.” Emery was then asked if Watkins had refused to play, to which he said: “I think you can call him and you can call his agent and he can respond.”

The Guardian have contacted Watkins’s agent for comment.

“He [Watkins] can only explain his answer, I can’t,” Emery added, after being asked if he felt let down by Watkins.

Emery reported that Madjo would be out for “two weeks more … more or less” while attacking midfielder Johan Manzambi – who has been the club’s marquee summer signing – would “need maybe some days more [than that]”. He was unclear about a timeframe for Abraham’s return.

Quick Guide How do I 

Emery talked up the resistance of his players in the second half against Brighton and said he was optimistic about finding solutions for the season ahead. But he returned to the difficult preparations for the opening fixture, noting that: “Two strikers are injured and another striker gives his answer.”

The head coach added: “This problem [with the transfer market] … we had every season and every season we overcame it. It’s something we have to accept and always we reacted, especially the players. This is something hard for us every year but we are calm. With this result, it’s more difficult to explain but calm, work, be positive and find solutions for the next week and after the transfer window.”

Sports.title: Newcastle and Liverpool crank up the entertainment for emotional send-off | Sam Dalling
Sports.content:
It’s 4.35pm on Tyneside. William Osula sets Anthony Elanga away, slightly right of centre and just short of 50,000 draw collective breaths. Pace is no issue; Elanga has no shortage of that, and Milos Kerkez won’t catch him.

But Newcastle fans have seen this clip before and remember the ending. Muscles tighten, cheeks clench, as they brace themselves for it to start again like it carried on before. (Yet) another memeable‑moment inbound. A tiny part of each of them, though, thinks: “Wait, hang on, this is a new season, a fresh start.” The slate is not just clean but has been entirely replaced and is now AI-operated.

Elanga takes a touch, a tad heavier ideal but it pushes the ball away from Alisson. A moment of composure follows and Newcastle lead. An entirely goalless league season passed after Elanga’s £55m transfer from Nottingham Forest and now, within five minutes of a new one, his drought is broken. Elanga missed a much easier opportunity against Aston Villa on the 2025-26 opening day, and his confidence never recovered. Can you walk back through a sliding door?

Nearly two hours later, there remain just a few precious seconds for Liverpool to salvage something. Victor Muñoz is brought down clumsily by Lewis Hall. Dominik Szoboszlai converts the resulting penalty. 2-2.

Muñoz apparently gave Newcastle positive noises about joining them during summer. Then, in a flexing of financial muscle, Liverpool met the Osasuna forward’s release clause and to Anfield he went. What was that about sliding doors?

View image in fullscreen Liverpool’s Víctor Muñoz – a summer target for Newcastle – is brought down by Lewis Hall to hand the visitors a late penalty. Photograph: Ian Hodgson/AP

Those two goals bookended an afternoon that was, if you want to do go down that road, a fitting tribute to the recently departed Kevin Keegan. Entertaining but flawed.

As a term, legend is so chronically overused now that it is meaningless. But Keegan is a prime example of the word’s proper application. Shortly before kick-off everyone present paid an emotional tribute to him. Legend. Hero. King. All subjective labels essentially turned objective.

With Liverpool, Keegan’s seven trophies in six years – including three titles and the European Cup – set the club up to be the behemoth they now are. Across three spells at Newcastle, he jabbed syringes of hope into a flailing, helpless shell.

St James’ Park is not quite the house that Keegan built, but it is no stretch to say it is the house built because of him. Without his steering Newcastle to Second Division safety in 1992 as manager, the club in its current guise might not exist.

So, why does Keegan remain so adored? He is in effect a symbol of what football once was and should still be, can be even. Maybe. Forget spreadsheets, financial acronyms and PR-doused messaging. Ignore expected this and that, low blocks and cancelling each other out. Find the joy. Forget perfect; take a risk. Failure and fallibility? Both absolutely OK.

Those are sentiments Andoni Iraola and Matthias Jaissle would do well to remember as they look to settle themselves into new gigs. The former, with Liverpool being champions two seasons ago, will be under the greater pressure. A repeat of his start at Bournemouth, where he won only at the 10th time of asking, would be difficult to tolerate.

There were promising signs for Iraola, sure. Jérémy Jacquet grew into his debut. Cody Gakpo had only just whipped a strike narrowly off target before his fine equaliser just after half-time. Rio Ngumoha was quiet but that he has impressed sufficiently to start the season opener is itself a plus.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Florian Wirtz (centre) and former Newcastle man Alexander Isak again both struggled to make an impact for Liverpool. Photograph: George Wood/Getty Images

But there were familiar failings, too. The full-backs looked shaky and Iraola needs more (much, much more) from both the sums and the whole of the £241m Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak combo.

Isak is about as popular in Newcastle as government-mandated balaclava wearing in a heatwave would be, but the stick-cum-abuse he received didn’t seem to bother him. However, what should keep Isak up at night is how he can and must refind the level that rightly saw him tagged one of the Premier League’s best forwards not so long ago. A skied left-footed effort was the closest he came to silencing the heckles.

Jaissle is likely to get more slack. Everyone is aware of what Newcastle have, where they are and, most pertinent, what they have lost. Something fresh was absolutely needed but that requires time and patience. There are, and will continue to be, warts, imperfections, things that Bruno Guimarães might have done.

A midfield pair sold for north of £180m were replaced on Sunday by a double pivot with a combined aged of 38 and less than 50 league starts. Lewis Miley and Sean Steur looked the part but made mistakes. That they did so seeking the positive option will only endear them to fans. As will more similar performances from Yoane Wissa. A player who last season looked sluggish and largely static, was suddenly full of everything in the No 10 role.

A decent start. Room for improvement. Apply that to both sides.

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 3: Birmingham City
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 12th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 1st (WSL2)

Prospects

Founding members of the Women’s Super League when it launched in 2011, Birmingham are back in the top flight after four years in the second tier, having won promotion as WSL2 champions on the final day of last season. After a decent summer transfer window, Birmingham look to have a fighting chance of staying up, and perhaps even surprising a few teams, while off the pitch they are the best-equipped of the three promoted sides to cement themselves in the top division.

Forwards Lily Crosthwaite and Wilma Leidhammar and defender Neve Herron, are all 23-years-old and likely to continue improving. Birmingham have also added players with WSL experience, such as the former Brighton goalkeeper Sophie Baggaley and the centre-back Millie Turner.

Inconsistency was nearly their downfall last season; they won the most games in WSL2, but also lost six times. They delivered under pressure, boosted by the performances of Leidhammar after her club-record arrival in January, ensuring they avoided a repeat of the heartbreak of 12 months earlier when they missed out on promotion on the final day. Nonetheless, Birmingham are still a long way off from the days when they were runners-up in the top tier and their first two away fixtures are against Manchester City and Chelsea. They also host fellow promoted sides Crystal Palace and Charlton relatively early in the campaign and those home fixtures could be key to building confidence.

Off-field picture

Birmingham’s women’s team were sold to the club’s ownership group in February, with Shelby Companies Limited – an affiliate of Knighthead Capital Management – owning 97%. The remaining 3% was purchased by investors including the former England midfielder Karen Carney and the four-time grand slam tennis champion Kim Clijsters. The club appear to be in a relatively healthy position with ambitious owners determined to reestablish the 2012 FA Cup winners as a regular, competitive presence in the WSL. They train at the recently renovated Knighthead Performance Centre, on the same site as the men’s team’s former Wast Hills training base, with a new gym among other extensive refurbishments.

The manager

Amy Merricks has been in charge since April 2024 She holds a Uefa Pro Licence and was 30 years old when she was appointed by Birmingham. She has previously coached within the England youth setup as well as at Gillingham, Millwall and Brighton, where was stepped up to be interim manager three times.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Lisa Naalsund arrives from Manchester United to boost Birmingham’s midfield. Photograph: DeFodi Images/Getty Images

Birmingham have recruited players with international experience, including the Canada defender Marie Levasseur from Montpellier, but their two most eyebrow-raising additions are Turner and Lisa Naalsund from Manchester United. They were starting members of United’s FA Cup-winning side of 2024 and played in a Women’s Champions League quarter-final as recently as April. Naalsund will be an influential force in the midfield – she has won 39 caps and was part of Norway’s squad at last year’s Euros.

Stat attack

Birmingham topped WSL2 last season despite not scoring the most goals or conceding the fewest. One stat they led was big chances, Opta’s metric for opportunities where it is reasonable to expect the attacker to score. While their tally will be much harder to repeat in the top flight, their attacking process looks in good order.

Set for a breakthrough

There is plenty of excitement at Birmingham about another of their new signings, the 19-year-old France youth forward Chancelle Effa Effa, who arrived from Le Havre for a fee understood to be about €120,000 (£100,000) this month. She broke into Le Havre’s first team at the age of 15 and scored 17 times in 28 games for France’s Under-17 and Under-19 teams, having helped France win 2023’s Under-17 Euros.

What they say …

“We know it’s going to be a massive challenge, but it’s a challenge that, as players, you thrive upon. As long as we can take that togetherness, that relentlessness, into the games, I’m sure we’re going to be just fine” – Chelsea Cornet.

Where are they playing their home games?

Birmingham play their home fixtures at St Andrew’s, which has been the women’s team’s home since 2021. They set a club record attendance for a women’s game there on the final day of the 2024-25 season – 8,749. Long-term, the club have announced plans to build a new women’s team stadium as part of the ‘Sports Quarter’, which also includes the proposed 62,000-seater men’s team Powerhouse Stadium as well as an indoor arena, training ground facilities and a new railway station.

Sports.title: Maresca concedes Manchester City ‘a work in progress’ after hair-raising escape
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca said Manchester City remain a “work in progress” after Sunday’s last-gasp win over Bournemouth at the Etihad Stadium.

Marc Guéhi’s 85th-minute equaliser and Josko Gvardiol’s 91st-minute winner gave City’s new manager victory in his first game, after Marcus Tavernier’s first-half strike for the visitors.

Maresca thought his side performed similarly to last Sunday’s 3-0 Community Shield loss to Arsenal. “I feel in the same position as after Arsenal,” the Italian said. “It’s normal you judge after results but I don’t see big changes. Unfortunately, this is a work in progress and I’m looking for solutions. For sure when you win games it helps.

“If you think of the Premier League – it won’t happen that you will concede nothing. The goal we conceded was their first shot. They had two or three dangerous moments but it’s how you react. We’ve still got [Erling] Haaland, Elliot [Anderson], Marc [Guéhi], Nico O’Reilly [who all started], who are in pre-season still. It’s a huge difference in terms of physicality and we are going to get better and better.”

Before the game City unfurled a huge tifo bearing his image that said: “Welcome back Enzo.” He said: “It is the perfect day. I was very pleased to see the banner when the game started. We gave them [fans] the joy at the end. It was quite emotional. The spirit was fantastic. It’s a game we deserved to win [but] you don’t need to wait for the last five minutes. We missed chances, then they scored and it became more complicated.”

Maresca fielded Guéhi in an unfamiliar midfield role. “I know Marc from [ Crystal] Palace and I always thought he could play as a midfielder because he is very good,” the manager said. “So we tried it for a few days and I think he was quite good. He gives us a solution for the future,.”

In his first game managing Bournemouth, Marco Rose came close to leading them to a first away win against City. “We’re competitors, we came here to win for the first time,” said the German. “We were in a good way to do so. But we did many good things. We have a lot of things to improve. At the end, how the game went was quite unlucky to lose that way. We had two situations – one corner kick and one attacking [move] – when we defended too passively.

Sports.title: Journey to Wembley: After a fortnight of fretting over floodlights on the fritz, Nelson's FA Cup journey ends at Witton Albion - where home fans toasted victory with pina coladas!
Sports.content:
Journey to Wembley: After a fortnight of fretting over floodlights on the fritz, Nelson's FA Cup journey ends at Witton Albion - where home fans toasted victory with pina coladas!

It’s the annual pina colada festival in the Witton area of Cheshire – the song about the drink, which topped the US charts in the late 1970s, was written by someone local to the place and they’ve spotted the commercial opportunity – so there are people walking around dressed as pineapples and wearing big yellow glasses on Saturday lunchtime. But life has not exactly been a cocktail party for Nelson, an East Lancashire ninth tier club, just lately.

They breeze through one of the challenges which faces them after arriving to face opponents one step above them in the pyramid. Their new yellow away kits for the season haven’t arrived and last season’s issue, which they’re still using, don’t have a No 18 jersey – needed today because you’re allowed seven subs in the FA Cup. Someone finds a white marker pen and inks the number on to a plain yellow away shirt. Wearing numbers on your back is mandatory in the tournament.

This is a minor obstacle compared with the floodlight problems which has been testing Nelson minds since we left them celebrating extra preliminary round victory at their ‘Little Wembley’ ground two weeks ago. That was the first part of our journey to Wembley told in 13 instalments, following a club as far as they go and then picking up with the team who knock them out, all the way to the final.

They’d signed off on a £30,000 contract, helped by FA grants, to replace the system of lights which had started to fail during evening games, only to find that the new ones still didn’t work.

The approved contractors didn’t seem to have mentioned that the cables and wiring supplying the lights also needed ripping out, and yet were sending the club legal letters demanding payment, as Nelson’s directors sought advice from the FA about the black hole they risked disappearing into.

Inside the home dressing room at the Bedspace Trust Community Stadium

Nelson captain Bill Priestley receives some treatment ahead of kick-off

A home steward - proudly sporting Witton Albion's colours - tucks into a pie at half-time

When we caught up with Nelson at their league away game at Charnock Richard in Lancashire, last Tuesday night, the floodlights were the prime topic of conversation as the players arrived in the car park. There had even been talk of a temporary ground move, which did not exactly delight the North West Counties League. Nelson’s proactive club sponsor Monks Contractors had offered supplying temporary structures.

In the end, they just went to work again. Volunteers helped dig two 100m trenches to lay the new cabling to the new lights and on Wednesday, they flicked the switch once more. ‘Let there be light?’ The look on Nelson director Rob Doherty’s face as the visiting contingent are welcomed into Witton’s snug little boardroom suggests so. ‘As of three days ago, they were working,’ he relates. The FA provided emergency funding.

Both these teams badly want to win this FA Cup Preliminary Round game. In his extremely modestly proportioned office Witton manager Benny Harrison, whose day job is a teacher at a special educational school, reflects at 2pm on the profound effects Marine experienced after playing Tottenham in the Third Round in 2021. The windfall helped win them two promotions in three years.

But as the rival teams’ executives gather in that boardroom, there’s a sense of mutual empathy about the existential threats which can be just around the corner for any non-league club.

‘There’s what goes on out on the pitch, and the fans and all that the lovely stuff,’ says Witton director Paul Sanderson, when Nelson relate their floodlight troubles. ‘And then there’s survivability stuff that fans don't know about. Trying to navigate things that can threaten your existence if you’re not prepared for anything.’

Nelson were on a precipice before new co-owners Stewart Fort and Chris Price arrived three years ago, invested and built up the team of volunteers who are their lifeblood. But Witton’s excellent little club museum, charting a 139-year history and signposted ‘Probably the best non-League football museum in the world’, shows that they’ve also ridden football’s rollercoaster.

The museum chronicles the club’s journey to the 1992 FA Trophy final at Wembley, where they lost to Colchester. That period, which included a brief stay in the Vauxhall Conference, saw them splashing the surplus earned after selling their old ground to Sainsburys and building a new one, on players. The rewards were painful temporary. Witton struggled when the money ran out and the new stadium required major repair sooner than anticipated.

The sun’s out, though, and the FA Cup is blowing everyone’s troubles away. ‘Welcome to the best football competition in the world by a long chalk,’ states the stadium announcer. The appropriately named Witton groundsman James Spruce is reversing his mower out onto the excellent playing surface, his partner Katy Hulse is nursing a pina colada and her friend Barbara Bazley is watching the warm-up.

Groundsman James Spruce applies the finishing touches to the playing surface

Katy Hulse (left) enjoys a pina colada with her friend Barbara Bazley

Albion statistician Phil Chadwick has helped to curate one of the best club museum's in non-League

Nelson's 87-year-old superfan Harry Manning’s immaculate handwritten notes will be converted into a match report for the local Nelson Leader

‘When you make s*** decisions, it goes pear-shaped, so if someone makes a s*** decision, back them up and help sort it out,’ shouts assistant coach Liam Lishman, as he puts the squad through their paces. Thursday’s training session focussed on not allowing Freddie Garbutt, Witton’s towering 22-year-old striker, the chance to control and shoot.

At Charnock Richard, Nelson won 2-0, led by their own dangerous target man Sefton Gonzalez, who scored and hurled himself through his trademark somersault. Today, goalkeeper Chris Thompson is back after a bout of sciatica. There’s optimism in the air.

Against the backdrop of the chemical plants in salt-mining territory, Nelson discover what they’re up against in Garbutt and Witton’s attacking pace. Nelson wing-back Darren Holden, outstanding in the previous round and at Charnock in midweek, is operating in his own half far more, protecting Nelson territory, yet removing one of the Lancashire team's attacking dimensions.

Jamie Edwards, Nelson’s force field, draws a sharp save and Gonzales has just headed a great opportunity into the ground when Witton’s Garbutt leaps to meet a corner and send his team ahead.

He’s one of only two players Witton have signed up to a contract, protecting his match fee if he’s injured and protecting the club if someone else tries to sign him, Witton chairman Graham Wood relates, back in the boardroom at half-time.

The winners today will collect £1,444 in prize money and that would be just as precious to Witton, a fan-owned club with 400 registered shareholders, none of them hugely wealthy, who are currently trying to make a community football facility.

Nelson players warm up at the side of the pitch before kick-off

Witton Albion play in the Northern Premier League Division One West, one divsion higher than Nelson

Visiting goalkeeper Chris Thompson keeps a Witton Albion player at bay

Freddy Garbutt's first-half goal settled the game and sent Witton through to the next round of the FA Cup

Home boss Ben Harrison addresses his players at full-time

‘That will bring us an income to put back into the club,’ says Wood, who has helped bring a commercial sponsorship deal with a locally based homelessness charity.

Nelson dominate a second half in which Holden is pushed forward more, encouraged by his wife Abi, who is live tweeting the match for the club’s website with another volunteer, Amy Holden, and taking photographs for next week’s match programme and the website.

In the main stand, 87-year-old superfan Harry Manning’s immaculate handwritten notes, which will be converted into a match report for the local Nelson Leader, reflect the growing frustration. The ‘18’ inked onto sub James Hooper’s jersey is impressive. But it’s raining in Nelson hearts when the whistle blows and they tumble out of the competition.

Manager Arron Ripley stands in the sun-dappled centre circle ten minutes later and reflects on the way his ambitious side are evolving. ‘Last year we’d have kept launching it in a situation like that but we’re looking after the ball. We look like we’re enjoying it. We just weren’t clinical enough.’

Nelson can return fortified to their league campaign, confident, in so many ways, that the lights will stay on.

Sports.title: England cricketer Brydon Carse handcuffed after nightclub incident - with former captain Ben Stokes spotted watching on
Sports.content:
England cricketer Brydon Carse handcuffed after nightclub incident - with former captain Ben Stokes spotted watching on

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

English cricket is dealing with yet more embarrassing headlines after footage emerged of fast bowler Brydon Carse handcuffed by police outside a Derby nightclub late on Saturday.

Carse, who was part of England’s squad for the first two Tests against Pakistan and their leading wicket-taker during the Ashes defeat in Australia, was released without charge, having been out celebrating with Durham team-mates following their win over Derbyshire in the county championship.

A short video posted on social media showed Carse, 31, surrounded by four policemen outside the club, with fellow Durham stars Ben Stokes and Matthew Potts in the background. One of the policemen is heard to say: ‘Just get him over there.’

It is unclear why Carse was placed in handcuffs, and he is understood to have returned to the team hotel soon after.

The England and Wales Cricket Board said: ‘We are aware of an incident which is reported to have taken place in Derby [on Saturday] night, and are currently investigating. We will provide a further update when possible.’

No decision has yet been made over whether Carse will be removed from England’s 16-man squad for the second Test against Pakistan at Lord’s, starting on Thursday, while the ECB and the independent Cricket Regulator investigate the incident.

Brydon Carse was spotted in handcuffs surrounded by police outside a nightclub in Derby

The news comes not long after England’s new Test captain, Joe Root, abolished the team curfew that had been in place since the Ashes defeat in January, insisting his players should be trusted to behave like ‘grown adults’.

That followed a string of drink-related incidents over the past year that have sparked fresh debate about cricket’s relationship with alcohol.

In October, white-ball captain Harry Brook was punched by a nightclub bouncer on the eve of a one-day international in Wellington, New Zealand – an incident the ECB hushed up until the story broke on the last day of the fifth Test against Australia at Sydney in January.

In the meantime, England’s Ashes squad spent four high-profile days between the second and third Tests in the Sunshine Coast resort of Noosa. Opening batsman Ben Duckett was filmed by a member of the public slurring his words during a late-night exchange, while observers likened the trip to a ‘stag-do’.

In June, Stokes and fast bowler Gus Atkinson missed the second Test against New Zealand after they broke the team curfew at a west London nightclub celebrating England’s first-Test win at Lord’s. They both claimed they didn’t know the curfew still operated after the end of a home Test, and Stokes retired from international cricket soon after.

Carse, who has won 14 Test caps, has been in trouble with the authorities before, having been suspended for three months in 2024 for historic betting offences, which involved placing 303 bets on matches between 2017 and 2019.

Sports.title: 'No chance!': Peter Schmeichel is shot down live on TV by Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle on Man United's hopes of signing Lewis Hall
Sports.content:
Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle hilariously dismissed Man United's hopes of signing Lewis Hall live on TV.

Speaking in the aftermath of his side's 2-2 draw with Liverpool at St James' Park on Sunday, Jaissle was conducting a pitchside interview with Viaplay.

As the conversation turned to the transfer market, Jaissle was pressed on whether he hoped Newcastle would do any further business during what has been a turbulent summer for the club.

Key players Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon have already departed, and there has also been speculation over the futures of other stars including Joe Willock, Tino Livramento and Hall.

And when questioned on his aspirations to sign more players, Jaissle responded: 'I think it will be a stressful period for the sporting director, because we have some needs.

'But if we bring players in maybe there will also be some players who go out.'

Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle shot down Man United's hopes of signing Lewis Hall

Hall has been linked to United this summer, but Jaissle insisted the left-back is going nowhere

Former Man United keeper Peter Schmeichel, who played 398 times for the club, then cheekily said: 'We are looking at your left back.'

That comment was in reference to Hall, with United having made enquiries for the defender this summer.

But to that, Jaissle said: 'No chance, no chance,' as he chuckled.

Daily Mail Sport reported earlier this month that Hall has been on United's radar as it is clear they need to strengthen that position, with Luke Shaw, now 31, in the final year of his contract while youngster Harry Amass has been told he may be best leaving for first team football.

Hall, 21, has three years left on his current deal, and would require a substantial fee, with the defender now seen as one of Newcastle's biggest assets after joining from Chelsea in 2023.

United, meanwhile, feel they are light in the position. Shaw started all 38 Premier League matches last season, though there is no obvious back-up, with Patrick Dorgu viewed as a winger by Michael Carrick.

Jaissle's comments came after an impressive opening day performance from Newcastle as they drew 2-2 with Liverpool.

They had looked set for all three points after goals from Anthony Elanga and Joe Willock had them 2-1 ahead, but Dominik Szoboszlai equalised with a penalty in the 99th minute.

'In the end, I am a bit disappointed,' the German said after the game. 'But there is also some brightness, definitely, because the guys were doing an amazing job for over 90 minutes.

'We are a young squad and they really left their heart on the pitch and this is something we can build on.

'I'm proud. We are proud to see a unit on the pitch. The guys were trying to do it the intense way that we wanted to play. Front-footed, vertical in our approach.

'This, after such a short amount of time, I'm really happy. I felt the goosebumps straight away. You get energy from the stands and you just want to deliver it on the pitch. This synergy will be something special.'

Sports.title: 'Come on, that's ridiculous!': Man United boss Michael Carrick snaps at ex-player interviewer as pressure hits on first question about his team's 'passion' after collapsing at promoted Hull City
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick snapped at a reporter's 'ridiculous' opening question after Manchester United's shock defeat by Hull City on Saturday.

The United manager was affronted when asked if his players had lost against the newly promoted club due to a lack of 'passion'.

United's Premier League season got off to a nightmare start as goals from Semi Ajayi and Nobel Mendy – both stemming from set-pieces – put them to the sword in Yorkshire.

Carrick was interviewed afterwards by Viaplay broadcaster Jan Age Fjortoft, the Norwegian who played for Swindon, Middlesbrough, Sheffield United, and Barnsley in the 1990s.

'Would you accept that there was a lack of passion in the first half?' asked Fjortoft.

'Oh come on, that's ridiculous,' Carrick hit back.

Michael Carrick said it was 'ridiculous' to suggest his Manchester United team lacked passion in their 2-0 defeat by Hull City

He was vexed by the question posed by Viaplay reporter and former play Jan Age Fjortoft

“Come on, that’s ridiculous.”



Michael Carrick wasn’t happy when asked if there was a lack of passion from #mufc in their first half vs Hull.



via @ViaplayFotball pic.twitter.com/zyca5r5iSr — utdreport (@utdreport) August 23, 2026

'That's not how you would assess it?' asked Fjortoft.

Carrick replied: 'Come on, you played football, you understand, that's a ridiculous thing to say. Just because you got beat doesn't mean you don't care about it.'

Fjortoft said: 'I'm not saying that you didn't care about it. If you look at it, they came with passion, that's what I mean. I understand that you care about it, but would you accept that they took you on that front, so to say?'

'No, no. Their two goals came from set plays. Other than that, we had opportunities,' Carrick said. 'That was where the game was. I don't think it was passion or anything to do with that. I think it was just their moment that made the difference in the game.'

Fjortoft said: 'Is it these duels? Is that what you mean? That these two duels were the goals? Because they had chances. There were consequences there from the game that you could see that they would get at you.'

'It’s a game of football, it’s a Premier League game,' Carrick replied.

'It’s their first game at home, and we’ve seen it many times before. You know, I said it before the game because it was always going to be a tough game.

'And set-plays, yeah, that’s it. We’ve been decent over a period of time at dealing with them, and today we didn’t.

Any title talk for Manchester United was quickly dulled by their lacklustre performance

Semi Ajayi gave the hosts the lead after a kerfuffle in the box in the 17th minute

Nobel Mendy made matters worse for United when he added Hull's second after 38 minutes

Marcus Rashford came off the bench wearing the number nine shirt but was unable to change the match

'We can look into that, we can dissect it. We certainly won’t get carried away with the positives or the negatives. We never do. So I think we can stay calm and understand what we need to get better at.'

It was a humbling experience for Carrick, who lost just two of his 17 matches in interim charge of United.

They started with a new-look midfield in the form of Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, but neither was overly convincing and the former even got nutmegged at one point.

Carrick did a fantastic job to lead United into the Champions League and the hope is that they will imitate that. Carlos Baleba is soon arriving from Brighton for £70million to further bolster their midfield.

Reporting on the match at the MKM Stadium, Daily Mail Sport's Manchester United reporter Chris Wheeler called any talk of a title challenge a 'joke'.

Wheeler wrote: 'Even in his worst nightmares, Carrick couldn't have foreseen this: an opening-day humiliation at the hands of a team that sneaked into the Premier League via the Championship play-offs in May, and have been prepped for their return to the top-flight with a summer spend of just £70million on 12 players – the same as it is costing United to sign Carlos Baleba from Brighton.'

He added: 'After a summer of guarded optimism over the signing of Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, the new midfield failed to launch.

'Both players were replaced midway through the second half on their Premier League debuts with United two goals down, having been eclipsed by Matt Crooks and Slater, a mere £50,000 signing from Sheffield United in 2022.

'Instead, it was the business that United haven't done that becomes the main talking point. The new striker that hasn't arrived. The missing defensive cover for Luke Shaw. Baleba, the third midfield signing, coming in too late to start the season.

Considering Carrick only lost two of his 17 games after taking over in January, this was a serious setback. He talked in the week about touting United as title contenders being 'a jump'. On this evidence, it's a joke.'

Sports.title: Mutiny-hit Match of the Day review: BBC try to go with same old, same old amid Alan Shearer backing out - and no sign of the 'modernisation'
Sports.content:
Before the action, we had that lovely old intro, old clips, old voices, old logos, old Kenneth Wolstenholme telling us from August 1964: 'Welcome to Match of the Day.'

Ah, familiarity, our old friend. Despite an addiction to trying to fix what is not broken, the BBC begin each and every MOTD by celebrating how long this staple of Saturday nights has been on our screens, since a time when Wolstenholme was being beamed to us in black and white.

It was at least with relief that the Beeb stuck with this theme of familiarity for their first broadcast of the 2026-27 season, if accompanied by some apprehension over whether that feeling would last.

They had advertised their new line-up this last week, after all, telling us to expect to see Thomas Frank, Toby Alderweireld, Robbie Keane and Ashley Young on our screens while simultaneously plugging their four new YouTube shows in a bid to tap into the young'uns.

Got to modernise. Go after the audience that apparently doesn't think terrestrially.

But this particular MOTD was more a case of same old, same old, and not only because it started with that vintage montage and theme tune which, if they tried to bin next in favour of some modern track, I'd be tempted to launch a petition of my own.

The BBC stuck with a sense of familiarity for the first Match of the Day of the season

I would launch a petition if they ever changed the show's opening, writes Kieran Gill

The Beeb did not want to suddenly beam fresh faces into our living rooms. They saved the new blood, and scrutiny, for another time. Instead we saw those we know and trust.

Mark Chapman was in the hot seat. We know Chappers. We like Chappers. He, along with Kelly Cates and Gabby Logan, were chosen well as Gary Lineker's successors.

After a week in which we learned there is discontent behind the scenes at MOTD at the direction of this crown jewel's travel, Chapman's tongue-in-cheek opener was: 'Happy new season. Match of the Day returns. We're all smiles here. Just look at Alan Shearer and Wayne Rooney.'

More familiarity. We like them, too. They add to the broadcast. We could watch the highlights online if we wanted, hours before MOTD. We tune in because it adds analysis in between the action, including the stylish statistical graphics they show, and that is what we want.

When we will next see Shearer in one of these seats, who knows. We are told he has scaled back his contractual commitments, and as well as giving him back his weekends by only doing one show a month if that, he supposedly has beef with those above him.

In his place, Frank should be a good addition. He has authority. Despite what happened with Tottenham Hotspur, he is a fine, modern, intelligent coach, and impressed during the 2026 World Cup, which the BBC predominantly covered from Salford as we know.

Also entering via the revolving door, Alderweireld and Keane can expect their takes on Spurs will end up being separate stories online, especially if they are controversial.

Rooney branding Manchester United's defending as 'schoolboy' on Saturday will have had the odd news editor tempted to ask for copy to be bashed up, I'm sure.

Alan Shearer and Wayne Rooney are good pundits, but we will see a heavily revolving cast

Yet it will be intriguing to see how they all click together and if there is chemistry, the type that Shearer, Richards and Lineker forged over time spent working together. Apparently that concern surrounding camaraderie forms part of the mutiny occurring within MOTD.

Millions still trust their Saturday nights in the hands of the BBC. Myself included, having watched this show since my parents let me stay up late enough to do so.

Those of us who love the company of MOTD never want it to go the same way as Football Focus, its sister show which ended in May after 52 years on air.

Changing it too much would be a risk. At least the Beeb saw enough sense to show us what we wanted to see on this occasion as we settled in for Hull's big win on their return to the Premier League and the other highlights thereafter. On to what next week brings.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick must make his mark as capitulation in dismal defeat by Hull raises fresh concerns over this Man United squad's ability to build on his achievements, writes CHRIS WHEELER
Sports.content:
When Michael Carrick celebrated his return to Old Trafford in January with back-to-back wins against Manchester City and Arsenal, the message from the head coach was calm and consistent. 'Nobody is getting carried away,' was Carrick's mantra at the time.

So he was never likely to have a public meltdown at the MKM Stadium on Saturday after Manchester United suffered a shocking defeat at Hull City, losing to a newly-promoted team on the opening weekend for the first time in the club's history.

As bad as the result and United's performance were, Carrick's approach remained the same as it was seven months ago. Calm down, it's just one game.

He is right, of course, but Carrick has also been around United long enough to know that you are only ever one game from a crisis.

Lose to Ipswich in United's first home game of the season on Sunday, and Carrick's softly softly approach will be drowned out by the alarm bells ringing around Old Trafford.

The 45-year-old's placid exterior has always masked his real emotions, first as a player and now as a coach. At United, his calm demeanour and measured approach have been a welcome antidote to the emotional incontinence and public self-flagellation of his emotional predecessor Ruben Amorim.

Michael Carrick exuded calmness despite seeing Manchester United lose 2-0 at Hull City

The 45-year-old hides his emotions a lot better than his United predecessor Ruben Amorim

Nobody who knows Carrick would doubt the competitive edge and hunger to win that was seared into the heart of all Sir Alex Ferguson's teams - and which he must imbue into the squad that surrendered so tamely on Humberside.

The players certainly got the message after Carrick suffered his first defeat in charge at Newcastle in March, but the manner of their capitulation to Hull has raised fresh concerns over the ability of this group to build on what he achieved in the second half of last season after replacing Amorim.

Managers react differently to defeat. Erik ten Hag took his players on a 13.8km run the day after United lost their first away game of the season 4-0 at Brentford in 2022 to make up for the overall distance they had lagged behind their opponents - a result just as shocking as this defeat at Hull. Amorim damaged a TV during a dressing-room rant after his team lost at home to Brighton in January last year.

The challenge for Carrick this week is to strike the right balance. He is the last man to press the panic button - certainly after one game - but he also has to make it abundantly clear to the players and supporters that Manchester United losing to Hull City is not acceptable.

At the MKM Stadium, he was asked if the cool-headed approach that has served him so well thus far might actually be viewed negatively by fans expecting a few choice words from their head coach.

'I know there's a lot goes on outside of our football club, yeah,' Carrick said with a smile. 'I understand. I understand the responsibility I've got, but it doesn't make me do things differently just because of that.

'I'm talking to you quite calmly, but I'm not exactly calm inside and enjoying the day, you know? So there's a big difference. I played here for a long time. You don't get to play here for a long time without just going day by day, the results, the ups and downs, but you just carry on as normal. It's 100 per cent not that, trust me.

'It just doesn't mean that we all have to shout and scream and create some chaos just because of it. Inside we're hurting. The boys know, and we need to get better. But the calmness doesn't mean that there's no emotion in it, for sure.

'It's not a nice feeling at all. It doesn't mean it's going to change the direction of how we're going as a team or as a football club. It's one game and results can happen in football, we all understand that. It's not nice when they do, but it does happen. We can be better, and we will be better.'

Reflecting post-match, Carrick insisted that his side know they have to be better after losing

Youri Tielemans was worryingly ineffective in midfield for Manchester United on his debut

United couldn't be much worse, in fairness, but at least Carrick will have a stronger squad available against Ipswich.

Carlos Baleba won't be available once his £70million move from Brighton goes through due to an ankle injury, but Kobbie Mainoo will have benefitted from another appearance off the bench at Hull, and Mason Mount could be fit again after impressing in pre-season until he was injured in the friendly against Paris Saint-Germain.

The two midfielders United have already bought for a total of £85m so far this summer, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, were worryingly ineffective at Hull.

The minor nature of the injury Amad Diallo suffered in training late last week suggests he could return on the right flank, potentially releasing Bryan Mbeumo to play through the middle again after Matheus Cunha struggled there on Saturday. Benjamin Sesko is another option after making his first appearance of the summer off the bench due to a shin problem.

Lisandro Martinez and Diogo Dalot could also return to the line-up after another week of training following their late return from the World Cup, in place of Ayden Heaven - who struggled against Hull's combative striker Oli McBurnie - and Noussair Mazraoui.

Carrick has no shortage of options. He just has to get the balance right on and off the pitch.

Sports.title: Alexander Isak's Newcastle return was full of vitriol and vicious noise - the £125m man looked paralysed by pressure in performance that will not have endeared him to ambivalent Liverpool fans, writes CRAIG HOPE
Sports.content:
Four, four-letter words. Love. Hate. King. Isak.

Just when we thought the most emotionally-charged collective of the afternoon would be the minute's applause for Kevin Keegan, Alexander Isak stepped from the line of red jerseys to take kick-off.

How foolish of the visitors. How naive to play so willingly into the hands - and mouths - of their hosts. As if they needed any extra encouragement. They had already hissed their hatred when Isak left the team bus. This time, he could not hide behind his AirPods.

From Keegan to Isak, The Messiah to The Pariah, this was a different noise entirely. Hostile does not come close. This was vicious. This was vitriol. The Toon Army had waited a year to take aim at their former striker and, when the moment came, they did not miss. It set the tone for what followed.

The home crowd had to wait only four minutes more for Isak's first touch to go wrong. Sixty seconds later and, for Newcastle at least, everything felt so right. The breakaway goal was the sort that used to involve Isak - fast, direct and ruthless.

How fitting, then, that it was a Swede who scored. Anthony Elanga was bought last summer to play with his compatriot, before he defected to Merseyside. Unlike Keegan, Isak is not loved by both sets of supporters. In fact, you wonder if Liverpool's are even that keen. His performance here would have done nothing to endear him. It said everything that those in black and white loved it, as Keegan might say.

Alexander Isak endured a difficult afternoon on his first return to Newcastle since leaving

His long-awaited return to St James' Park saw him greeted by a vitriolic and vicious reception

Indeed, there were two moments to rival Newcastle's goals for noise, and they both, to little surprise, involved Isak. First, after a challenge by Lewis Hall to leave the Premier League's most expensive player clutching his ankle, new Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle, standing only yards away, threw his arms in the air. Not in protest at Isak staying down, but in invitation of a little more Geordie scorn for this fallen foe. They duly obliged. Isak did not like it and was quickly on his feet to let the German know. Not that he cared.

Jaissle, you suspect, will care for little beyond that which affects him and his team. For 95 minutes, he got the better of fellow managerial debutant Andoni Iraola on the pitch, and when it came to animation and aggression, the touchline too. His cajoling, his snarl and disregard for the boundaries of his technical area will quickly win him friends on Tyneside. Mocking their enemy with not hurt, either. That brings us to the second explosion of noise.

At 2-1 in the 69th minute, Isak was presented with his first big chance. It would prove to be his last. Those in the low rows of the Leazes End were ready to bury their heads in their hands - Isak had a clear sight at goal from 14 yards - only to use those same palms as a form of protection. Isak's shot flew hopelessly into the stands.

As the clock then ticked beyond the last of five added minutes, it felt like Isak's miss would be Liverpool's last inglorious act in front of goal. When they then won a penalty, you wondered whether he would take it. You wondered, too, whether his own fans would have wanted him to - the odds on redemption felt considerably longer than those on ridicule. Dominik Szoboszlai was a wiser choice and, with his blast, the points were shared.

Maybe that is what Keegan would have wanted, albeit without the reminder of a stoppage-time goal from Liverpool. The sight of him slouched behind the Anfield advertising hoarding in 1996, following Stan Collymore's 92nd-minute winner in the 4-3 classic, will forever capture the ecstasy and agony of Keegan and his great Entertainers side, who were all present here.

Newcastle fared better in terms of result this time, but the hurt was just the same. They had deserved to win. They had done what teams are told to avoid - they had played the occasion. They played it with, at times, some beauty. But more so, a brutal intensity that suggests they will not be feeling sorry for themselves on the back of a turbulent summer.

The challenge, of course, is to replicate that when the likes of Bournemouth and Hull City come to St James' Park in the coming weeks. There will be no occasion to play then, no former hero to vilify or emotional current to ride. The emphasis will be on breaking teams down as opposed to running them over.

Still, Newcastle's supporters would have left this opener more enthused than Liverpool's. The Reds were unconvincing and Isak was not alone in appearing paralysed by pressure. The man who now wears his old No 9, Yoane Wissa, was the game's best player, save for the miss that would have made it 3-1 four minutes from time.

Newcastle fans paid homage to Kevin Keegan before the match following his recent death

Before the match, Newcastle supporters unfurled a Keegan quote about dreaming big

Before the game, a Keegan quote was unfurled across the Gallowgate End. 'I want people to dream about their football club. They should. We should all be dreamers at heart. Some people are the opposite and say, "we can't do that". But when you ask them why they can't give a reason. Well, I say, "why not?".'

Until the very last kick, at least, this was the dream the Geordies had imagined - and the nightmare they had wished upon Isak. Then came the equaliser. Four, four-letter words had framed the afternoon. Four goals settled it.

And, for Newcastle, there was one more. Pain.

Sports.title: Lewis Hamilton's sarcastic Dutch GP radio remarks addressed by Ferrari boss
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton's sarcastic Dutch GP radio remarks addressed by Ferrari boss

Lewis Hamilton was left frustrated during the Dutch Grand Prix and made his feelings clear over the radio, with Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur now addressing the situation

View 2 Images Lewis Hamilton was not happy with his Ferrari team (Image: Getty Images)

Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur has played down Lewis Hamilton's frustrated radio outbursts during the Dutch Grand Prix. The seven-time former world champion narrowly missed out on a podium at Zandvoort on Sunday, eventually crossing the line in fourth place.

‌



Boasting a four-lap tyre advantage over Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc, Hamilton was significantly faster than the Monegasque driver on Lap 42 and urged his team to allow him past for what was then second place. Leclerc was in no rush to comply, however, leaving Hamilton visibly irritated and unable to conceal his frustration over team radio.

‌



The Brit sarcastically said: "Great way of wasting time guys, good job."

‌



Yet to pit for fresh rubber, Hamilton had been leading the race while eventual winner Lando Norris and Kimi Antonelli were closing in rapidly behind him, prompting the 49-year-old to question the team's strategy.

He said: "Are you using me as a guinea pig or what? What's going on? How long will you have me stay out?"

Vasseur has now addressed Hamilton's radio messages in comments made to GPblog.

‌



View 2 Images Fred Vasseur is not concerned by Hamilton's comments (Image: Getty)

The 58-year-old said: "We didn't want to tell him the strategy at this stage because we didn't want to disclose it to the competitors.

"Because we wanted to keep him on track until the end but he was able to keep Antonelli behind him and I think it would have been the right call."

‌



Addressing the earlier drama with Leclerc, he added: "Charles was supposed to pit, we extended one lap and it was a kind of confusion but I'm not worried about this. Everybody will be back in the briefing, they will have a clear picture about the race."
