World.title: JAMB Unveils O’Level Upload Online, Ends CBT Centre Visits
World.content:
* Candidates can now verify, upload results from home



Kuni Tyessi in Abuja

The Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) has introduced an online system allowing candidates seeking admission into Nigerian tertiary institutions through the 2026 Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME), to verify and upload their O’Level results from home.

The new service, which initially covers results issued by the West African Examinations Council (WAEC), is expected to reduce candidates’ dependence on Computer-Based Test (CBT) centres for O’Level result uploads, particularly during periods of high patronage.

Under the arrangement, JAMB will electronically verify candidates’ results directly with the relevant examination bodies before the results are uploaded to their profiles.

The board, in a statement on Monday by its Acting Director, Public Affairs and Protocol, Dr Fabian Benjamin, said the initiative was designed to make its services easier, faster, safer and more convenient while eliminating challenges associated with the traditional manual upload process.

According to JAMB, the system will also address cases involving misplaced or mixed-up paper certificates, submission of unverified or fraudulent results, as well as errors in the manual entry of subjects and grades.

With the integration of JAMB’s e-Facility platform with examination bodies, candidates’ results can now be checked against records held by the issuing bodies before being downloaded into their JAMB profiles.

The board said the innovation formed part of its renewed customer-focused service delivery agenda under its sixth Registrar, Prof. Segun Aina, with technology being deployed to reduce unnecessary physical visits, queues and paperwork.

How to verify, upload results

JAMB explained that candidates would first be required to obtain a result verification code by visiting the designated result verification portal.

Candidates with two O’Level sittings are required to log into their JAMB e-Facility dashboard and select ‘2026 UTME O’Level Upload’.

After entering the verification code, the two verified results will be displayed, enabling candidates to select the required subjects.

The board said candidates must select a minimum of five and a maximum of nine subjects, with no subject selected more than once, before clicking ‘Apply the O’Level Results’.

A notification will be sent to candidates upon the successful completion of the upload.

JAMB said the new verification service would provide a particularly useful alternative during periods when CBT centres experience heavy patronage, long queues or network-related difficulties.

The board said it would continue to strengthen collaboration with examination bodies and other government agencies while deploying technology to simplify its processes and improve the overall candidate experience.

It said the development underscored its determination to place candidate convenience and efficient service delivery at the heart of its operations.

The latest innovation marks another step in JAMB’s digital transformation, moving a process that previously required physical intervention towards a technology-driven system that allows candidates to complete critical admission-related processes remotely.

World.title: Eid ul Mawlid: IPCR Calls on Nigerians to Reject Hate Speech, Embrace Dialogue
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The Institute for Peace and Conflict Resolution (IPCR) has urged Nigerians to reject hate speech, inflammatory rhetoric and violence, calling instead for dialogue, tolerance and mutual understanding as Muslims across the country celebrate this year’s Eid ul Mawlid.

The institute said the commemoration of the birth of the Holy Prophet Muhammad provides an opportunity for Nigerians to reflect on his teachings and exemplary life, particularly his emphasis on compassion, justice, forgiveness, peaceful coexistence and respect for human dignity.

In a statement issued on Monday, the Director General of IPCR, Dr. Joseph Ochogwu, urged Muslims and Nigerians of all faiths to use the occasion to strengthen national unity and promote peaceful relationships within families, communities and the wider society.

According to the institute, Nigeria’s religious, ethnic and political diversity should be regarded as a source of strength rather than a basis for division, stressing that differences in identity must not become triggers for violence.

IPCR specifically called on religious leaders to use their platforms to promote peace, tolerance and responsible citizenship, particularly against the backdrop of the social, economic and security challenges confronting communities across the country.

It also charged political, traditional and community leaders to demonstrate responsible leadership by discouraging inflammatory statements, hate speech and other actions capable of deepening divisions or escalating tensions among citizens.

The peace institute further urged Nigerians to make dialogue the preferred means of resolving disagreements, warning that sustainable peace could not be achieved through confrontation, violence or the exclusion of others.

IPCR said the values associated with Eid should extend beyond the celebration, urging Nigerians to demonstrate compassion towards vulnerable members of society, support those in need and engage in acts capable of strengthening social cohesion.

Peace should, according to the institute, become a shared responsibility among citizens, with Nigerians drawing inspiration from the life of Prophet Muhammad to promote justice, kindness, patience, forgiveness and respect for others.

The institute congratulated Muslims on the occasion and called on all Nigerians to work collectively towards building a united and inclusive society where every citizen can live with dignity, security and hope for a better future.

World.title: Oil Theft: Navy Arrests Three Suspects, Impounds Vehicles in Imo
World.content:
Sylvester Idowu in Warri

Operatives of the Nigerian Navy Oguta have arrested three suspected oil thieves and impounded two vehicles allegedly used for economic sabotage in Imo State.

The suspects and their vehicles were intercepted and arrested last Friday at Ejemekuru-Obudi-Agwa road in conjunction with the Nigerian Army personnel from 342 Artillery Brigade while on routine patrol.

THISDAY gathered that the combined security operatives, while on routine patrol intercepted a tipper truck with registration BLF 217 XA and a Toyota Hiace bus with registration EHM 36 XA Imo, transporting bags containing approximately 8500 litres of illegally refined petroleum products suspected to have been sources from illegal refineries.

Consequently, three suspects identified as Okolo Somtochukwu aged 30 years, Chimezie Emeodi aged 39 years and Uche Onyedikachi aged 25 years, all from Imo State, running the tipper truck, were apprehended.

It was further gathered that the driver and occupant of the Toyota Hiace bus however escaped into the bush while a manhunt has been launched to apprehend them by the naval operatives.

Commander, Naval Base Oguta, Commodore Sabo Tanko Lengaya, while commending the personnel, said the operation was consistent with the Nigerian Navy’s objectives for internal security aimed at denying criminal elements freedom of action in Imo State.

“This operations represent a significant success in the ongoing efforts by Naval Base Oguta to combat crude oil theft and other acts of economic sabotage targeted at critical national assets in furtherance of the Nigerian Navy’s strategic mandate within its area of operations,” he said.

Commodore Lengaya noted that the timely interception of the suspects and recovery of the suspected illegally refined petroleum product has denied the criminal syndicate the opportunity to further their illegal activities and it is expected to provide valuable intelligence for follow-on operations against other members of the network.

World.title: 2027: As Tinubu Constitutes Campaign Council, Banks on Mbah in S’East…
World.content:
That President Bola Tinubu of the ruling All Progressives Congress constituted his Campaign Council at the weekend ahead of the January, 2027 poll, appears good on paper, but the taste of the pudding will be in the eating, writes Deji Elumoye.

The lifting of ban on presidential campaign by the Independent National Electoral Commission effective August 19, 2026 set the stage for the 2027 presidential contest. Various political parties and their presidential candidates are beginning to put their houses in order.

Although the opposition appears fragmented, especially with the collapse of the much-expected coalition under the platform of African Democratic Congress (ADC), President Bola Tinubu, has left no one in doubt that he is not under any delusion that the 2027 election contest would be a walk in the park. After all, one of the agelong cardinal rules of politics is not to underestimate your opponent.

It was not surprising, therefore, that he went all out in constituting a 233-member All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council. The number and calibre of personalities empaneled clearly show a determination to successfully navigate the presidential election challenge and its numerous landmines. To underscore his understanding of the task before the party, Tinubu named himself at the helm of his reelection bid as the Chairman of the Campaign Council (PCC).

He will work with a body of advisers namely pioneer national Chairman of the APC, Chief Bisi Akande; former Ogun state Governor, Chief Segun Osoba; ex-Imo State Governor, Senator Rochas Okorocha; former national Chairmen of APC, Senator Abdullahi Adamu, and Mai Mala Buni and former presidential aide, Senator Florence Ita-Giwa.

According to a statement released by presidential spokesman, Bayo Onanuga, on Saturday, the PCC also has the Vice President Kashim, Kashim Shettima and the APC National Chairman, Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, as Vice Chairman I and Vice Chairman II, respectively, while Governor of Imo State, Senator Hope Uzodimma is to serve as the Secretary. APC National Secretary, Senator Ajibola Bashiru and Special Adviser to the President, Hadiza Bala-Usman, will serve as deputy Asistant Secretaries.

Also, former Governor of Zamfara State and incumbent Senator, Yari Abdullaziz, will serve as the Director-General of the PCC, President of the Senate, Senator Godswill Akpabio; House Speaker, Hon. Tajudeen Abbas; and Governor of Yobe State, Mai Mala Buni, were appointed Deputy Director-Generals each in the South and North zones. They are to work with Senator Bamidele Opeyemi and Senator Jibril Barau in the South and North, respectively.

Governor of Enugu State, Dr. Peter Mbah, was appointed as Zonal Coordinator for South East, Governor Bassey Out of Cross River, and Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu of Lagos were named the Coordinators for South South and South West Zones, respectively. Other Zonal Campaign Coordinators are Governor Umar Bago of Niger (North Central), Senator Ali Modu Sheriff (North East) and Governor Ubah Sani (North West).

Former National Chairman of the APC, Senator Adams Oshiomhole will serve as Deputy Director-General in charge of Mobilisation, while the President’s Chief of Staff, Hon. Femi Gbajabiamila, will serve as Deputy Director-General, Administration.

A ranking member of the National Assembly, Hon James Abiodun Faleke, who played a pivotal role in the 2022/2023 campaign, has returned as Deputy Director-General for Election Planning, Coordination and Monitoring, working with Senator Olushola Adeyeye in the South West, Dr Ngozi Olejeme in the South South, Senator Uche Ekwunife in the South East, Muntaqha Rabe in the North West, Ahmed Muhammed Ketso in the North Central, and Senator Sani Danladi in the North East.

Muiz Adeyemi Banire will lead the legal directorate as director, with Dr Liman Hassan and Babatunde Ogala as deputies. Other members are Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Prince Lateef Fagbemi, former governor Ibrahim Shema, Worgu Boms and Dr Kingsley Tochukwu Udeh.

Tinubu has charged Members of the Council to work tirelessly to overcome those, who want to take Nigeria backwards and ensure victory for the APC in the January 16, 2027 polls.

“We have delivered on our campaign promises and set our country on a path of economic progress. We are definitely out of the dark tunnel and are now at the cusp of reaping the benefits of a prosperous economy that will benefit all Nigerians.

“As we march into the campaign season, we have many achievements to trumpet—let us confidently showcase our record and inspire hope in every corner of our nation. Let us soundly defeat all those forces who plan to take our country backwards,” he charged the team.

Meanwhile, Mbah’s appointment as the Coordinator for APC’s PCC in South East has underhandly caught the attention of political observers and analysts. And the reasons are not far-fetched.

The APC has serially recorded its worst presidential results in the South since first outing in 2015. While ex-President Goodluck Jonathan of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) got 2,464,906 votes (about 92.5 per cent), the eventual winner, former President Muhammadu Buhari of the APC garnered 198,248 votes (about 7.5 per cent) of the votes cast in the region in the 2015 presidential election. In 2019, APC’s Buhari polled 403,968 votes whereas the PDP’s Alhaji Atiku Abubakar got 1,693,485.

APC recorded its worst results in the region in 2023. Entangled in internal squabbles by principal actors, plus the Mr. Peter Obi wave fueled by the perceived denial of PDP’s ticket, the Labour Party garnered 89.42 per cent of South East votes, while Tinubu struggled with 127,605 votes (5.83 per cent). Enugu State contributed only 4,772 votes to Tinubu, the least nationally.

South East sentiments towards APC was not equally helped by what they saw as Buhari’s scorched mistreatment of the region as par his ontroversial “95 per cent and 5 per cent” statement. For instance, for Buhari’s eight years, the South East was not considered fit for the headship of any security or paramilitary agency.

For these and more reasons, Tinubu needed someone that could turn around the fortunes of the party in the region. Although Mbah joined the APC in October 2025, less than a year ago, he has obviously earned Tinubu’s trust and appears to have learned the art of APC’s internal politics quite fast. This fact is underscored by the emergence of his preferred candidates as members of the Zonal Executive Committee at the South East APC congress as well as during the national convention in Abuja, which notably produced Dr. Ben Nwoye as the Deputy National Chairman (South).

There has since been a steady effort to build peace among party leaders and buoy up public goodwill towards the APC.

The President must also have considered good governance quotient, as Mbah resonates among Nigerians as one of the revelations in the current dispensation, thus a poster boy for the party both in the South East and nationally.

Only recently, Enugu was named the fastest-improving state in the Philips Consults 2026 State Performance Index, that measured governance, performance, and development across the states of Nigeria. It is measured based on five indicators: citizen satisfaction, debt sustainability, revenue growth, fiscal transparency, and internally-generated revenue relative to federal allocations.

And according to the report, Enugu State’s emergence as the fastest-improving state reflects deliberate governance, strong fiscal discipline and sustained implementation of reforms.

Indeed, Enugu State, under Mbah’s leadership, has witnessed deliberate reforms and investment in education, security, health, transport, housing, agriculture, road infrastructure, among others – a fact attested to by the President himself when the governor led a delegation of who-is-who in Enugu State to pay him a thank you visit at the State House in Abuja in April, 2026.

“The future of this country rests on people like you with the commitment, great vision, and seriousness that you have embarked upon since you assumed the office.

“You have been a transformative leader, and we genuinely appreciate what is evolving in Enugu today in a manner that we have witnessed a rapid development of the state,” the President had said.

With the PCC constituted, the taste of the pudding will now rest in the eating. Will the PCC deliver Tinubu’s second term? Can Mbah and other South East APC leaders turn around the party’s fortunes in the region come 2027? Only January, 2027 poll can tell.

World.title: TETFund: Lighting Up Nigeria, Projecting a Culture of Excellence Across Africa and the World
World.content:
By Eniola Olakunri

“Nigeria must begin to reflect excellence, discipline, and integrity in all aspects of national life….the era of dilapidated public facilities must give way to infrastructure that mirrors the dignity of the Nigerian people.”

— Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, President and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, Federal Republic of Nigeria

It is no gainsaying that the Tertiary Education Trust Fund (TETFund) is kinetically transforming Nigeria’s public tertiary education landscape and contributing significantly to the enormous national machinery being deployed to accelerate the country’s socio-economic development.

Indeed, TETFund’s evolving story is increasingly becoming one of vision, intervention, innovation and excellence – an institutional success story that is beginning to resonate well beyond Nigeria’s borders.

There is an instructive lesson from the remarkable transformation of Dubai.

In his book, My Vision: Challenges in the Race for Excellence, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Ruler of Dubai and Prime Minister and Vice President of the United Arab Emirates, observed that at a certain stage in Dubai’s development, the emirate essentially stopped competing with others and began competing with itself.

That mindset was pivotal.

Having moved ahead of many of its regional peers, Dubai’s challenge was no longer simply to catch up with anyone else, but to continuously surpass its own achievements. Its remarkable transformation subsequently became a source of inspiration for other countries in the region.

The ripple effect is evident across the Middle East. Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman, among others, have unveiled ambitious development visions designed to diversify their economies, invest in human capital, accelerate innovation and reduce dependence on traditional sources of revenue.

Saudi Arabia’s futuristic NEOM project, Qatar’s aggressive investment strategy, Bahrain’s Vision 2030, Kuwait’s Vision 2035 and Oman’s Vision 2040 all speak to a region increasingly determined to compete not merely with others, but with the limitations of its own past.

Therein lies an important lesson for Nigeria – and, indeed, for TETFund.

TETFund, established by Nigerian law to provide intervention and support for the development of tertiary education, appears to have entered a phase where it is not merely fulfilling its statutory mandate but increasingly competing with its own records of achievement.

The Gambian Minister of Higher Education, Research, Science and Technology, Hon. Prof. Pierre Gomez, fourth from right and TETFund’s Executive Secretary, Arc. Sonny S.T. Echono (fourth from left), in a group photograph with their respective teams during the visit.

The Fund is progressively raising the bar on what is possible in Nigeria’s public tertiary institutions, intervening in infrastructure, research, innovation, academic staff development, teaching and learning facilities and other areas critical to restoring and sustaining standards.

Its reach extends beyond conventional universities, polytechnics and colleges of education and include top-tier educational institutions operated by the nation’s security agencies – the Army, Navy, Air Force and Police.

The significance of this should not be underestimated.

For decades, the conversation around public education in Nigeria was dominated by the challenges of decaying infrastructure, inadequate facilities, insufficient research capacity and the persistent erosion of standards.

TETFund has emerged as one of the principal instruments through which government is confronting these challenges.

More importantly, however, Nigeria may now be exporting an education intervention model that other African countries consider worthy of emulation.

From Nigeria to The Gambia and Beyond

A compelling indication of this emerging influence came recently when The Gambia announced its intention to understudy the TETFund model.

The Gambian Minister of Higher Education, Research, Science and Technology, Hon. Prof. Pierre Gomez, led a high-powered delegation to TETFund’s headquarters in Maitama, Abuja, where they were received by the management team led by the Executive Secretary, Arc. (Dr.) Sonny S.T. Echono.

Prof. Gomez disclosed that The Gambia had established its own Tertiary and Higher Education Trust Fund (THET), modelled substantially on Nigeria’s TETFund experience.

The delegation therefore sought TETFund’s cooperation and support in opening its institutional doors and sharing its experience with officials of THET, who are expected to undertake a study tour of the Fund’s operations.

According to the Gambian delegation, the country had consistently followed TETFund’s activities through its website, social media platforms and other communication channels and had become convinced that establishing a similar intervention mechanism would provide an added fillip to the Gambian government’s efforts to transform its tertiary education sector.

The proposed collaboration is expected to encompass areas such as research and capacity development and, importantly, strengthen the already existing diplomatic relationship between Nigeria and The Gambia.

That is a significant endorsement.

It means that an institution created primarily to address Nigeria’s own tertiary education challenges is now attracting attention as a reference point for education-sector intervention elsewhere in Africa.

And The Gambia is not alone.

Tanzania’s Education Authority (TEA), Ghana’s Education Trust Fund (GETFund) and Sierra Leone’s Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) are among institutions whose mandates and activities reflect similar efforts to strengthen tertiary education through structured intervention and funding mechanisms.

Nigeria, through TETFund, is therefore increasingly participating in a broader African conversation about how to sustainably finance, modernise and reposition higher education for the demands of the 21st century.

From Infrastructure to Innovation

TETFund’s mandate is broad and consequential.

It encompasses essential physical infrastructure for teaching and learning, instructional materials and equipment, research and publication, academic staff training and development, as well as other areas considered critical to improving and maintaining standards in higher education.

Over the years, the Fund has continued to deepen its intervention across Nigerian tertiary institutions.

And the next frontier appears increasingly to be research, innovation and the commercialisation of knowledge.

In a bold move to unlock Nigeria’s vast human and natural resources, stimulate innovation and accelerate socio-economic transformation, TETFund recently approved N7.5 billion for 174 cutting-edge research projects under the 2025 National Research Fund (NRF) Grant Cycle.

That intervention represents more than a financial commitment.

It is a recognition that Nigeria cannot educate its way into prosperity merely by producing graduates. The country must also produce ideas, technologies, intellectual property, solutions and enterprises capable of solving its most pressing developmental challenges.

The Fund’s support for research into vaccines for diseases such as COVID-19 and Lassa fever further demonstrates the potential of tertiary institutions to become engines of national problem-solving rather than simply centres for the transmission of knowledge.

Similarly, the provision of substantial innovation funding to university students signals a shift from the traditional model in which students are expected merely to graduate and search for employment.

The emerging model is one in which young Nigerians can be encouraged and supported to become creators, innovators, employers and entrepreneurs – even before leaving university.

That is precisely the kind of thinking required to build a knowledge economy.

The National Research Fair

TETFund’s planned second National Research Fair, expected in November, provides another important platform for this emerging ecosystem.

The Fair offers an opportunity to identify, showcase and support innovative ideas from across the country, regardless of the social or economic background of their originators, provided they successfully navigate the established expert evaluation process.

Such platforms matter because many potentially transformative Nigerian ideas never progress beyond laboratories, lecture rooms, notebooks and prototypes.

The challenge is to create pathways through which research can move from idea to prototype, prototype to product, and product to enterprise.

A properly structured research and innovation ecosystem can strengthen Nigeria’s knowledge economy, improve industrial competitiveness, create employment and provide practical solutions to some of the country’s most urgent developmental problems.

Excellence Has No Finish Line

For the Board and Management of TETFund, excellence appears to have no finish line.

The Fund seems increasingly determined to challenge itself at every turn – to exceed previous accomplishments, close the door against institutional complacency and demonstrate that what was once considered impossible can become achievable through vision, discipline, resources and purposeful execution.

Its ultimate ambition should therefore be viewed beyond the immediate construction of buildings or provision of equipment.

The bigger opportunity is to help transform Nigeria into a global powerhouse in knowledge, research, innovation, science, technology and human capital development.

And there is a sense of urgency about this.

Nigeria cannot afford to wait indefinitely.

The country possesses an enormous reservoir of youthful talent, intellectual capacity, natural resources and entrepreneurial energy. What is required is the institutional architecture to convert these assets into sustainable national prosperity.

TETFund is one of the institutions positioned to play a defining role in that transformation.

Its growing impact is therefore not simply about the number of projects commissioned, buildings constructed, researchers supported or institutions reached.

It is ultimately about changing the possibilities available to the Nigerian student, researcher, academic and innovator.

Nigeria’s Opportunity to Lead

TETFund may well have started as an intervention agency designed to rescue Nigeria’s tertiary institutions from years of infrastructural and developmental neglect.

But the trajectory today suggests something considerably bigger.

The Fund is increasingly demonstrating that a Nigerian public institution can build systems, break its own records, institutionalise excellence and become a reference point for others.

The emerging interest from African countries is particularly instructive.

If The Gambia is looking towards Nigeria for lessons; if other African education institutions are studying similar intervention models; and if Nigeria is beginning to export not just people and culture but also institutional solutions, then TETFund has entered a new phase of relevance.

This is perhaps one of the most compelling dimensions of the Fund’s evolution.

Nigeria has for too long been accustomed to importing models, ideas and institutional frameworks from abroad.

There is absolutely nothing wrong with learning from successful countries.

But there comes a point when a nation must also begin to develop solutions worthy of emulation by others.

TETFund appears to be approaching that point.

With the support of its Board of Trustees under the leadership of the Right Honourable Aminu Bello Masari and the focused management team led by Arc. (Dr.) Sonny S.T. Echono, the Fund has an opportunity to deepen this trajectory and establish itself not merely as Nigeria’s foremost tertiary education intervention agency, but as an African reference institution in education financing, research intervention and human-capital development.

The challenge now is to sustain the momentum, institutionalise the gains and ensure that excellence becomes not an occasional achievement but a permanent culture.

For TETFund, the race is no longer simply to catch up.

The race is to continuously outdo itself.

And if it succeeds in doing so, Nigeria will not merely be lighting up its tertiary education system.

It will be lighting up Africa – and projecting a distinctly Nigerian culture of excellence to the world.

*Eniola Olakunri , Public Sector Analyst and CEO, Write Affairs, writes from Abuja.

World.title: DSS, Other Security Forces Neutralise Two Suspected Kidnappers, Rescue Abducted Man In Imo
World.content:
The Department of State Services (DSS), in collaboration with other security forces and local vigilantes, has rescued a 29-year-old man abducted by suspected kidnappers in Orlu Local Government Area of Imo State.

The victim was abducted last Tuesday around Afor-Ogidi Market in Isiala Amaifeke Community, Orlu LGA, while returning home from the International Market, Umuna, Orlu, according to a security source.

The source said the assailants, who were armed with assault rifles and operating on two motorcycles, blocked the victim’s vehicle, seized him and took him to an undisclosed location.

Following the abduction, the kidnappers contacted the victim’s family and demanded a ransom of N15 million for his release.

However, in the early hours of Thursday, security operatives rescued the victim at Ihioma Community, Orlu LGA, during a coordinated intelligence-led operation involving the DSS, other security forces and local vigilantes.

The operation also resulted in the neutralisation of two suspected members of the kidnapping syndicate, while two high-calibre weapons and ammunition were recovered.

The rescued victim was subsequently secured by the security forces and reunited with his family.

The source said the operation was among several efforts demonstrating the sustained collaboration and growing synergy among security agencies to curb criminal activities, dismantle kidnapping networks and prevent the country from becoming a safe haven for perpetrators of violent crime.

World.title: Atiku Doubles Down on Plan to Restore Fuel Subsidy
World.content:
*Says Tinubu took from poor, gave to his rich friends

*Yilwatda: Atiku’s proposal troubling, suspicious*Olawepo-Hashim: Ex-VP is father of subsidy removal, recent U-turn dishonest



*Donald Duke canvasses economic reset, says policies worsening hardship



*Idris: Restoring fuel subsidy will reverse Nigeria’s economic gains

Chuks Okocha, Emmanuel Addeh, Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja and Ayodeji Ake in Lagos

Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar yesterday doubled down on his proposal to restore a targeted petrol subsidy, accusing President Bola Tinubu of running a contradictory economic policy that removes support from poor Nigerians while granting tax credits, concessions and other incentives to major investors in the petroleum industry.



Atiku, through a statement issued by his Senior Special Assistant on Public Communication, Phrank Shaibu, described the federal government’s claim that petrol subsidy had been abolished as one of the biggest economic frauds being sold to Nigerians, arguing that public resources were still being deployed to cushion costs and support investment in the same sector.

The former vice president said the Tinubu administration had transferred the burden of economic adjustment to households, even as it provided fiscal support to major petroleum investors.



“Tinubu stood at Eagle Square and declared that subsidy was gone. Petrol prices exploded, transportation costs soared, food prices followed, businesses buckled and household purchasing power collapsed. Nigerians were told there was no alternative and that enduring this pain was the necessary price of economic reform.



“But when major oil investors knock on Tinubu’s door, the sermon changes. Suddenly, government intervention is good economics; tax credits are necessary; fiscal concessions are strategic; and private investment must be ‘de-risked.’ Apparently, subsidy is only evil when poor Nigerians benefit from it,” he stated.



Atiku questioned the rationale for providing fiscal incentives to petroleum investors while rejecting what he described as targeted intervention to reduce the burden of high energy costs on households.

He specifically cited the government’s Deep Offshore Oil and Gas Projects Incentives framework, under which qualifying petroleum developments can receive production tax credits, arguing that the policy demonstrated that government intervention remained part of the administration’s economic approach.



The former vice president also challenged the administration’s explanation of energy-security expenses recorded by the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC), arguing that the figures showed that public resources continued to absorb petroleum price differentials despite the declaration that subsidy had been removed.



According to Atiku, NNPC’s 2023 accounts recorded approximately N4.84 trillion as energy-security expenses and related shortfalls, while its 2024 audited financial statements recorded about N7.13 trillion under energy-security expenses.

He said NNPC had explained that the expense arose partly from the difference between the exchange rate used to determine the regulated PMS ex-coastal price and the prevailing exchange rate when import obligations were settled.



Atiku maintained that the description of the expenditure as an energy-security expense or shortfall did not alter its economic effect.

“Nigerians do not eat semantics. Whether the government calls it subsidy, under-recovery, shortfall or energy security, public resources were being used to bridge a gap between economic cost and the price at which petrol was sold. You cannot abolish subsidy at the podium and resurrect it in the accounts under an alias,” he said.



The former vice president accused the administration of operating what he described as two economies in one country, with market-driven policies imposed on households while investors received fiscal incentives designed to reduce investment risks.

“The government can protect a multibillion-dollar oil investment from risk, yet it says protecting the Nigerian worker from crushing hardship is bad economics,” Atiku said.



“It can bend policy to make every barrel of crude more profitable, but tells a struggling mother that making the litre of petrol she needs to take her children to school more affordable is irresponsible,” he added.

He argued that the success of economic reform should be measured by its impact on citizens rather than by the removal of a particular policy. “Economic reform is not a competition over how much suffering a President can impose on his citizens. Removing subsidy without adequate buffers while simultaneously providing fiscal cushions to investors in the same petroleum industry is not courage. It is selective economics dressed up as reform,” he argued.

Ex-VP Says He Will Rejig Old Subsidy Regime

Atiku, however, clarified that his proposal did not amount to a return to the previous subsidy regime, which he described as opaque and vulnerable to abuse.

“This is precisely why the Atiku Economic Recovery Plan rejects Tinubu’s false choice between the corrupt subsidy regime of yesterday and the cruel shock therapy of today. Atiku is not proposing a return to an unlimited, opaque and corruption-ridden subsidy racket.



“What he proposes is a targeted, capped, transparently budgeted and independently audited intervention with a clearly defined exit mechanism, accompanied by accelerated domestic refining, competition, mass transportation and measures to restore household purchasing power,” the statement added.

He said the same principle used by the government to reduce investment risks could be applied to households bearing the consequences of high petrol prices.



“If the government can legitimately de-risk investment, why is it economic heresy to de-risk survival?” he asked.

Atiku said he supported foreign investment and performance-based incentives for businesses but opposed what he called unequal treatment between corporate investors and ordinary Nigerians.

He called on the federal government to disclose the beneficiaries and value of major petroleum tax credits, remissions and other incentives, alongside the investments delivered in return.

“These concessions belong to the Nigerian people and must never become instruments of patronage dispensed behind closed doors,” he said.



Atiku said the ultimate test of Tinubu’s economic policies should be whether Nigerians were better off, businesses were becoming more productive, jobs were being created and household incomes could meet basic living costs.

“The Atiku Economic Recovery Plan is founded on a fundamentally different philosophy: markets must work, investment must earn a fair return and public finances must be protected, but the Nigerian citizen must remain the ultimate beneficiary of economic policy,” he said.

Yilwatda: Proposal Troubling, Suspicious

But the National Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, yesterday rejected Atiku’s proposal to reverse the removal of petrol subsidy, describing it as a troubling policy U-turn that raised questions about the opposition’s preparedness to govern Nigeria.

Yilwatda spoke during a visit to the headquarters of the City Boy Movement in Abuja, where he inspected the organisation’s facilities and interacted with its leadership.



In a statement issued by his Special Adviser on Media and Information Strategy, Abimbola Tooki, the APC chairman said Nigerians deserved more than election-season declarations, particularly on a policy with major implications for public finances.

He said any proposal to restore a costly subsidy regime must be subjected to rigorous scrutiny because of the enormous fiscal burden subsidies had placed on public finances and the distortions they had created in the economy.

Yilwatda said the opposition had been challenged repeatedly over the past three years to tell Nigerians what it would do differently if entrusted with power, but that no serious, coherent and convincing alternative had emerged.



He said it was therefore suspicious that, after more than three years without a comprehensive governing agenda, Atiku was presenting a policy about four months before the 2027 general election that could reverse what he described as hard-won economic adjustments.

“Economic policy cannot be reduced to election-season promises. Nigerians deserve to know precisely where the money will come from, what sectors will bear the cost and whether such a policy can be sustained without reopening the fiscal pressures that necessitated reform in the first place,” Yilwatda said.



He maintained that subsidy removal was a difficult but necessary decision, although its consequences required complementary measures to cushion the impact, expand social intervention and strengthen productive sectors.

According to him, the real test of leadership was not the ability to promise immediate relief for electoral advantage, but the courage to take difficult decisions, explain them honestly to citizens and remain committed to policies capable of producing sustainable growth.



Yilwatda warned that reversing the reforms without a credible alternative could undermine investor confidence, worsen fiscal pressures and jeopardise the gains being pursued by the administration.

He urged Nigerians to scrutinise competing economic programmes ahead of the 2027 elections and distinguish between policies designed to address structural problems and promises that could provide short-term political appeal while creating longer-term fiscal difficulties.



The APC chairman also criticised what he described as ideological and organisational inconsistency within the opposition, arguing that politicians who continually move from one political platform to another could not credibly claim to offer the stability and clarity required to govern a complex country.

He said the 2027 election should be a contest of ideas, competence and credible policy alternatives, rather than a competition over who could make the most attractive promises at the last minute.

Olawepo-Hashim: Atiku’s Recent U-turn Dishonest

For his part, the presidential candidate of the Accord Party, Dr. Gbenga Olawepo-Hashim, described Atiku as the “father of subsidy removal” in Nigeria’s Fourth Republic, accusing him of dishonesty for reversing his position without apologising to Nigerians.

Olawepo-Hashim, who has consistently opposed subsidy removal, said in an interview last week that subsidy should be restored on petrol and other strategically important products as part of measures to protect citizens and productive sectors from excessive economic shocks.

He, however, faulted politicians who previously advocated subsidy removal but were now reversing themselves without acknowledging their earlier positions.

“Some candidates who campaigned in the last election to remove subsidy are now reversing themselves without even regretting their earlier display of ignorance and lack of compassion for the people,” he said.

Olawepo-Hashim specifically criticised Atiku for changing his position without accounting for his earlier advocacy.

“Atiku’s recant on subsidy removal without an apology is dishonesty. If you change your position because circumstances or evidence have changed, tell Nigerians why you changed. There is nothing wrong with changing your mind. What is wrong is pretending that you never held the position in the first place,” he said.

According to him, Atiku, Tinubu and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi all campaigned on subsidy removal during the 2023 presidential election, while he, Omoyele Sowore and Prince Adewole Adebayo opposed the policy.

Olawepo-Hashim said Atiku’s position on subsidy removal predated the Tinubu administration, describing the former vice president as one of the earliest major advocates of subsidy removal and wholesale privatisation during the Fourth Republic.

“The truth of the matter is that Atiku, before Tinubu, on the national political scene, has been the father of the idea of subsidy removal and wholesale privatization in this republic, he and his so-called economic team. “We combatted them vigorously during the early period of the Obasanjo government,” he emphasised.

He recalled that in 1999, when Atiku was vice president and headed the economic team under former President Olusegun Obasanjo, the administration increased petroleum product prices and removed subsidy.

Olawepo-Hashim said he and other PDP officials publicly opposed the decision, while the National Assembly also passed resolutions against the policy, forcing the executive to reverse its decision.

“We opposed subsidy removal when it was politically inconvenient to do so. We did not suddenly discover the suffering of Nigerians because another election is approaching,” he said.

Olawepo-Hashim said his proposal was not for a return to an uncontrolled subsidy regime but for a targeted and transparent system that would protect citizens and productive sectors from severe price shocks.

“Our position is simple: restore subsidy on petroleum products and other strategic products where necessary, but do it intelligently. Subsidy should be targeted at protecting the Nigerian economy and Nigerian people, not at enriching intermediaries,” he added.

He proposed that any subsidy regime should be based on targeting, transparency, measurable economic outcomes and strict accountability rather than open-ended payments to importers or politically connected intermediaries.

“Our own government would identify strategic products and sectors where price shocks have economic wide consequences, establish clear eligibility criteria, publish the fiscal cost and beneficiaries, and periodically assess whether the intervention is delivering measurable economic benefits,” he said.

Olawepo-Hashim pointed out that stronger domestic production should also be an essential component of any sustainable subsidy policy.

“The objective would be to use subsidy as a bridge to greater domestic productive capacity, not as a permanent excuse for dependence on imports,” he said.

He added that the 2027 presidential election should be defined by competing ideas and credible economic programmes rather than political imitation.

“Nigeria needs originality, courage and compassion in leadership. We cannot continue recycling people because they have the biggest megaphone. We must begin to ask who said what first, who stood by the people when it was difficult, and who has a credible plan to rebuild the economy.”

Duke to Tinubu: Reset Economy, Policies Worsening Hardship

Also, former Cross River State Governor and presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP), Donald Duke, has called for a fundamental shift in Nigeria’s economic direction, arguing that the country would not benefit from a continuation of the Tinubu administration’s policies.

Duke said Nigeria needed imaginative and strategically designed policies capable of driving sustainable growth, developing its natural resources, harnessing human capital and reducing poverty.

“The Nigerian economy will not benefit from the continuation of the Tinubu administration’s economic policies,” Duke declared.

“The strength of our economy will be reinforced by imaginative, strategically-designed policies that address growth,” he added.

The former governor said Nigerians deserved an administration with policies designed to address growth and alleviate what he described as the current crushing level of poverty.

“Nigerians deserve an administration strategically-designed with policies that address growth and alleviate the current crushing level of poverty,” he said.

Duke urged Nigerians to move beyond what he described as “pandering debates” over the economy, insisting that the country needed informed and growth-oriented policies that would deliver tangible improvements in citizens’ lives.

“The nation must move beyond pandering debates to adopting well-informed and growth-oriented policies,” he said.

He argued that the performance of the economy should not be measured primarily by government revenue or foreign reserves but by indicators that reflected the welfare of citizens.

“The yardstick of measuring the wellbeing of our economy shall not be based on the manipulated volume of our foreign reserves, but rather on employment indices and income per capita,” Duke said.

He was particularly critical of the handling of petrol subsidy, arguing that the arrangement that existed before the Tinubu administration had been replaced by what he described as a poorly managed alternative that benefited government finances while increasing the economic burden on citizens.

“The fuel subsidy scam which preceded the Tinubu administration has been replaced by an even more poorly-managed option which makes more devalued money for the governments, impoverishes its citizens and depletes the economy,” he said.

Duke maintained that Nigeria must move beyond recurring political arguments and subject its economic policies to scrutiny, with greater emphasis on sustainable growth, productive use of natural resources, job creation and higher incomes.

He said the PRP would prioritise the productive use of Nigeria’s natural and human resources as part of its economic approach. “Quality of the livelihood of Nigerians shall remain our goal,” Duke said.

Idris: Restoring Fuel Subsidy Will Reverse Economic Gains

Meanwhile, Information and National Orientation Minister, Mohammed Idris, has warned that any attempt to restore fuel subsidy would reverse the economic gains recorded under the reforms of the Tinubu administration, arguing that the policy would recreate the fiscal pressures and distortions that made the subsidy regime unsustainable.

Idris, in an op-ed yesterday, said the hardship associated with the reforms should not be addressed by dismantling them, but by accelerating the delivery of their benefits to Nigerians through improved public services, job creation, infrastructure and better living standards.

“The above illustrates an important point: restoring subsidy would almost instantly return Nigeria to the economic conditions of 2022, recreating the same fiscal pressures, distortions, scarcity and incentives for arbitrage that made the old system unsustainable in the first place.

“We are not claiming that the reforms have solved all of Nigeria’s economic challenges; there is indeed still much work to be done to translate improved fiscal capacity into better services, jobs, infrastructure and living standards. But the proper response to the hardship associated with reform is not to dismantle the reform; it is to accelerate the benefits – which remains what the Tinubu administration is resolutely focused on.

“The objective is clear: to move public resources away from subsidising consumption and towards investing in the Nigerian people and the productive foundations of lasting prosperity,” he explained.

World.title: Iran Parliament Dares Trump, Approves Strait of Hormuz Fee for Ships
World.content:
*Hardline security chief issues stark warning to Gulf nations

*Pentagon: 774 US casualties recorded in Iran war *America turns on economic pressure

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

Iran’s parliament has moved to strengthen Tehran’s control over shipping through the strategic Strait of Hormuz, approving a provision that would allow the country to charge vessels from countries it authorises to transit the waterway, as the United States prepares to intensify economic pressure on Tehran.



The development came as Iran’s newly appointed Supreme National Security Council secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, issued a stark warning to Gulf countries against joining Washington’s economic campaign, threatening that Tehran would prevent oil from leaving the Persian Gulf if regional states supported the US.



The moves have further raised the stakes in the conflict between Iran and the United States, with shipping through the Strait of Hormuz already severely disrupted and global energy markets exposed to the possibility of prolonged supply constraints.

The Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission approved Article 3 of a proposed law on the security and development of the Strait of Hormuz.



The provision would permit Tehran to collect fees from vessels belonging to countries that Iran authorises to pass through the waterway.

The proposed charges would cover maritime and navigation services, environmental services, fuel supplies under special circumstances, insurance, safety and security services, as well as other services provided to vessels during transit.



Commission spokesperson Hassan Qashqavi said the authorised vessels would be required to pay for the services.

“Based on Article 3, a fee will be charged for services including maritime, environmental, fuelling under special conditions, insurance, safety, and other services provided in the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. The payments could be made in Iranian rials or another currency designated by Tehran.



The measure is contained in a proposed “Strategic Action Plan to Ensure the Security and Development of the Strait of Hormuz,” with Iranian state media reporting that the parliamentary commission approved the provision on Sunday.

However, the proposal must still be considered by the full parliament before being forwarded to the Guardian Council, which reviews legislation for compliance with Iran’s Constitution and Islamic principles.

Where disagreements remain between parliament and the Guardian Council, the Expediency Council could be called upon to resolve them.



Qashqavi maintained that the proposed legislation recognised freedom of navigation under international law while also protecting the sovereignty and security interests of countries bordering the Strait of Hormuz.

He referred to the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and cited Oman’s position on the relationship between international maritime rules and national sovereignty.



“The Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz have their own rules and conditions, and in this regard, after accepting the 1982 Convention on the Law of the Sea, the country of Oman immediately issued a political declaration emphasising that the provisions of this convention should not violate the country’s national sovereignty and national security,” he said.



The proposed fee regime comes at a time when Iran is already exercising greater control over access to the waterway.

Tehran has allowed some vessels to transit the strait while restricting wider commercial movement. It recently granted permission for a number of Iraqi oil tankers to cross Hormuz, underscoring the selective nature of access during the conflict.

Rezaei Threatens Gulf States



As Tehran moved to formalise its control over the waterway, Iran’s security chief, Rezaei, warned Gulf countries against supporting Washington’s economic campaign.

“If the countries surrounding Iran join the Americans in their economic war, not a drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz,” Rezaei said, according to Iran’s Tasnim news agency.



“We will also target other oil export routes from the Persian Gulf,” he added.

The warning came as President Donald Trump’s administration prepared to move the conflict into a new phase centred on economic pressure, sanctions and restrictions on countries and companies continuing to trade with Iran.

Rezaei also criticised Trump’s handling of the conflict, arguing that the US attacks had increased global interest in acquiring nuclear weapons.



“Trump’s recklessness, with his attacks on Iran, has increased the desire of people around the world to acquire nuclear weapons, especially when they saw that membership in the International Atomic Energy Agency and the (Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty) NPT was ineffective in preventing attacks from the United States,” he said.



“Trump has created nuclear insecurity instead of nuclear security,” he added.

Rezaei said Iran had accepted international nuclear safeguards, remained a member of the NPT and complied with inspections.

“Iran is the only country that is ahead of all other countries in its commitment to nuclear regulations,” he said.

Pentagon Records 774 US Casualties

Meanwhile, American military casualties in the war with Iran have risen to 774, including 18 deaths, according to the latest figures from the Pentagon’s casualty reporting system.

The Defense Casualty Analysis System showed that 756 US service members have sustained injuries since the war began on February 28. The figures are now divided into two reporting periods, reflecting the changing diplomatic and military circumstances of the conflict.



The first period, designated Operation Epic Fury, accounts for 14 deaths and 417 wounded personnel.

Seven of the deaths in that category were classified as hostile deaths, including service members killed in action or those who subsequently died from their wounds.

The remaining seven deaths were attributed to accidents or undetermined causes, with the US Air Force and Navy accounting for a significant proportion of the fatalities.

A second category, titled Overseas Operations, records casualties from July 7, following the effective collapse of the memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran and one day before Trump formally declared the ceasefire “over”.

That period has recorded four hostile deaths, all involving US Army personnel, and 341 wounded service members.

The US Army has suffered the highest number of casualties across the two reporting periods, recording 11 deaths and 589 injuries.

US Shifts to Economic War

The casualty figures came as the Trump administration prepared to intensify economic pressure on Tehran after months of direct military confrontation.

The United States is expected to target Iran’s economy and countries that continue to trade with Tehran, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expected to unveil details of the new measures.

The strategy is expected to combine additional sanctions, a naval blockade and pressure on countries buying Iranian commodities, particularly oil.

China, India, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates could face pressure because of their economic relationships with Iran. China is expected to be a particular focus because it remains the main buyer of Iranian oil.

The administration’s objective is to force Tehran to accept an agreement on Washington’s terms without relying exclusively on continued large-scale military operations.

However, analysts have warned that the strategy could produce the opposite result by encouraging Iran to retaliate militarily rather than capitulate.

World.title: Kaizer Chiefs target ‘not worth the fuss’
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs are being tenuously linked with Thembinkosi Lorch. Here’s why he was never worth the fuss, even at age 33.

Lorch is overrated and always has been

Thembinkosi Lorch spent the better part of two years on the treatment table leading up to 2023. In the 2022-23 campaign, he made just 12 appearances in the league, exactly 40% of the Betway Premiership season, and made just 15 league outings in the season before that. Was Lorch ever worth the trouble? Even when fit and available, he couldn’t string consistent performances together, and his direct output of goals and assists wasn’t good either. Chiefs’ links to 33-year-old Lorch seem ill-advised.

Mshini’s Kaizer Chiefs stats are worrying

Meanwhile, Nkosingiphile Ngcobo’s dismal Chiefs stats merit closer observation. The attacking midfielderhasn’t managed more than two goals in a single season since 2020-21. He’s only scored two goals in his last three Betway Premiership seasons combined, and was excluded altogether against Sundowns in a recent 1-1 draw. The writing could be on the wall for Mshini.



When is Chiefs’ next match?

The Glamour Boys are next in action on Wednesday, 26 August, with an away clash against Richards Bay at 19:30. Chiefs are two points behind their tally at this equivalent stage last season, when they won their first three league encounters.

World.title: Springbok team to face All Blacks in Cape Town attended these SCHOOLS
World.content:
Rassie Erasmus has named his Springbok team to face the All Blacks at the Cape Town Stadium on Saturday. The squad attended these schools. Image: Charmaine Visser

Pieter-Steph du Toit is on the verge of joining an elite group of Springboks when South Africa face New Zealand in Cape Town on Saturday, 29 August.

Kick-off is at 17:10.

EXCLUSIVE | The ‘curse’ of the Springbok centurion club



The utility forward is set to earn his 100th Test cap, becoming only the 11th player in Springbok history to reach the milestone.

Meanwhile, prop Ox Nche is also in line to celebrate a major career achievement, with the front-rower set to earn his 50th Test cap at the Cape Town Stadium.

The milestones will add extra significance to a match in which the Springboks are desperate to respond after suffering a record 33-16 defeat to the All Blacks in Johannesburg last Saturday.

Leading South African bookmakers Sportingbet have installed the Springboks as 1.40 favourites to level the four-Test series, while the All Blacks can be backed at 3.00.

The draw after 80 minutes is on offer at 16.50.

In terms of handicap, Sportingbet believe South Africa are 5.5-point favourites.



SURVEY | Rate the referee and TMO: Springboks vs All Blacks

Siya Kolisi could return

Coach Rassie Erasmus has largely retained the team that featured in the opening Test, although there are several changes to the starting XV and replacements.

Siya Kolisi has been bracketed with Paul de Villiers at flank and will need to come through training before being confirmed in the starting line-up.

If cleared, Kolisi will join Du Toit and Jasper Wiese in the loose trio.

Handre Pollard will start at flyhalf alongside Cobus Reinach at scrumhalf, while Ethan Hooker comes into the backline after Cheslin Kolbe suffered a niggle.

Hooker’s inclusion will see Kurt-Lee Arendse switch to the right wing, with Damian Willemse completing the back three.

Du Toit will captain the Springboks on his landmark appearance.

Should Kolisi take his place in the starting XV, South Africa will field their most experienced starting team ever, with a combined 1 012 Test caps.

Deon Fourie returns

The replacements also feature a notable change, with veteran Deon Fourie included at the age of 39.

Fourie will provide front-row cover alongside Gerhard Steenekamp and Thomas du Toit, while Lood de Jager and Cameron Hanekom provide further forward options.

Andre Esterhuizen, Morne van den Berg and Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu complete the bench.

Fourie is the only player in the matchday squad who did not feature in South Africa’s last two Tests against Argentina and New Zealand.

His most recent appearance for the Springboks came in the 2023 Rugby World Cup final.
