World.title: Mundubile petition window closes as courts shut for business
World.content:
The window for losing presidential candidate Brian Mundubile to petition the results of the August 13 general election closes today amid the closure of court premises in Lusaka and several other parts of the country, with police deployed at some of the affected judicial facilities.

The developments have placed particular attention on the Constitutional Court because today marks the final day on which Mundubile can challenge the election of President Hakainde Hichilema. There had been no confirmation by Sunday evening that Mundubile had lodged his petition.

Under Article 105 of the Constitution, a challenge to a presidential election result must be lodged within seven days of the declaration. President Hichilema was declared winner on August 16 with 2,965,326 votes against Mundubile’s 1,856,217, making today the final day available for a petition to be filed.

The Supreme Court premises in Lusaka have been closed today for what has been described as “security reasons”, while reports indicate that the High Court and Constitutional Court premises have also been affected. Police tape has been placed around parts of the court premises, restricting access.

Some Local Courts have equally been closed, with scheduled cases adjourned to later dates. Information circulating around the Judiciary indicates that the affected courts will remain closed until further notice.

The closure has immediately raised questions over how litigants with time-sensitive matters are expected to access the courts, particularly Mundubile, whose constitutional window for challenging the presidential election expires today.

The situation is not confined to Lusaka. High Court premises in Ndola, Chipata and Livingstone have also been reported closed or inaccessible, with police officers deployed at the facilities.

In Chipata, the High Court premises were sealed off by armed police officers, with no one being allowed access. Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer Robertson Mweemba referred questions concerning the closure to the Zambia Police Service spokesperson.

In Livingstone, the High Court premises were also closed, with a heavy police presence guarding the area. Similar scenes were reported at the Ndola High Court, where police officers were deployed around the premises.

The simultaneous restrictions at judicial premises have attracted political attention because they have occurred on the final day available for Mundubile to commence his presidential election challenge.

Former politician Muhabi Lungu said he personally visited the High Court premises in Lusaka and found the gates closed and police tape around the facility.

“The High Court premises are closed. Gates closed and are yellow police like tape, the one we see in the movies that screams ‘Crime Scene, do not pass beyond this point’,” Lungu wrote.

Lungu said he had passed the High Court at about 07:45 hours and later returned to the premises, expressing shock at what he witnessed and the information he subsequently received.

Phoenix FM Zambia also reported that the High Court, Constitutional Court and Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security premises were visibly closed with tight security, pointing out that the development had occurred on August 24, the final day for Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance presidential candidate Mundubile to file his challenge against the August 13 presidential election results.

The closures come at a difficult moment for Mundubile, who contested the election under the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) banner backed by the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance.

Mundubile is reported to have sought protection at United Nations agency premises in Lusaka following security operations after the election. As of Sunday evening, he had not lodged the anticipated presidential petition, according to sources close to the matter.

His position has also become more complicated following developments within his political camp. NRPUP Secretary General Nonde Mubanga announced on Sunday that the party was withdrawing from the Tonse Alliance, saying the party needed to reposition itself around its own long-term objectives.

NRPUP president Ezra Tembo, the party’s legally registered leader and newly elected Member of Parliament for Dag Hammarskjöld, has separately conceded the presidential election outcome and called on Zambians to give President Hichilema and the UPND space to govern.

Resolute Party president Martin Phiri and Tonse Alliance Secretary General Chris Zumani Zimba have also distanced themselves from pursuing a legal challenge. Zimba has warned against continuing with confrontational post-election politics and has instead advocated political dialogue and reconciliation between the competing political camps.

Civil society lawyer Linda Kasonde, who had been exploring a separate citizen-led petition, also said last week that she did not have sufficient evidence to proceed with such a challenge.

Against that background, the closure of court premises today has introduced another dimension to the approaching deadline.

Opposition-linked statements circulating online have accused Chief Justice Mumba Malila, as head of the Judiciary, and Judiciary administrators of deliberately closing the superior courts to prevent Mundubile from filing his petition. Other statements have accused President Hakainde Hichilema of directing the closure.

The Judiciary has cited security reasons for the closure. However, the timing has led to demands for a fuller explanation of what security circumstances necessitated closing the courts on the final day for filing a presidential election petition and what arrangements, if any, have been made for urgent and constitutionally time-bound filings.

Social media commentator Andrew Kazembe raised concerns about the implications for judicial independence, arguing that if courts were closed in circumstances that prevented a lawful election petition from being lodged, serious constitutional questions would arise regardless of which political party or candidate was affected. He called for transparency over who authorised the closures and the reasons behind the decision.

Mwamba Payne Kapema similarly linked the court closures to allegations of election rigging, writing that the developments reinforced her concerns over the handling of the election.

The dispute follows the declaration of President Hichilema as winner of the August 13 presidential election. Final consolidated results from all 226 constituencies gave Hichilema 2,965,326 votes, or 60.49 percent, against Mundubile’s 1,856,217 votes, or 37.87 percent.

Mundubile and sections of the opposition have disputed the fairness of the electoral process and raised allegations concerning vote counting, verification and result management.

Opposition representatives have also alleged that the Electoral Commission of Zambia halted vote counting at a stage when Mundubile was leading, and have linked that interruption to their broader complaints about the final results.

The appropriate forum for determining such allegations would ordinarily be the courts, where claims can be supported by evidence, challenged by respondents and determined under the Constitution.

That is what makes today’s closure particularly consequential. Beyond the political arguments surrounding the election itself, the immediate question is whether Mundubile has practical access to the Constitutional Court registry before the seven-day period expires.

The Wake Up Campaign for a Better Zambia has separately urged Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu not to rush into seeking asylum and instead allow the police to clear them of any allegations through established legal processes.

Government has yet to issue a detailed statement addressing the court closures and their relationship, if any, to today’s petition deadline.

The Judiciary and Zambia Police Service are now expected to clarify the security circumstances behind the closures, which judicial facilities are affected, how long the restrictions will remain in place and, most importantly, whether arrangements have been made to receive urgent filings despite the physical closure of the premises.

For Mundubile, however, the constitutional clock continues to run.

With the petition window expiring today and court premises in Lusaka, Ndola, Chipata and Livingstone closed or under restricted access, attention now turns to whether Mundubile will manage to lodge his presidential election petition before the deadline and whether the Judiciary will explain how access to the Constitutional Court is being maintained on the final day available for the challenge.

World.title: Women volleyball team leaves for Nairobi
World.content:
The Zambia Women’s National Volleyball Team this afternoon left the country for Nairobi, Kenya for the 2026 African Volleyball Confederation, African Women’s Volleyball Nations Championship.

The continental championship will run from , August 23rd to September 5th, 2026, in Nairobi, with Zambia aiming to make a strong impression at the competition.

Zambia Volleyball Association (ZAVA) has stated that the 14-member squad is headed by setters Sally Bwalya and Annie Kalaba, while the middle blockers are Mwelwa Ngosa, Isabel Mudenda, Jane Kamwa and Limpo Mombotwa.

The outside attackers are Alice Nankamba, Naomi Kahalu, Betina Zulu and Beene Matongo.The association said the team also includes opposites Lubasi Nakena and Beatrice Besa, as well as liberos Tendai Zulu and Belia Ngoyi.

And Coach Arnold Simulezi, who will be assisted by Lloyd Mweemba and Monde Akalaluka, has assured that the girls are ready for the championship after seven days of training.

Meanwhile, ZAVA described Zambia’s participation in the continental championship as an important milestone in the continued development and promotion of volleyball in the country.

The association has also recognised the support of the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts, the National Sports Council of Zambia, sponsors, partners, stakeholders and the media in promoting national sport.

World.title: Pule Urges Opposition to Respect Election Outcome
World.content:
Christian Democratic Party President Professor DANIEL PULE has called on all opposition leaders to respect the outcome of the 2026 General Election and move on.

Professor PULE says petitioning the election results could delay national reconciliation, unity, peace and development.

He has further cautioned that, given the current political atmosphere, a petition could risk the lives of innocent citizens and trigger unnecessary disturbances.

Professor PULE says the Christian Democratic Party, having participated in the elections, is confident that Zambians have spoken through the ballot and chosen to retain President HAKAINDE HICHILEMA for a second term.

He has congratulated the President-elect on the victory in the just-concluded General and Presidential Elections.

In a statement released to ZNBC News, Professor PULE said the time has come for Zambians to put the past behind them, unite and focus on rebuilding the country.

He said Zambia needs healing more than ever and has urged political leaders to put national interests above personal interests.

Professor PULE has emphasized that campaigns are now over and all Zambians should focus on building the country, stressing that Zambia is bigger than any individual or political party.

He has reaffirmed the Christian Democratic Party’s commitment to a peaceful, united and prosperous Zambia.

World.title: UPND Urges Commonwealth, EU to Apply Consistent Standards
World.content:
The United Party for National Development -UPND- has called on the Commonwealth and European Union to apply consistent standards when addressing alleged security threats and political violence in Zambia.

UPND Media Director MARK SIMUUWE says international organisations should be careful not to issue statements that may appear to support or ignore terrorism, insurgency or violence.

Mr. SIMUUWE says the same measures applied to such threats in other parts of the world should equally apply to Zambia.

In a statement to the media, Mr. SIMUUWE said the Commonwealth and EU should be concerned by reports of the alleged militarisation of an opposition political party and activities that may threaten national security.

He added that political affiliation should not shield anyone from scrutiny where there are credible allegations of organised violence or unlawful possession of military weapons.

Mr. SIMUUWE said the UPND supports fair investigations and respect for people’s rights, but the law must apply equally to everyone regardless of political affiliation.

He said political parties should not have armed or military groups, and any claims of terrorism, violence or illegal possession of weapons should be properly investigated by the law.

Mr. SIMUUWE has called on the Commonwealth, European Union and other international partners to support Zambia’s democratic institutions while respecting the country’s independence.

World.title: NRPUP Pulls Out of Tonse Alliance
World.content:
The National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity -NRPUP- has, with immediate effect, pulled out of the TONSE Alliance.

NRPUP Secretary General NONDE MUBANGA announced the development at a press briefing this evening.

Mr. MUBANGA said this follows the NRPUP’s careful consideration in collaboration with stakeholders.

He also said the party has objectively made the decision to pull out of the TONSE Alliance owing to the prevailing circumstances in the nation.

Mr. MUBANGA said the party will, in due course, chart the way forward on its political affiliation.

World.title: Buyzed Campaign Founder salutes re-election of President Hichilema
World.content:
BuyZed Campaign Founder, Evans Ngoma, has noted that the re-election of President Hakainde Hichilema as Zambia’s President for the second term, entails his responsibility to further unite the country and deliver development as demonstrated in his previous term.

Speaking during a press briefing in Lundazi District in Eastern Province, Mr Ngoma who also congratulated President Hichilema, called for calm, responsible political conduct and, thorough, professional and impartial investigations into allegations of political violence, and any attempts to undermine Zambia’s democratic process and national security.

Mr Ngoma stated that while serious allegations must not be swept under the carpet, investigations must be guided by evidence, due process and the constitutional principle that every suspect is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

“Let the evidence speak and let the law take its course,” Mr Ngoma said.

He also urged all political leaders and their supporters to desist from using misinformation, disinformation and inflammatory rhetoric that could heighten political tensions and create hostility among Zambians.

And Mr Ngoma charged that being in opposition should never become a licence to deliberately mislead citizens, spread fear, promote hatred or create conditions capable of disturbing national peace.

He further commended National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) President Ezra Tembo for demonstrating statesmanship by accepting the election outcome announced by the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ), congratulating President Hakainde Hichilema and the United Party for National Development (UPND) on their victory.

He says such political maturity is important for Zambia, particularly following a highly competitive election.

Mr Ngoma welcomed Mr Tembo’s call for Zambia to move beyond electioneering and concentrate on economic and social development.

He said once elections are concluded, elected leaders must return to work and serve the people who gave them the mandate.

“Elections must have a beginning and an end. Members of parliament must return to their constituencies and represent the people. Mayors and council chairpersons must lead development in their respective councils, while councillors must serve their wards,” he added.

Mr Ngoma said Zambia needs a strong but responsible opposition that provides constructive checks and balances while supporting policies and programmes that advance the national interest.

He cited the Constituency Development Fund CDF) as an example of a development programme that should be supported when it benefits citizens, regardless of political affiliation.

He says Zambia’s peace is bigger than any political party or individual political ambition.

He therefore urged Zambians across the political divide to remember that political fortunes can change, with one party in government today and another tomorrow, but that the people remain neighbours, relatives, workmates and citizens of the same Republic.

Mr Ngoma further implored political leaders and citizens to put Zambia first, respect constitutional institutions, allow investigations to proceed without interference, and resolve political differences through lawful and democratic means.

World.title: Late Mbala mayor-elect put to rest
World.content:
Mbala Mayor-elect Steward Simutenda, who died on Wednesday, August 19, 2026, has been put to rest.

Scores of Mbala residents turned up at Mbala Central Seventh Day Adventist Church, to pay their last respects to the late Mr Simutenda.

Speaking during the church service, Seventh Day Adventist Church Pastor, Bryson Katele encouraged the family and believers to find solace in God.

Pastor Katele urged mourners to remain firm in their faith, saying death is not the end for those who believe in God.

And speaking at Mutambalike Cemetery, where the late Mr Simutenda was laid to rest, United Party for National Development (UPND) Saise Lawmaker Remmy Sikazwe described the mayor’s death as shocking.

Mr Sikazwe commended Mbala residents for demonstrating unity during the funeral.

“This gathering has demonstrated the unity that exists among the people of Mbala, and we should continue with this spirit of togetherness even beyond the funeral,” said Mr Sikazwe.

Meanwhile, Mbala Central Member of Parliament Raphael Chilufya urged the bereaved family to remain united during the difficult period.

Mr Chilufya pledged to work with the family and the people of Mbala in honour of the late mayor, stressing the importance of supporting one another.

And Mbala District Commissioner, Jestus Sikazwe, in a speech read on his behalf by Mbala District Livestock Coordinator, Jones Kabaso said the late mayor-elect was a dedicated individual who demonstrated commitment in serving the community.

The District Commissioner said Mr Simutenda’s dedication to public service and community development will be remembered by the people he served.

“He was passionate about working for the people even during his time as Councillor for Kazimolwa Ward, as well as through his personal business activities,” he said.

Mr Simutenda died on Wednesday, August 19, 2026 at Mbala General Hospital after an illness

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 24, 2026
World.content:
30 Killed as Rubbish Mound Collapses in Guinea

At least 30 people have been killed and 22 injured after a mound of rubbish collapsed onto homes at a major waste site in Conakry, Guinea, following heavy rain. Six of the injured are in serious condition. Fears remain that the death toll could rise. Rescue teams, including the military, have been searching through the debris with excavators for survivors. Prime Minister Mamadou Oury Bah visited the site to oversee the response. The government had recently ordered the expulsion of nearby residents in informal housing due to a fear of collapses . A similar landslide at the waste site killed 10 people in 2017.

DR Congo and M23 Rebels Agree on Peace Roadmap

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Democratic Republic of Congo government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group have agreed on a roadmap for peace talks after five days of negotiations in Switzerland. The deal includes a mechanism to monitor ceasefire violations and sets timelines for negotiations under a 2025 US-brokered peace framework. However, disagreements remain over sanctions, detainees and political reforms. The latest negotiations were attended by M23, the government of DR Congo, Qatar, the US, the Republic of Togo, the African Union Commission and host Switzerland. Fighting has continued in eastern DR Congo despite previous ceasefire commitments, with the conflict having killed thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.

Mogadishu Home Demolitions Spark Clashes

The demolition of homes in Mogadishu's Tookiyo neighbourhood has sparked clashes between government forces and residents resisting the operation, with nearly 10 people reportedly injured. Authorities began demolishing homes as part of efforts to reclaim land considered government property. Residents have said that they have lived in the area for decades and are demanding clarity over land ownership and a proper legal process. Concerns are growing over further violence and displacement. The Somali government has yet to issue an official statement on the reported injuries.

Nigeria Police Rescue 75 Kidnap Victims

Nigerian police have rescued 75 people, including men, women and children, after they were kidnapped from commercial buses in Kaduna State. The victims, identified as Fulani travellers, were abducted by gunmen on August 19. They were held inside a cave in a mountainous forest near Birnin Gwari. Police, acting on intelligence from the local transport workers' union, raided the area and forced the kidnappers to flee, rescuing all 75 victims unharmed. Authorities urged residents to remain vigilant and share information with police while warning against vigilante action. They further warned members of the public against taking the law into their own hands, cautioning that vigilante actions or reprisals could escalate violence and result in the loss of innocent lives.

Close 

Mystery Elephant Deaths Alarm Kenya Conservationists

Since June, at least 20 elephants in Kenya's Amboseli ecosystem have died after developing symptoms of extreme weakness and paralysis, leaving conservationists and Maasai communities searching for answers. The Kenya Wildlife Service has said that toxicology tests found high levels of cyanide in some carcasses, raising suspicions of pesticide poisoning. However, local wildlife experts dispute the theory. They said that scavengers feeding on the carcasses have not shown signs of poisoning. Authorities have said that there is currently no evidence of an infectious disease. Investigations continue to determine what is killing the elephants.

World.title: South Africa: Cape Town Taxi Violence Sparks Talks - South African News Briefs - August 24, 2026
World.content:
Cape Town Taxi Violence Sparks Talks

The Western Cape Department of Mobility is engaging taxi industry stakeholders following a recent flare-up of taxi-related violence in Cape Town, reports EWN. Four men were killed and two wounded in two separate shootings. An informal trader was also shot dead at Dunoon Taxi Rank. The latest violence comes weeks after authorities mediated a deadly dispute between four taxi associations over routes in the southern suburbs. The department has said that it is working with stakeholders on measures to restore stability. The South African National Taxi Council (SANTACO) is attempting to facilitate peace talks between rival associations.

Three More Arrested Over Boxer Zolani Tete Murder



Eastern Cape police have arrested three more suspects in connection with the murder of former two-division boxing world champion Zolani Tete, reports SABC News. This brings the total number in custody to four. Tete, 38, was shot dead outside his home in Mdantsane. A 27-year-old woman travelling with him was wounded and remains in hospital. One of the suspects, a 22-year-old man, has been charged with murder and attempted murder and is due to appear in the Mdantsane Magistrate's Court. Police say further arrests are expected.

Steve Biko Death Inquest Set to Resume

The reopened inquest into the death of anti-apartheid activist Steve Biko is set to resume at the Gqeberha High Court, nearly five decades after he died in police custody, reports EWN. Biko was arrested in August 1977 and died weeks later from severe injuries sustained in custody. A 1977 inquest accepted the police account that he had been injured in a scuffle, and no one was prosecuted. The new inquest will examine whether any acts or omissions surrounding Biko's death amounted to criminal offences, potentially providing long-awaited answers to his family and the country.

World.title: Africa: The Deadly Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak Can Be Stopped
World.content:
Dr Mohamed Janabi (WHO Regional Director for Africa -left), Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus (WHO Director-General - center), and Dr Jean Kaseya (Director-General of Africa CDC -right) at a press briefing in Kinshasa during a joint high-level mission to Uganda and DRC on 4 and 5 August 2026.

guest column

Each time we travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), we first go to listen.

In Bunia, we have met dozens of community representatives: survivors, women, young people, local organisations, health workers and leaders from affected areas. Their message is direct: involve us. We know our communities. We know where families seek care, how information moves and why trust is breaking down. Give us the means to help drive the response. They are right.

Ebola spreads through communities, and communities hold the knowledge required to stop it. They can identify illness early, alert health teams, help identify and trace contacts, challenge dangerous rumours and support families through access to treatment and safe, dignified burials. The response always moves faster when communities lead alongside national authorities and health workers.



Communities are not just part of the response. They are at its heart." - Tedros

One hundred days ago, the Government of the DRC declared the country's 17th Ebola outbreak following confirmation of the Bundibugyo virus. WHO subsequently declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, followed by Africa CDC's declaration of a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security.

Priorities are clear: reach every affected area, protect frontline workers and turn commitments into action.

The scale of the emergency is immense. As of 21 August 2026, the DRC has reported 5,290 confirmed cases and 2,516 deaths across 56 health zones. This is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak recorded, and it is moving faster than any previous one. It is being fuelled by insecurity caused by decades of armed conflict that have undermined law, order and social services and displaced more than a million people.

At the centre of the response are the people who show up every day. Health workers care for patients. Laboratory teams identify the virus. Contact tracers follow its path. Community health workers build trust where fear and misinformation have taken hold. Burial teams help families honour their loved ones safely and with dignity.

They are working under extraordinary pressure, often in insecure and hard-to-reach areas. Some have contracted Ebola in the line of duty.

Their service must be met with action: safety, protective equipment, training, sufficient medical supplies, timely payment, psychosocial support and access to rapid diagnosis and high-quality supportive care if they fall ill. The safety of frontline workers is central to stopping transmission.

The response has made progress. Under the leadership of national authorities, Congolese responders, WHO, Africa CDC and partners have expanded surveillance, deployed laboratories, supported treatment centres, reinforced infection prevention and delivered essential supplies.

Uganda has interrupted locally acquired transmission of the virus. Several health zones in northern Ituri province and South Kivu have also interrupted transmission. These experiences prove that the outbreak can be stopped more quickly when rapid detection, decisive national leadership and close cooperation with communities break the chains of transmission. But the continued emergency in Ituri and five other provinces demands urgently scaled up action.

To turn the corner, surveillance teams are being expanded and equipped to detect cases early and rapidly identify contacts. Safe clinical care and infection prevention measures are being increased wherever people seek treatment. More risk communication and community engagement teams are being deployed to reach out to communities to empower them to participate in the response and address barriers to care. More safe and dignified burial teams are working to prevent transmission associated with deaths. Special efforts are being made to reach vulnerable populations and communities in insecure and hard-to-reach areas.

But despite all these efforts, more is needed. We need to scale our response by two to three times current capacities, across all the response pillars.

Front-line workers' safety is essential to stopping Ebola.

Health facilities require urgent protection from infection. As of 20 August 2026, 158 health workers have been infected and 45 have died. Every facility in an affected or high-risk area needs trained staff, protective equipment, clean water, sanitation and functioning infection-prevention systems.

National and local teams need predictable funding for surveillance, laboratories, treatment, logistics, infection prevention and community engagement. Frontline workers must be paid on time. Local organisations need direct support to work consistently with communities. Supplies must arrive before stocks run out.

Delayed financing costs lives. Fragmented financing leaves gaps. Ebola exploits both. On the ground we at WHO and Africa CDC have established tight integration among health and relief organizations working with the government. Donors therefore need to support and enhance that integration, rather than support siloed and disconnected efforts.

Cross-border also coordination must remain strong. People move within and between countries to trade, work, study, seek care and support their families. Borders must serve as bridges for coordinated public health action. This does not require closing borders or imposing blanket travel and trade restrictions. Such measures can disrupt response operations and livelihoods without stopping transmission.

Close 

The priority is coordinated surveillance, rapid information-sharing and prepared health services along movement routes. Find every case. Follow every contact. Break every chain of transmission, protect every health and frontline worker, save lives and ensure that no community is left behind. Bring testing, and treatment closer to every affected community. Bolster cross-border coordination. Scale up international support. Turn every pledge into action.

African leadership and international support are necessary.

WHO and Africa CDC will continue working with the DRC, neighbouring countries, communities and partners to deliver on these priorities. Our responsibility is to bring the full strength of international and continental cooperation behind the nationally led response.

Uganda and areas in DRC have shown how the course of the outbreak can be turned, through rapid detection, decisive action and close cooperation with communities. But these measures must be delivered at scale. Success depends on sustained national leadership, continental solidarity and international support. We must rise to this challenge, together.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is Director-General of the World Health Organization. Mohamed Yakub Janabi is Regional Director of the World Health Organization African Region. Jean Kaseya is Director-General of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

World.title: Congo-Brazzaville: Congo's Wealth Is Not Yet Power
World.content:
guest column

Across Africa, the decisive economic contest lies between raw material and finished product. For cotton, it is the distance from fibre to fabric. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, it is the distance from mineral and hydropower wealth to electricity, industrial capacity and productive work. The sectors differ, but the development question is the same: who captures the value created between extraction and the final product?

The Democratic Republic of Congo contains a startling share of the raw materials on which the modern economy depends. It is the world’s leading producer of cobalt. It has vast copper deposits, one of the planet’s great river systems and a population of roughly 100 million people, most of them young. On a map of the energy transition, the country appears indispensable.

On a map of lived prosperity, it looks very different. Only about 21 per cent of Congolese people have access to electricity, according to the World Bank. Poverty remains deep, insecurity persistent and the state distant or predatory for many citizens. The country’s most important economic question is therefore not how much wealth lies beneath its soil or runs through its rivers. It is whether that wealth can be converted into power, production and broadly shared opportunity.

That distinction separates endowment from development. Congo has never lacked resources. It has lacked the durable institutions and infrastructure that allow resources to become public value.

An extractive inheritance

The origins of that failure reach back to the formation of the state itself. Under King Leopold II, the Congo Free State became synonymous with forced labour and brutal extraction. Coercive labour practices persisted after Belgium assumed direct colonial rule in 1908, and a genuinely free labour market emerged only slowly before independence in 1960, according to academic research cited in the original manuscript.

The colonial economy was designed to remove value and administer territory, not to cultivate a broad Congolese political, managerial and technical class. At independence, the country inherited immense land and mineral wealth but little indigenous administrative capacity. A World Bank historical assessment cited in the manuscript describes both the shortage of trained Congolese personnel and Belgium’s effort to retain influence through technical advisers placed alongside key officials.

The crisis that followed independence, the assassination of Patrice Lumumba, Mobutu Sese Seko’s long authoritarian rule and the Congo wars deepened those institutional weaknesses. Mobutu did not invent the extractive state, but his personalised system entrenched it: institutions weakened, patronage expanded and public resources served political survival. Later conflicts and regional interventions fragmented authority further and allowed armed groups to flourish.

This history matters not because it condemns Congo to failure, but because it explains why geology alone has proved such a poor development strategy. Resources create possibilities. States, markets and public institutions determine who captures them.

From quarry to factory

The scale of the opportunity is nonetheless exceptional. The US Geological Survey estimated that in 2024 the DRC accounted for about 75 per cent of global cobalt production and roughly 55 per cent of global reserves. It was also the leading producer of tantalum and among the leading producers of copper, diamonds, tin and other strategic minerals.

These materials sit inside the energy, electronics, telecommunications, defence and manufacturing supply chains that are reshaping global commerce. Yet the familiar model remains one in which the highest-value activity occurs elsewhere. Minerals are extracted in Congo; more sophisticated processing and manufacturing take place abroad.

The policy choice is often described as one between exporting minerals and exporting products. But moving from one to the other requires more than declaring an industrial ambition. Copper processing, battery materials, electrical equipment, construction inputs, machinery and chemicals all require dependable electricity, transport, skills, capital, enforceable contracts and access to markets.

The real transition, then, is not simply from “quarry” to “factory”. It is from an extractive system to a productive one. The measure of success is not how many tonnes leave the ground, but how much capability, employment and domestic value are created before they leave the country.

The river and the grid

Congo’s most consequential industrial asset may be the one that flows through it. The Congo River and its tributaries give the country extraordinary hydropower potential. The Inga site alone has an estimated capacity of about 42,000 megawatts, which the World Bank describes as one of the world’s largest hydropower opportunities.

That number is dazzling. The national power deficit is sobering. With electricity reaching only about one in five people, the first claim on Congo’s hydropower future must be domestic: households, schools, clinics, farms and businesses that cannot develop without reliable power. The country’s National Energy Compact aims to raise access to 62 per cent by 2030, potentially reaching about 82 million people, according to the World Bank.

Power is also the bridge between Congo’s mineral base and its industrial ambitions. A processing plant cannot run on geological promise. Mines, smelters, factories and cities need generation connected to functioning transmission and distribution networks. The Inga opportunity therefore cannot be judged only by installed capacity. It must be judged by whether electricity reaches Congolese users reliably and affordably.

Regional trade could extend the value of that system. The DRC participates in the Southern African Power Pool, and electricity from Inga has historically been supplied to countries including South Africa and Zimbabwe. The World Bank has identified stronger transmission links between Inga, Zambia and the wider southern African market as strategically important.

The proposed Inga 3 project illustrates both the promise and the uncertainty. World Bank analysis cited in the manuscript places its possible generation between 2 and 11 gigawatts, depending on the final design. Congo’s position could eventually allow power to move across southern, central and eastern African pools. But “could” is the operative word. Regional electricity trade depends on finance, transmission lines, credible contracts, regulatory alignment and political confidence—not capacity estimates alone.

World Bank/ Ai Generated Congo at the centre. Country and river geometry: Natural Earth.

Europe’s interest, Congo’s choice

The strongest European connection is not a speculative cable from the Congo River to European homes. It is the prospect of a different industrial relationship. Europe seeks secure supplies of critical minerals and lower-carbon industrial inputs. Congo needs energy, jobs and greater value addition.

If renewable power can be combined with copper, cobalt and other minerals, Congo could produce more of the intermediate goods required by the energy transition. That would allow trading partners to buy higher-value Congolese output rather than raw material alone.

But the arrangement will be developmental only if industrial capacity takes root inside Congo. Supply security for foreign buyers is not the same as prosperity for Congolese citizens. The terms of contracts, the distribution of rents, local skills, environmental safeguards and the strength of domestic suppliers will decide whether a new mineral boom merely modernises extraction or changes the structure of the economy.

A young country needs work

The urgency is demographic. A World Bank assessment cited in the manuscript estimates that almost 65 per cent of the population is under 25. About 22 million people were aged 15 to 24 in 2025; that figure is projected to reach roughly 26 million by 2030. About a third of young people are neither in education, employment nor training, while roughly 40 per cent struggle to find work.

A young population is neither automatically a dividend nor inevitably a danger. It becomes an economic advantage when education, electricity, investment and functioning markets allow people to be productive. Without those conditions, demographic scale can intensify exclusion and instability.

This is why Congo’s industrial debate must be about jobs as much as exports. Capital-intensive mining can generate revenue without employing people on the scale the country requires. Processing, construction, energy, logistics, agriculture, services and regional manufacturing offer a broader employment base—but only if skills policy and industrial policy are designed together.

Peace as economic infrastructure

No such strategy can succeed while conflict continues in the east. Violence is first a human catastrophe. It is also a destruction of economic possibility: roads go unbuilt, schools are disrupted, responsible investment becomes harder and informal or illicit systems gain ground.

The IMF has identified governance weaknesses, mineral dependence, youth exclusion, conflict and the regional dimensions of insecurity among the DRC’s drivers of fragility. The implication is that peace cannot be treated as a security file isolated from economic policy.

The DRC and its neighbours have a material interest in replacing the economics of conflict with the economics of connection. Electricity links, roads, railways, ports, digital networks, agricultural value chains and lawful cross-border trade can raise the opportunity cost of destabilisation. Integration is no guarantee of peace. But an economy organised around shared production and exchange offers a stronger foundation than one organised around contested extraction.

Finance, and the test of delivery

Development institutions have begun to finance parts of this agenda. As of September 2023, the African Development Bank’s active DRC portfolio consisted of 27 operations worth about $1.45bn across transport, information and communications technology, energy, water and sanitation, and agriculture. Its 2023–2028 country strategy focuses on industrialisation, employment, infrastructure, agricultural value chains, human capital and the business environment.

The energy commitments cited in the manuscript include $22.4mn in parallel AfDB financing alongside $73.1mn of World Bank support approved in 2014 for Inga-related technical assistance. In December 2024, the AfDB was appointed mandated lead arranger for the $340mn Moyi Power Metro-Grids project, intended to bring cleaner, more reliable electricity to more than one million people in three cities.

These commitments show that Congo’s needs are recognised. They do not, by themselves, prove transformation. Portfolios, strategies and mandates are inputs. The meaningful outputs are functioning grids, reliable transport, competitive firms, transparent institutions and work that pays.

The missing chain

Congo’s agenda is often presented as a list: better mining contracts, more roads and rail, stronger security, technical education, regional power links, a better business climate. Each item is necessary. The more difficult insight is that they are interdependent.

Electricity without transmission cannot power a factory. A railway without predictable freight may not be financeable. Mineral processing without skills and reliable energy will not compete. Investment without accountable institutions can reproduce the very extractive bargain Congo needs to escape. Peace without legal economic opportunities may remain fragile.

The country therefore needs more than projects. It needs a sequence: secure productive regions; improve public institutions and contract transparency; expand electricity access and transmission; connect mines, farms and cities to markets; build technical capabilities; and use mineral and energy policy to support industries that can compete.

None of this is quick. Nor is it guaranteed. The same resources that make Congo strategically valuable also intensify struggles over rents and influence. Large infrastructure can create debt, displacement and governance risks if projects are badly designed. Regional interconnection creates opportunity, but it also requires patient diplomacy and institutions able to enforce agreements.

Yet the alternative is not stasis. Global demand for strategic minerals is placing Congo closer to the centre of the world economy. The country can remain indispensable as a source of raw materials while its citizens remain excluded from the value those materials create. Or it can use this moment to negotiate a more productive bargain.

The real test will not be whether the Democratic Republic of Congo finally “wakes”. Countries are not giants in fairy tales. They are political economies, built through choices and constrained by institutions.

Congo already has the assets. What it has not yet secured is the chain that joins them: peace to investment, power to production, minerals to industry, and national wealth to household prosperity. Building that chain would not merely alter Congo’s fortunes. It could change the economic geography of Africa.

World.title: Zambia: Hichilema Wins a Stronger Mandate, but Zambia's Democratic Test Isn't Over
World.content:
analysis

Late reforms and weak checks on power expose democratic fault lines and raise the stakes for Hichilema's second term.

Zambia's 13 August election delivered a second five-year term for President Hakainde Hichilema. With last-minute changes to electoral law and a fragmented opposition, the result was not unexpected.

Hichilema secured 60.5% of the vote, against National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) candidate Brian Mundubile's 37.8%. The expanded National Assembly now has 226 directly elected members (up from 156) plus 40 proportional representation (PR) seats reserved for women, youth and people with disabilities. Constitutionally, the president can appoint up to 11 MPs, bringing the total to 277 seats.

So far, Hichilema's United Party for National Development (UPND) has won 138 seats, the NRPUP 60, with independents and smaller parties winning the rest. With the UPND's presidential seats and expected 24 of the 40 PR seats, the ruling party has 160 (62% of the house). Even so, the opposition retains a substantial bloc.



Roughly 57% of registered voters participated, down substantially from 70% in 2021 - likely reflecting living-cost frustrations and unequal campaign conditions.

Other issues also marred the polls, among them a 14 August raid by Zambian security forces on a Lusaka property, in which former transport minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot and killed. Eleven people, including senior opposition figures, were arrested for possessing military-grade weapons for an armed insurrection. Mundubile denied the claims, but he and senior opposition figures now face treason charges.

There is a striking coincidence between this situation and Hichilema's arrest after the 2016 election for allegedly endangering the president by obstructing his motorcade. Hichilema was held in a maximum-security facility for over 100 days until the Commonwealth intervened. The Commonwealth Secretariat has again expressed concern over the current post-election climate.

Several election observers noted that Zambia held a largely peaceful vote - but on an uneven playing field. The European Union (EU), Southern African Development Community and African Union-Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa missions all raised concerns about the implementation of last-minute electoral reforms.

The Constitutional Amendment Act No 13 (2025) created the new 226-seat parliamentary map. Allocations were done in April, with PR seats approved in May - three months before polling. Critics say adding most new constituencies in UPND-leaning rural areas benefitted the party.

Also, the PR system discouraged parties from nominating women for constituency seats, seeing seats reserved for women as a substitute for women's representation rather than being complementary. Female candidacy fell to 12.5% from 21.1% in 2021.

The change in electoral rules so close to the polls created uncertainty for parties, voters and election administrators (UPND was the only party to file a candidate for all available seats). The observer missions said electoral reform should strengthen competition, not leave the rules contested just before voting.

Hichilema's campaign also benefitted from his position as head of government. EU observers documented the use of state resources at campaign events and found that presidential and vice-presidential visits were exempt from the Electoral Commission of Zambia's (ECZ) five-day campaign timetable that applied to other candidates. Some unscheduled visits by Hichilema or his running mate resulted in opposition events being blocked or cancelled.

Transparency International Zambia's independent monitoring matched the ECZ's tallies within 1.1%, but flagged unsealed ballot boxes (which risk tampering) and delayed announcements in 32 of 221 constituencies checked. The Christian Churches Monitoring Group found turnout implausibly exceeding its estimates in 30 constituencies.

On 14 August, the ECZ suspended counting for around six hours over reports of violence against polling staff and theft of marked ballots. At the same time, Mundubile, citing his party's parallel count, pre-emptively claimed victory - a statement that ECZ warned candidates against making.

The NRPUP says it will challenge Hichilema's win in court, which could extend Zambia's transition period from seven to 15 days, as occurred after the closer 2016 polls. However, the 2026 winning margin is far larger - over a million votes (22.6%) compared to just over 100 000 (2.7%) in 2016. A recount probably wouldn't close that gap, and a costly court-ordered rerun would be disruptive.

The economic vote was likely decisive in giving Hichilema his second term. Although the president's macro-economic record on debt restructuring, lower inflation and improved relations with international lenders has not improved household welfare, more immediate and visible interventions gained traction among voters.

These include the Constituency Development Fund, which increased from K1.6 million ($84,160) per constituency in 2021 to K40 million (US$2.1 million) in 2026, higher student allowances at public universities, reduced power cuts and improved fertiliser payments in rural areas.

Mundubile's Tonse Alliance showed that anti-UPND sentiment could be consolidated into a real presidential challenge, inheriting strongholds of the former ruling Patriotic Front. The alliance's 60 parliamentary seats give it a base, but a coalition built mainly on opposing the incumbent doesn't constitute a governing alternative. Creating one requires a formal party structure with an agreed-upon line of succession, not centred on an individual.

Close 

A policy platform on jobs, energy and living costs that voters can organise around beyond opposing Hichilema is also vital. Finally, legal challenges to the election result must be based on evidence, not merely grievances, to prevent a court defeat that would cost the opposition what credibility it has left.

For the UPND, the stronger mandate gives the party the space to deliver on energy, jobs and living costs. It also creates a heavier duty to strengthen parliamentary scrutiny rather than rush legislation through with little debate, as occurred with the recent electoral reforms.

Zambia has shown democratic resilience, but the polls exposed real vulnerabilities. Hichilema enters his last term with a stronger mandate and fewer institutional checks on how he uses it. The test is no longer whether he can win elections, but whether he leaves behind a system that enables his successor to fairly compete in the democratic spirit the country is known for.

David Willima, Researcher, Climate Risk and Human Security, ISS Pretoria

Zenge Simakoloyi, Research Officer, Africa Peace and Security Governance, ISS

World.title: South Africa: World's Largest Research Funder Lifts Ban On South Africa
World.content:
Many clinical trials were halted, and many researchers were retrenched when the NIH stopped funding

The United States National Institutes of Health (NIH) has lifted its ban nearly 18 months after an order to stop work with South Africa.

The funding ban created a crisis for HIV and TB research, including NIH grants and US Agency for International Development aid.

Many of the world's major advances over the past two decades in understanding the science of HIV arose from South African scientists and from studies conducted here, the vast majority of them funded by the NIH.

The United States National Institutes of Health (NIH) has lifted its ban on South Africa, nearly 18 months after its February order to stop work with South Africa created a crisis for HIV and TB research.

In January 2025, the United States began halting funding of South African projects, including NIH grants and US Agency for International Development (USAID) aid.



The scientific journal, Science, reported that an internal memo dated 17 August, signed by NIH director Jay Bhattacharya, had lifted the ban. We have since obtained the memo, which is marked "Not for distribution outside government". It states funding for "meritorious research projects" in South Africa may proceed.

The memo states that NIH grants are "distinct from the objectives traditionally associated with foreign aid or assistance".

A brief from May 2025 by Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders), US advocacy organisation Treatment Action Group, and the South African Medical Research Council (SAMRC) found that critical research initiatives and decades of investments in research infrastructure were affected by the NIH stop-work order.

The brief noted that research in South Africa, mostly led by South African scientists with NIH funding, has in the past two decades "shaped global health policies that have revolutionised TB and HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care, benefiting both the local population and communities worldwide, including people who live in the United States".

Ntobeko Ntusi, president and CEO of the South African Medical Research Council, confirmed that the decision comes after 12 months of negotiating with the NIH "to reverse their position on South Africa".

"Part of the mandate of the NIH to engage in international research collaborations should be viewed in light of the fact that South Africa is one of only few countries that co-funded biomedical research with the NIH, rather than merely being a recipient," said Ntusi.

"I welcome this apt decision of the NIH because no country can ever solve the challenges of global health alone ... We need scientific collaboration to drive scientific progress," he said.

Linda-Gail Bekker, director of the Desmond Tutu HIV Centre, said the centre had to retrench people when the funding stopped, since it was largely NIH funded. It had a partnership with NIH for decades.

Bekker said there has been a long hiatus from receiving research protocols from their networks in the US, such as the Advancing Clinical Therapeutics Globally (ACTG), HIV Vaccine Trials Network (HVTN), and others.

She said their networks are coming to the end of seven-year trials for their clinical trials units. "We haven't had confirmation that South Africa will be included. But we feel more optimistic than we did before," said Bekker.

She said they have received some funding from the SAMRC in reprieve of the lost NIH money but not anywhere close to the same volume.

In August 2025, the SAMRC announced that it had raised around R600-million in rescue funds to support research projects and groups affected by the cuts. This amount includes around R400-million from National Treasury, R100-million from the Gates Foundation, R100-million from the Wellcome Trust, and R14.4-million from the ELMA Foundation.

Bekker said the scientific advancements in South African HIV and TB research are also "good for the whole world" and the benefits have been "bidirectional".

Landon Myer, at UCT's School of Public Health, warned that South Africans should be "cautiously optimistic". He did not think things were going back to the way they were before NIH funding halted.

Close 

Myer said it was difficult to know what the memo means in practice. "Time will tell," he said.

Within the NIH there have been a large number of layoffs and resignations and budgets have been limited, possibly undermining their bureaucratic capacity, he said.

Myer confirmed Bekker's view that many of the world's major advances over the past two decades in understanding the science of HIV arose from South African scientists and from studies conducted here, the vast majority of them funded by NIH.

The memo also stated that the Fogarty International Center is "no longer supporting research training and career development applications from South Africa" due to SA being an upper-middle-income country. Myer said over decades the Fogarty training invested heavily in South African scientists which in turn led to so many "scientific accomplishments" here.

Co-published with Spotlight

World.title: Uganda: I'm Alive and Well Because of Jesus - Janet Museveni
World.content:
Kampala, Uganda — First Lady Mama Janet Museveni made a major public appearance on Sunday after more than five months away from the public spotlight due to health challenges, telling worshippers that 2026 will forever remain the year God "delivered" her life from the jaws of death.

Mama Janet was speaking during the consecration of her daughter, Patience Kokundeka Museveni Rwabwogo, as Bishop of Covenant Nations Church at Maya-Luzira in Kampala.

Although she made a brief public appearance several days ago during a reception for visiting American evangelist Bishop Dr LaDonna C. Osborn, Sunday's ceremony marked her first appearance before a huge gathering since her prolonged absence.

Mama Janet delivered a prayer lasting more than 14 minutes, which she used to publicly reflect on her health ordeal, Uganda's history and the growth of the church, while thanking Ugandans and Christians who prayed for her during her illness.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

She said she was grateful that people for whom she had prayed over the years, including widows, orphans and vulnerable Ugandans, also remembered her in her hour of need.

The First Lady also linked her recovery to her Christian faith, describing Jesus as "the healer, the great physician" and quoting Isaiah 53:5 on healing.

Her prayer also became a reflection on the history of Uganda, with Janet crediting God for guiding the country through years of civil war, HIV/AIDS, insurgencies, poverty and the challenges of rebuilding after conflict.

She praised President Yoweri Museveni for leading the country through what she described as a 40-year journey of rebuilding and recovery.

"It was your presence that defeated the innumerable challenges we have faced these past 40 years," she said, citing the war in northern Uganda by the Lord's Resistance Army and other conflicts.

Mama Janet said she was particularly thankful that Uganda had transformed from a war-ravaged country into a nation supporting regional peace and hosting refugees from neighbouring countries.

On the consecration of her daughter, she said it is a moment of great honour and joy for the family.

"Today, we celebrate the consecration of our daughter, Patience, to the office of a bishop," she said. "We are overwhelmed with joy and thanksgiving at the great honour you have bestowed over us in choosing one of our children to serve you in this capacity."

She said Patience answered the call to ministry 20 years ago and prayed that she and her husband, Odrek Rwabwogo, would receive "a fresh anointing of the Holy Spirit" to continue their work.

She also prayed for Covenant Nations Church to expand beyond Uganda while remaining grounded in prayer, love, and the preaching of what she called the undiluted word of God.

At the conclusion of the prayer, President Museveni ionately recognized his wife before stepping onto the podium to deliver what he described as his "brief speech." Museveni began by thanking God for his wife's recovery and also acknowledged the medical personnel and their children who supported her during her illness.

The President then commended Patience on becoming a bishop, saying the development represented a significant milestone for his family.

Museveni traced his family's encounter with Christianity, saying his ancestors had lived in the region for millions of years before the arrival of Islam and Christianity. He said Islam arrived in Uganda in the 1840s, followed by the Anglican Church in 1877 and Catholic missionaries in 1879.

According to Museveni, his great-grandparents and grandparents did not join the church nor the colonial administration, with his own family only embracing Christianity in 1947.

Museveni also praised his daughter's biblical knowledge, revealing that he had spent 12 years studying the Bible but found himself learning new things from Patience's writings.

He said he was particularly surprised by her explanation of the descendants of Lot and Esau, which led him to conclude that his daughter had studied the Bible more deeply than he had.

Close 

"So I said, this young person has really read the Bible much more than myself, I surrendered," he said.

Museveni said Patience would bring "a lot of energy" to the church and thanked Bishop Osborn and Nigerian preacher Pastor Enoch Adeboye for travelling to Uganda for the consecration.

He also used the occasion to call on religious leaders to focus on the substance of Christianity.

The ceremony was attended by Vice President Jessica Alupo, ministers, Members of Parliament and religious and cultural leaders.

Among those present were Pastor Robert Kayanja, Prince Wasajja Kiwanuka representing the Buganda Kingdom, and representatives of the Anglican, Catholic and Muslim communities.

The consecration also attracted religious leaders and dignitaries from Uganda and abroad, as Covenant Nations Church marked 20 years since Patience began pastoring the church.

As a gesture of support to his daughter, Museveni announced that he and Mama Janet would give Patience 50 cows.

World.title: Guinea: Garbage Collapse at Landfill Kills Dozens
World.content:
Heavy seasonal rains caused a mound of garbage to collapse, burying dozens of people and nearby homes before the break of dawn.

At least 30 people have died after a landfill collapsed in Guinea's capital, Conakry, officials said on Sunday.

Heavy rains overnight caused a large mound of rubbish to collapse at the Dar Es Salam landfill, burying nearby homes before dawn.

At least six other people were seriously injured.

Guinea's minister for territorial administration, Djenabou Toure, visited the site, where workers used excavators to search for more bodies.

Landfill was slated for closure

The government had recently ordered the expulsion of nearby residents in informal housing due to a fear of collapses.

Balde Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the Military Engineering Battalion, said the Dar Es Salam site had been slated for closure on Sunday.

Heavy seasonal rains have been known to trigger collapses at landfills in some countries, with Uganda and Ethiopia suffering similar tragedies in recent years.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: Thune-aligned groups unleash historic war chest to defend Senate majority: 'Winning message'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), a top GOP campaign group aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., announced that it and other allies have raised over $500 million ahead of the 2026 U.S. Senate elections, setting new records as they look to defend a Republican majority in the upcoming midterms.

Despite a historical precedent that sets long odds for the president’s party in the midterms, Republicans have built a war chest in recent months to put Democrats on the defensive in the House and Senate.

"Thanks to Leader John Thune and our generous investors, Senate Leadership Fund and its affiliated groups have raised more resources than any other Senate effort in history," SLF Executive Director Alex Latcham said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

NRCC REPORTING RECORD $47.1 MILLION QUARTER, RECORD $28.1 MILLION RAISED IN MARCH

"However, we cannot slow down as Chuck Schumer and Radical Democrats seek to take our nation back to open borders, rampant crime and crushing inflation."

It's those elements the group hopes to put front and center.

In many of their materials, SLF looks to pin Democrats over their opposition to many pieces of President Donald Trump’s legislative agenda and past support for far-left policies.

Across races in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan and North Carolina, they are using ad campaigns to highlight elements like violence caused by soft-on-crime policies, opposition to wage hikes for veterans and past scandals that have followed some of the Democratic candidates.

HOW DEMOCRATIC LEADERSHIP SANK $40 MILLION MEANT TO DEFEND KEY SEATS ON A GAMBLE THAT BACKFIRED

"Logan was a casualty of an agenda," one featured interviewee said, recounting how his daughter had been killed by Alexander Dickey, a repeat criminal who had faced nearly 40 criminal charges.

In another ad, SLF reminded voters in Iowa how Josh Turek, a Senate hopeful who had won gold for the U.S. in the Paralympic Games, had missed over 50% of his votes while running his campaign.

"We expect our lawmakers to show up, yet liberal politician Josh Turek missed 58% of his votes in the Iowa legislature — votes to help veterans and fund schools, yet still collected his full taxpayer-funded paycheck," the ad states.

DEM SENATE HOPEFUL RIPPED AS 'ABSENTEE LEGISLATOR' AFTER MISSING NEARLY 60% OF VOTES

Latcham said he anticipates SLF’s layered strategy of messaging — and the resources needed to bring that message to voters — combined with the GOP’s candidate strengths will deliver wins in November.

"With incredible candidates, a winning message and record funding, we are confident that Senate Republicans will maintain their majority this November and continue to deliver for the American people," Latcham said.

World.title: Andrew feels ‘abandoned’ by royal family, rejects King Charles’ invitation over outcast fears: experts
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly feels "abandoned" by his family as his royal exile deepens.

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that friends are reportedly checking in regularly on the former Duke of York and "he's certainly not hiding away" from them.

"Rather than spending the summer at Balmoral hidden away with the rest of the family, Andrew seems to be opting for time abroad with friends," she said. "Allegedly, he feels abandoned by certain family members."

FORMER PRINCE ANDREW SPOTTED WITH BRUISE COVERING HALF HIS FACE AS MYSTERY INJURY SPARKS QUESTIONS

British royal expert Hilary Fordwich echoed Chard's sentiments, citing her sources.

"Andrew isn't important anymore," said Fordwich. "No one is very concerned about how he's feeling. However, it's important to ensure he doesn't cause any more damage to the monarchy."

WATCH: FORMER PRINCE ANDREW REMAINS IN DENIAL OVER EPSTEIN SCANDAL: AUTHOR

A friend of the ex-royal's told The Sun that "Andrew feels he's been abandoned" and "he feels like he is no longer part of the family."

"He was invited but has got no great desire to be at Balmoral as he has nothing to gain and would be treated as an outcast," the unnamed friend told the outlet. "What's the point, he feels, of going all the way there for a much-needed holiday and being treated as an elephant in the room?"

Andrew stepped away from royal duties in 2019 following a widely criticized BBC "Newsnight" interview in which he attempted to explain his friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

In 2022, he was stripped of his military titles and patronages by his mother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, as he faced Epstein survivor Virginia Giuffre's sexual assault lawsuit against him. Andrew and Giuffre settled out of court for an undisclosed sum that year.

Giuffre died in April 2025.

In October 2025, King Charles III stripped his younger brother's royal titles as Andrew faced renewed scrutiny over his ties to Epstein. The scrutiny intensified following the publication of Giuffre's posthumous memoir and the release of documents detailing Andrew's relationship with Epstein.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Buckingham Palace also served Andrew formal notice to surrender the lease on his longtime residence, Royal Lodge. His ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, was expected to make separate living arrangements.

On Feb. 19, Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office over an allegation that he shared confidential information with Epstein during his time as a U.K. trade envoy. He was released after being held for 11 hours in police custody. The investigation remains ongoing.

Andrew has repeatedly denied wrongdoing in connection with Epstein and the allegations against him.

"Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor obviously is feeling the contempt and distancing from other senior members of the royal family," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital.

"So his mental health will become more prevalent. Some of his favorite activities, like riding and shooting, may have been curtailed. The ongoing police investigation is a continuous worry for him. And still, his soulmate and former wife is being distant."

"Andrew is confined to a lonely existence," Turner continued. "Allegedly, he watches a TV channel which shows planes landing as one of his new methods of relaxation."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Andrew's friend told The Sun that the disgraced ex-duke rejected the king's invitation to Balmoral Castle because he feared he would be treated as an "outcast."

Every summer, the royal family gathers at Balmoral to spend time together privately. About 30 family members are expected to join the king for the traditional gathering this year. The Sun reported that the king is not believed to have seen Andrew this year, despite at times staying only a mile away from him.

"Why would Andrew reject an olive branch from his brother?" said Turner. "There's a mixture of anger at what happened to him, a disdain for Charles, which he may see as a weak man, and, no doubt, arrogance with his belief that he can do what he wants without punitive measures taken against him. Also add to the tension with Prince William. Andrew is boxed in."

"There will never be any public restoration for Andrew at all, not now with King Charles and certainly not when Prince William ascends to the throne," said Fordwich.

"If Andrew did decline an invitation from the king, it might just be Andrew’s classic self-concern that he’d feel too awkward knowing he wasn’t wanted by the extended family at large. The only family member, I believe, who had visited Andrew was Prince Edward."

The Sun reported that Andrew’s ex-wife and their two daughters have "avoided" his new home, Marsh Farm, where he’s "lonely."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Even as Andrew becomes increasingly isolated from royal life, one royal privilege reportedly remains intact.

The Daily Mail reported that Andrew remains on a confidential government list of royal family members with funeral plans prepared in advance. The arrangements are known as "bridge plans," with plans for senior royals named after bridges in the U.K.

When Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022, "Operation London Bridge" went into action. The plan for her husband, Prince Philip, was known as "Operation Forth Bridge" when he died in 2021.

The plans are kept confidential until the royal dies, People magazine reported. According to the Daily Mail, Andrew's funeral service is expected to be held at St. George's Chapel before he is laid to rest at the Royal Burial Ground at Frogmore in Windsor.

Retired Rear Admiral Chris Parry, who captained HMS Fearless, told the Daily Mail that he believes the Royal Navy would provide volunteers to serve as pallbearers at Andrew's funeral. Andrew served in the Royal Navy from 1979 to 2001.

"... He had a Falklands medal, and you can't take that away from him, and he deserves the credit for that," said Parry. "... If somebody said to me, 'Would you do it?' I'd do it."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Spencer Kuvin, an attorney who represented nine of Epstein's victims, told the outlet that "taxpayers should not ever be funding a funeral for a private individual."

"No public money should be used to benefit him during death," he said. "It’s an embarrassment to the Crown."

Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace for comment.

World.title: Baker busts common sourdough myth that keeps busy Americans out of the kitchen
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A loaf of sourdough can take three days to make. That doesn't mean you'll spend three days making it.

That's the distinction Kate Freebairn wants busy would-be bread bakers to understand.

Freebairn, a sourdough recipe developer and food blogger in rural Western Australia, says one of the biggest barriers keeping beginners away from sourdough is the perception that making it will take over their lives.

COSTCO SHOPPERS DIVIDED OVER NEW 'SOURDOUGH' BREAD AS CRITICS SAY IT'S NOT THE REAL THING

"I think that people think that sourdough is really difficult and that it takes a lot of time, but really, even though a loaf of sourdough might take three days to complete, the actual time that you'll have your hands in the dough might only be an hour," Freebairn told Fox News Digital.

Her debut cookbook, "Easy Sourdough on Any Schedule," is built around fitting bread baking into everyday life rather than fitting life around bread baking.

For someone working a typical weekday, Freebairn suggests feeding the starter before bed, mixing the dough over morning coffee and tending to it while the kids are having breakfast. The dough can ferment while its baker is at work, then be shaped and refrigerated that evening.

The next morning, "you can wake up, pop the oven on, make your coffee and bake a fresh loaf of sourdough," Freebairn said. "So, the actual time that you have your hands in the dough is very minimal."

Freebairn also points to potential health benefits as another reason to choose sourdough.

CLICK HERE TO 

Because it is naturally fermented, she said, "the microbes in the sourdough starter, they're already doing some of the digestion for you," adding that sourdough "tends to not spike your blood sugar" and "has lots of prebiotics, which are really good for gut health."

Her favorite benefit, however, is simpler.

"Probably the best thing is it really does taste better," she said.

Beginners don't need a kitchen full of specialized equipment, either. Freebairn said an old pickle jar can hold a starter, and an ordinary bowl can substitute for a proofing basket. Her own Dutch oven isn't an expensive status piece.

"I literally still to this day use a $30 Dutch oven I bought from Aldi," she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Perhaps the bigger investment is patience. Freebairn recommends beginners expect their earliest loaves to be imperfect and says it may take five to 10 attempts to start getting the hang of the process.

"There's a lesson in every loaf," she said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

It's advice that captures her approach to sourdough: Start with what you have, fit it around the life you're already living and don't worry if the first loaf isn't perfect.
