World.title: The Jewish-Mexican food traditions hiding in plain sight
World.content:
My friend Jorge Fitz once told me a story about his childhood visits to the town where his grandfather grew up, Juliantla, just outside of Taxco, Mexico. He remembers many particular things about the way the town celebrated festivities and holidays, but one thing that stuck out in his memory was a special braided bread they made called pan de Juliantla.

As an adult, Jorge said he started making Jewish friends, and when he saw pan de Juliantla on their tables, he wondered how they knew about it.

“Jorge, that’s challah bread,” they would respond.

He later learned that Juliantla is believed to be the first Jewish settlement in the Americas, complete with a spiritual cleansing bath known as a mikveh that dates back to the 16th century.

As far as Jorge could tell, a majority of the townspeople didn’t realize where many of their customs and food came from. He and his parents definitely didn’t know about their Jewish ancestry until much later.

Hearing this story illuminated just how deeply rooted Jewish food is in Mexican culture, so much so that even when origins have been forgotten, they remain an integral part of community life.

Waves of migration and a culinary legacy

The first Jews to grace Mexican shores sailed in on the ships of Spanish conquistadors during the 1500s and 1600s. They were fleeing the Catholic Inquisition of the Iberian Peninsula, but found little solace in the New World as the Inquisition migrated across the ocean.

Many of these early Jews “converted” to Catholicism while continuing to practice their own religion in secret. In Spanish, they are called “conversos,” or the converted. In English, we often refer to them as Crypto Jews.

With these Sephardim came cinnamon, grapes, figs, dates, almonds, cherries, apricots, olives and olive oil, nutmeg, ginger, cardamom and mustard, as well as black pepper, thyme, basil, clove, fennel, oregano, cumin and other Mediterranean spices.

They also had a strong tradition of pickling what they brought to the New World. In northern Mexico, cabrito, slow-roasted baby goat, is a traditional dish among the Sephardic Jews of the Iberian Peninsula. Similarly, the region’s dessert bread known as pan de cemita and la capirotada, a kind of bread pudding, are also attributed to those early Iberian Jewish immigrants.

The second wave of Jewish immigrants to Mexico arrived at the end of the 1800s from the failing Ottoman Empire. Jews who were part of the diaspora from Spain and Portugal, now living in the countries of the Levant, came because of economic opportunities in Mexico. They arrived from what is today Lebanon, Syria and Turkey, and because they were not fleeing persecution, their culture, religion and food were much more visible.

Preserving culture in the neighborhood oven

A third wave of Jewish immigrants came to Mexico during and between the two world wars. Some had plans of continuing on to the United States but were turned away at Ellis Island because of the Immigration Act of 1924, which severely limited the numbers of Southern and European immigrants allowed into the country.

These immigrants brought the Ashkenazi dishes of Eastern European countries like Poland, Ukraine and Germany — hearty soups and stews made with root vegetables like borscht, matza ball soup, gefilte fish, schmaltz (rendered chicken fat), tzimmes, gribenes and braised meats like brisket.

Food is paramount for any immigrant community trying to preserve their identity. The Jewish community was no different.

When Syrian Jews moved into Colonia Roma at the beginning of the 20th century, they not only built one of the city’s oldest synagogues but also opened a community oven down the street where special traditional breads were baked and sold to worshipers coming from services. At the local market were kosher butchers, while elderly folks sat in neighborhood cafes sipping thick, Turkish-style coffee and eating the sweets of home.

Unlike some of the immigrant groups I have researched, the diverse Mexican-Jewish community not only preserved the traditional dishes of their culture, but also, over the generations, adapted and innovated with local ingredients and cooking methods, creating a distinct Judeo-Mexican cuisine.

The fusion kitchen and home recipes

“Sabor Judío,” published in 2024, is a recipe collection by two authors whose Jewish grandmothers passed down handwritten recipe books. They gathered together a comprehensive archive of recipes from kitchens across the Mexican-Jewish community. Among the book’s pages are traces of many cuisines — Mexican mestizo, Spanish, Sephardic-Iberian, Sephardic-Middle Eastern and Ashkenazi.

Yiddish blintzes with huitlacoche (Mexican corn smut considered a local delicacy), matza chilaquiles, a variation of shakshuka with poblano peppers and Mexican oregano, and brisket tacos with three-chile salsa are all included in the collection. Irma Appel’s stuffed poblano peppers with guacamole include a smattering of gribenes (often referred to as Jewish bacon), and Pati Jinich, of PBS’s “Pati’s Kitchen,” provided her recipe for jalapeño-mushroom matza ball soup.

Then there are traditional Mexican recipes that the Mexican-Jewish community has adopted as their own, cooking them for high holidays and other festivities. That includes nopal and tomato salad made in advance to eat cold during Shabbat, or ceviche with prepared horseradish on top, supposedly invented during a Passover Seder.

Not everything is kosher, but the community’s many identities are on full display.

Scanning through the menus of Jewish restaurants in Mexico City, however, it’s hard to find the fusion dishes represented in “Sabor Judío.” For whatever reason, these dishes hold sway in family kitchens, but haven’t yet made it to commercial dining rooms.

Where to find Jewish food in Mexico City

Maybe the world isn’t ready for spicy gefilte fish?

That’s not to say that you can’t get glimpses of them — the salami chilaquiles at Klein’s in Polanco is a delicious example. You’ll also find chiles making guest appearances in the Israeli dishes at Merkava, and kosher cafe Guacho Grill has al pastor tacos made with fish and chicken, as opposed to the traditional pork.

So maybe fusion is yet to take off in restaurants, but at places like Klein’s or Niddo, which once described itself in an interview as Jewish-Mexican-Canadian, diners will at least find Jewish and Mexican dishes coexisting on the table.

Plenty of other expressions of Jewish food can be encountered throughout the city — Mendl, for instance, has incredible U.S.-style deli sandwiches and bagels with lox. And at Pat Patz, chef Mijeal Seidel has a labneh recipe that he adds dill to as a shout-out to his Eastern European side, along with tons of other dishes worth exploring.

You may have to make some fusion dishes at home, but a taste of Jewish-Mexican heritage is definitely available across Mexico City.

Lydia Carey is a freelance writer and translator based in Mexico City. She has published extensively both online and in print, sharing her insights about Mexico for over a decade. She lives a double life as a local tour guide and is the author of “Mexico City Streets: La Roma.” Follow her urban adventures on Instagram and see more of her work at mexicocitystreets.com.

World.title: How the Middle East has shaped Mexico for almost 2,000 years
World.content:
I’m sitting in the courtyard of Guanajuato’s Museo Iconográfico del Quijote, admiring the stone arches and columns, waiting for a chamber music concert to begin. I probably walk through at least one courtyard a day in Guanajuato because they’re everywhere in town – not just in museums, but in restaurants, universities, government buildings and parks. Even the classic Mexican colonial home has a courtyard with a fountain in the center, surrounded by rooms.

Mexican courtyards reflect the influence of the Moors, the North African Islamic group that ruled Spain for 800 years and whose ornate tilework, intricate geometric patterns and decorative calligraphy influenced the art and architecture of Spain. After the fall of the Moors in 1492, Spain continued to use Islamic patterns in its designs, creating a unique style that blended Islamic and Christian elements known as mudéjar, which later made its way to Mexico.

But it’s not just courtyards that bear the mark of the Moors. From architecture and folk medicine to crafts and textiles, here’s a quick roundup of the Islamic group’s lasting impact on Mexican culture.

Alhambrismo

This is an architectural style in Spain and Latin America inspired by the decorative Islamic arts of the Alhambra, a palace and fortress complex in Granada, Spain, with Moorish elements such as horseshoe arches, intricate stucco and colorful tilework.

A well-known example of this is the Kiosk of Santa Maria la Ríbera, an ornate octagonal pavilion made of wrought iron with a glass cupola dome on the top, in Mexico City’s Alameda Park.

Churches

In many colonial Mexican churches, you can see echoes of the mudéjar architectural style, including azulejos, blue-glazed tiles that adorn domes, bell towers and facades; intricate geometric carved-wood ceilings resembling inverted ship hulls; and arches and doorways.

Oaxaca’s famous Templo de Santo Domingo de Guzmán, for example, displays these design elements in the intricate geometric arabesque patterns on the ceiling and the genealogical tree of the temple’s namesake saint.

Inward-facing living

I remember when my husband and I first saw the house we bought in Guanajuato. Although one of its assets was a close-up view of the dome atop one of the city’s signature churches, San Francisco, we could barely see it from the tiny window in one of the bedrooms.

Unlike in the U.S. and Canada, traditional Mexican houses face inward, revealing their Moorish and Andalusian roots, with walled enclosures and internal gathering spaces.

Urban layouts

While Spanish colonial urban planning in the Americas officially ordered a strict grid system, some historic Mexican towns like Guanajuato and Taxco have narrow, winding streets, reflecting the medieval and southern Andalusian urban layouts shaped by centuries of Moorish influence.

Tiles, pottery and ceramics

Moorish craftsmen influenced Iberian ceramic styles, including tin-glazed pottery, by integrating geometric patterns and calligraphic bands into their work. When the craft was established in Puebla during the colonial period, artisans carried over these traditional Iberian-Islamic design elements, including abstract script borders and traditional brushstroke motifs.

Puebla’s famous Talavera pottery also blends Indigenous styles with Spanish and Moorish glazed-tile traditions.

Crafts and textiles

Mudéjar geometric inlaid woodworking and carpentry techniques influenced traditional lacquerware and furniture crafts in regions like Michoacán and Guerrero. Precise interlaced framing merged with Indigenous wood-carving and pre-Hispanic lacquering, creating colonial furniture like desks with repetitive geometric paneling and floral touches.

As for weaving, the traditional Mexican sarape displays complex linear, diamond and star-centered layouts that show cross-cultural parallels to Middle Eastern flat-weave blanket traditions.

Curanderismo (folk medicine)

Moorish and Islamic medical practices influenced curanderismo, the herbal medicine still widely practiced in Mexico. Ritual cleansing, petitionary prayers and talismanic magic elements arrived via Spanish traditions that had absorbed Moorish folk customs.

For example, the belief that the “mal de ojo,” or “evil eye,” can cause physical discomfort like fever, crying and restlessness was brought to the New World via Spanish and Moorish folk magic.

Middle Eastern influences beyond the Moors

Influential as the Moors were, they are not the only Middle Eastern influence in modern Mexico.

Following the fall of the Moors, many Sephardic Jews fled from the Middle East to colonial Mexico to escape the Inquisition. Later waves of Sephardic Jews arrived from the crumbling Ottoman Empire in the early 20th century. These communities established synagogues, cultural institutions and social networks, primarily in Mexico City.

While Mexico has seen periods of antisemitism throughout its history, modern Mexico hosts one of the largest and most vibrant Jewish communities in Latin America, mostly in Mexico City.

Meanwhile, the Lebanese diaspora in Mexico — currently standing at more than 500,000 descendants — has shaped the nation’s culture, cuisine and commerce since the late 19th century.

In the 1890s, they left to escape political oppression, heavy taxes, religious conflict and military conscription. At the same time, Mexico’s then-president, Porfirio Díaz, encouraged foreign immigration and trade, offering a welcoming environment and growing business opportunities.

During the period between the 1890s and 1930s, more than 100,000 mostly Lebanese immigrants arrived from Arabic-speaking nations, settling predominantly in the Yucatán, but also in Veracruz, Puebla and Mexico City.

In the early 20th century, the Lebanese community contributed around 50% of the total immigrant input to Mexico’s economy, and it remains one of Mexico’s most successful immigrant groups.

I’ve known for years that words like ¡ojalá!, albañil, and azotea are Arabic in origin, but I had no idea about other enduring Middle Eastern influences. The next time I use the Talavera dish I bought in Puebla, I’ll appreciate its ancient Moorish history, going back almost 2,000 years.

Louisa Rogers and her husband Barry Evans divide their lives between Guanajuato and Eureka, on California’s North Coast. Louisa writes articles and essays about expat life, Mexico, travel, physical and psychological health, retirement and spirituality. Her recent articles are available on her website, authory.com/LouisaRogers.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Fugitive swaps, a strawberry spat and a stronger peso
World.content:
Mexico and the United States spent the week of Aug. 17 trading shows of security cooperation, from fugitive handovers to a new drone-technology pact, culminating Wednesday in a federal operation in Michoacán that saw nine alleged members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel arrested and set off narco-blockades at more than 20 points across the state.

That cooperation ran alongside friction on other fronts. Mexico is contesting a proposed U.S. antidumping tariff on strawberry exports and objecting to Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Central America rather than home, as trade uncertainty lingers more than a month after the U.S. declined to renew the USMCA free trade deal in its current form. Domestically, the fallout from the U.S. visa revocation of former president López Obrador’s son continued to shadow the government’s messaging on fuel-smuggling enforcement. Against that backdrop, the peso’s push below 17 to the dollar stood out as a rare point of good economic news, as the central bank held its interest rate steady on lingering inflation concerns.

The week also brought a new Mexico-made electric vehicle, a national debate over kids and social media, and a presidential sick day. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Fugitive returns and a new drone pact mark security cooperation

Mexico and the United States kept up a steady drumbeat of security announcements this week. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said U.S. authorities returned three wanted fugitives to Mexico in a single day — one linked to the CJNG, one wanted for murder in Zacatecas and one for fraud — while separately handing over six more fugitives wanted for crimes including murder and firearms offenses. Jalisco police also captured Antoni Covarrubias, wanted for second-degree murder in California, in Puerto Vallarta, which Johnson called the ninth high-profile U.S.-targeted arrest in the state in recent weeks. At the same time, the U.S. and Mexico conducted a joint security exercise along the El Paso-Ciudad Juárez border, and the two countries signed a declaration of intent on drone technology that will let Mexico’s Defense Ministry access the U.S. Army’s marketplace for unmanned aircraft systems, though no models, quantities or purchases have been agreed.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch drew public praise from DEA Administrator Terry Cole at the 40th International Drug Enforcement Conference in Buenos Aires, where García Harfuch said U.S. agencies are processing 155 arrest warrants tied to Mexican investigations and reported that Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit has frozen more than 8.6 billion pesos in assets. He also cited a more than 50% drop in daily homicides, from 86 to 42, over the past two years, a figure attributed to his ministry’s own count of arrests and seizures.

The Michoacán operation capped the week’s security news: Soldiers and National Guard troops arrested nine people, including two women identified as relatives of CJNG plaza boss Heraclio “Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez, who evaded capture as the operation set off blockades that were largely cleared by Wednesday afternoon.

That flow of cooperation announcements ran alongside a separate dispute over fuel smuggling and politics. Sheinbaum said at Tuesday’s mañanera that fuel smuggling, or huachicol fiscal, is “practically over” in Mexico thanks to customs interventions and arrests — a claim she offered in the context of defending her government against opposition criticism. That criticism stems partly from the U.S. revocation of the visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, son of former President López Obrador, which Sheinbaum has called a political matter, saying he “was not” ever on authorities’ radar for criminal involvement. The fuel-trafficking case itself advanced this week when Rear Admiral Fernando Farías Laguna, accused of leading a Pemex-linked smuggling ring, was extradited from Argentina and jailed at the Altiplano maximum security prison. The case has damaged the Navy’s reputation and drawn indirect allegations, which Sheinbaum has rejected, involving López Beltrán.

Strawberries, Vietnam imports and a Canada call test trade ties

Mexico is contesting a U.S. Commerce Department finding that could impose antidumping tariffs on Mexican strawberries, which supplies 98% of U.S. strawberry imports. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard called the U.S. criteria “arbitrarily applied” and inconsistent with USMCA provisions; a final ITC ruling isn’t expected until early 2027, and the case could affect roughly 5,000 Mexican producers and 151,000 jobs if it proceeds. Sheinbaum has warned the case could set a precedent for challenging other Mexican agricultural exports.

Separately, Mexico’s imports from Vietnam more than doubled in the first half of 2026 to $18.4 billion, a jump that has raised suspicions — flagged in a recent White House report naming Mexico a “Tier 1” transshipment risk — that Chinese goods are being routed through Vietnam to dodge Mexico’s tariffs on non-free-trade-agreement countries. Mexico has denied being a transshipment hub for Chinese goods bound for the U.S.

Against that backdrop, President Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney discussed North American trade by phone on Thursday. Carney’s office said the two underscored the importance of renewing the USMCA pact soon, and separately thanked Mexico for deploying more than 400 firefighters to help combat wildfires in British Columbia. The call came as Trump-imposed tariffs on Canadian goods, delayed this week, loomed for Saturday absent a deal. (The U.S. tariffs on Canada ultimately went into effect after trade talks collapsed late Friday night.)

Peso strength collides with a cautious Banxico

The peso dropped below 17 to the U.S. dollar this week, dropping below 16.9 on Friday, largely on dollar weakness following a U.S. Treasury bond buyback announcement. The currency has appreciated nearly 6% in 2026, a gain Banxico credits with helping cool inflation.

Even so, the central bank held its benchmark rate at 6.5% earlier this month. In meeting minutes released this week, four of five board members cited persistent services inflation as a driver of that decision. Headline inflation slowed to 3.12% in July, but Banxico now doesn’t expect it to reach its 3% target until the fourth quarter of 2027. The bank also flagged Middle East tensions as an upside risk to oil prices. Separately, INEGI’s preliminary July data showed the economy growing 2.7% annually, which Rodríguez called “another piece of good news” following 2.1% growth in the second quarter.

Other business and finance news this week:

Mañanera themes: EVs, phone lines and a presidential sick day

On Monday, Sheinbaum said she opposes a social-media ban for minors like Australia’s, calling the idea “very problematic” and noting enforcement challenges, while Education Minister Mario Delgado announced a nationwide teacher consultation on classroom device rules ahead of the Aug. 31 school year.

At Thursday’s press conference, Sheinbaum unveiled a prototype of Olinia Carga, the government’s second domestically developed electric vehicle, a light-cargo EV that can carry 650 kilograms and will sell for around 150,000 pesos starting in late 2027. The same day brought a new arrest in the 2024 kidnapping case of Sinaloa Cartel figure “El Mayo” Zambada.

On Friday, Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez, standing in for an ill Sheinbaum, told U.S. Ambassador Johnson that Mexico disagrees with Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica rather than to Mexico.

Elsewhere, millions of Mexican cell phone lines were suspended after an Aug. 15 mandatory registration deadline passed, though regulators say most affected users can still recover service. Mexico also abstained from an OAS vote, which passed 29-1, to convene an emergency session on Nicaragua’s move to bar opposition candidates, with representative Alejandro Encinas citing Mexico’s non-intervention principle. Friday’s mañanera, run by Rodríguez after Sheinbaum announced she had the flu, also touched on new archaeological finds in a Chiapas cave tied to Zoque ritual traditions.

Regional news roundup:

And some good news to close out the week:

Looking ahead

Several threads left open this week are likely to develop further: Security cooperation with the U.S. continues to strengthen, while trade friction between the two countries shows no sign of easing. On a practical note, cell phone users facing the next registration deadlines — Aug. 31 for numbers ending in “1” — should act before their lines are suspended.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: From the archive: How to whistle like a true Mexican
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in January 2025 — is a perfect example, offering humorous insight into the fine art of whistling.

I have known no jealousy like the jealousy I feel when I hear Mexicans’ elaborate category of effortless whistles.

Okay fine, they’re not effortless. They just sound that way because they learned how to do it when they were kids. You know, like speaking Spanish.

Indeed, whistling is part of the language in some meaningful ways. There are specific whistles used for getting people’s attention. There are whistles for saying “Hey buddy, what’s up?” from across the street. There are whistles for saying, “But of course, my horse” — okay, maybe not exactly that, but a kind of “You know it!” with that adorable tone. There are whistles to say, “Wowza, nice butt, strange woman I don’t know!” Some whistles say, “Okay, back up your car now, a little more, a little more, a little more, stop!” There are even whistles to tell people where they can stuff it. Careful with those.

And I am going to learn them all.

A realistic goal

Well, I’m going to try. Forget turning my health or finances around; it’s too big a task. I need something I actually stand a chance at being able to bite off. Even though the prospect of practicing them takes me back to the deep humiliation I felt trying to string a four-word sentence together in Spanish while the three-year-old next to me rattled off deep, complex sentence after deep, complete sentence, I’m committed. I did it once, and I can do it again!

I won’t necessarily use them all, or use them frequently. In fact, I’m fairly certain that men whistle much more than women around here, anyway. Like cursing, it falls into a decidedly “male” category of behavior, and is seen as somewhat crass and unladylike.

I’ve also noticed that whistling is more prevalent among lower socio-economic classes than among the more well-to-do. Part of this is simply cultural habit, growing out of the need to communicate at great distances. It’s more pleasant sounding, and clearer, than shouting. If you’re willing to do some digging, there are actually some fascinating examples of whistles-as-language. There’s a cool short video about this below.

But I don’t need to be communicating over great distances in the Oaxaca countryside. I just want to have some fun.

Indigenous Whistle Language In Mexico

Watch this video on YouTube

And I don’t want to go too fast, but I’m also an eager learner. This video is pretty cute, by the way, as an introduction to the meanings of different whistles.

Here are the specific ones that I want to learn:

Learning how to whistle in Mexico (in different styles, for different purposes)

The whistle to get someone’s attention

Say you’re walking along a busy street and you need to get someone’s attention. Maybe it’s a vendor, or maybe a taxi that didn’t notice you! This whistle is perfect for it. It’s also important for me personally, because my voice does not carry at all. My loudest is not very loud, and the strain on my voice physically hurts! This can either be a quick low-high sound, or the more universally recognized high-low-slightly higher.

The ‘you can count on me, buddy’ whistle

I mostly want to learn this one because I think it’s both hilarious and adorable. My partner does this one sometimes, and even though it’s kind of a joke, I am 100% charmed.

‘Hey, friend on the other side of the street!’

Finally, I’ve just got to learn this whistle. It’s short and sweet, and I don’t care that I’ve hardly ever heard it from a woman’s lips.

So those are the three goals. Three distinct whistles — I can kind of do a “pucker” whistle now, but not very well — should be manageable in a year, right?

In the meantime, I’m dying to know: can you whistle? Can you do any specifically Mexican whistles? I especially want to know how many women out there can — please let me know in the comments!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Keep Colombia Wealth Tax for Quake Rebuild, Ocampo Says
World.content:
Colombia · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Ocampo urges keeping Colombia’s wealth tax for quake rebuild.

— How big The tax raised COP 1 trillion (US$328 million) in 2024.

— The real story Ocampo calls it the most progressive tax, offsetting hidden capital income.

— The catch Any reform applies only from 2027, not the current budget year.

— Who pays Only 32,397 taxpayers paid it in 2024, 0.5% of filers.

— What comes next Government wants to phase it out, but no bill exists yet.

A former finance minister argues the levy is the fairest tax in Colombia, while the government wants it gone.

The Centro Internacional business district in Bogotá, where much of the wealth the tax is meant to reach is managed.

Keep Colombia wealth tax to help rebuild after the earthquake, former finance minister José Antonio Ocampo says. Ocampo publicly urged the government not to abolish the levy, which he called the most progressive of all taxes.

Ocampo’s Call to Keep Colombia Wealth Tax

However, José Antonio Ocampo, a former Colombian finance minister, has urged the government not to scrap the Colombia wealth tax. Infobae Colombia reported his argument on Sunday 23 August 2026, citing a column he wrote in El Tiempo.

Still, Ocampo said the tax should not be eliminated because it is the most progressive and offsets under-declared capital income. Infobae summarized his position, saying that keeping the wealth tax would be indispensable to inject resources for completing reconstruction of affected areas.

Ocampo served as finance minister under the previous government and designed the current wealth-tax structure. His column in El Tiempo, cited by Infobae, underscores his authority on the matter.

The wealth tax, known as the impuesto al patrimonio, is an annual levy on net worth. Ocampo’s stance reflects his design of the current structure.

Government Wants to Phase Out the Levy

President Abelardo de la Espriella’s government has stated it wants to eliminate the wealth tax gradually. El Espectador reported that De la Espriella has repeated that the levy hurts investment and its contribution to revenue is marginal.

However, the tax remains in force for now. Although no bill number or official title has been identified, reporting says it would form part of a new tax reform.

However, the government’s plan to phase out the tax faces a timing hurdle. Any tax reform applies only from 2027, not the current budget year.

However, the government’s plan lacks a specific bill or date. Meanwhile, the tax remains in force for now.

Wealth Tax Raises Little Revenue

El Espectador reported that the Colombia wealth tax raised barely COP 1 trillion (US$328 million) in 2024. That was about 0.6 percent of DIAN revenue.

Meanwhile, another outlet reported slightly higher figures: COP 1.21 trillion in 2023 and COP 1.47 trillion in 2024. These two estimates should be considered separately, as they come from different sources.

In fact, the tax’s contribution to state coffers is small. Meanwhile, the tax’s low yield—about 0.6 percent of DIAN revenue—supports the government’s view.

Still, Ocampo argues the tax’s progressivity outweighs its modest financial return. In addition, the tax’s yield is small compared to total revenue.

As a result, its fiscal impact is limited.

Few Taxpayers Are Affected

Only 32,397 taxpayers paid the wealth tax in 2024, around 0.5 percent of individual income-tax filers, El Espectador reported. This shows the tax is narrow in its reach.

The finance ministry set marginal rates starting at 0.5 percent on net wealth above COP 3 billion. It rises to 1 percent above COP 5 billion.

For four years only, the top rate reaches 1.5 percent above COP 10 billion (US$3.28 million). In addition, the tax’s narrow base means few individuals bear its burden.

This is because the threshold starts at COP 3 billion (US$984,000), limiting it to the wealthiest. Meanwhile, the tax’s narrow base means few individuals pay it.

However, the threshold starts at COP 3 billion, limiting it to the wealthiest.

Fiscal Room Is Thin After Earthquake

Moreover, Mauricio Salazar Sáenz told Blu Radio that Colombia faces the earthquake with little fiscal room. He added that any tax change now applies to 2027; therefore, a reform will not raise money for the current budget year.

This timing problem means that even if the government moves to scrap the wealth tax, the fiscal benefit would not come immediately. Meanwhile, the need for reconstruction funds is pressing.

Salazar Sáenz directs the Observatorio Fiscal at Universidad Javeriana, a public-finance watchdog. His comments highlight the fiscal constraints facing the government.

In addition, Salazar Sáenz’s comments highlight the fiscal constraints. As a result, the government faces tough choices on tax policy.

Wealth Tax Is Progressive, Ocampo Says

Ocampo’s defense of the Colombia wealth tax rests on its progressivity. He argued that it helps compensate for the under-declaring of capital income, making it a fairer levy.

In his quoted words, the wealth tax should not be scrapped because it is the most progressive of all taxes. By contrast, taxes like the financial-transactions tax hit all users equally.

However, the wealth tax’s progressivity contrasts with the 4×1,000, which hits all users equally. This difference is central to Ocampo’s defense of the levy.

However, the wealth tax’s progressivity contrasts with the 4×1,000. This difference is central to Ocampo’s defense of the levy.

Financial Transactions Tax Also Under Scrutiny

The 4×1,000, formally the Gravamen a los Movimientos Financieros or GMF, is Colombia’s financial-transactions tax. It charges four pesos on every thousand pesos moved out of a bank account, which is 0.4 percent of each transaction.

A bill filed in the Cámara de Representantes, the lower house of Congress, sets out the burden and size of this levy. In addition, the GMF is 0.4 percent of each bank transaction, paid by the user.

It raised COP 14 trillion in 2023, equal to 5 percent of all revenue. In addition, the 4×1,000 raised COP 14 trillion in 2023, a significant sum.

Still, no executive proposal to repeal it exists, only a legislative bill. Meanwhile, the GMF’s revenue is significant, but no executive repeal exists.

Still, the tax remains a burden on all users.

No Executive Proposal to End 4×1,000

No document, statement, or bill from the De la Espriella government proposing to remove or change the 4×1,000 was identified. The only repeal text found is a 2024 bill filed by legislators, not an executive proposal.

Analysts are not on record saying the earthquake will sink proposals to remove the 4×1,000. Instead, they note that fiscal room is thin and any tax change lands in 2027.

Meanwhile, analysts note that fiscal room is thin and any tax change lands in 2027. Thus, the earthquake’s fiscal pressure does not automatically kill repeal efforts.

In addition, analysts note that fiscal room is thin. However, any tax change lands in 2027, not now.

Debate Over Colombia Wealth Tax Continues

The debate over the Colombia wealth tax is now tied to the earthquake reconstruction effort. Ocampo’s call to keep the tax contrasts with the government’s desire to phase it out.

In short, the fiscal pressure from the disaster may strengthen the case for retaining the wealth tax, at least for now. However, any change to tax policy will only take effect in 2027, leaving the current budget year unaffected.

In addition, the wealth tax is an annual levy on net worth, distinct from income tax. This distinction shapes the debate over its fairness and utility.

Meanwhile, the debate is tied to reconstruction needs. However, any tax reform will only apply from 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Colombia wealth tax?

The impuesto al patrimonio is Colombia’s wealth tax, an annual levy on the net worth of individuals above a threshold. It is distinct from a tax on income, targeting accumulated wealth instead.

How much does the wealth tax raise?

In 2024, it raised barely COP 1 trillion (US$328 million), about 0.6 percent of revenue administered by DIAN, according to El Espectador. A separate outlet reported COP 1.47 trillion (US$482 million) for the same year.

Who pays the wealth tax?

Only 32,397 taxpayers paid it in 2024, around 0.5 percent of individual income-tax filers. The tax applies to net wealth above COP 3 billion (US$984,000), with rates up to 1.5 percent for the wealthiest.

Why does Ocampo want to keep the wealth tax?

Ocampo argues it is the most progressive of all taxes and helps offset under-declaring of capital income. Infobae reported that he also sees it as indispensable for injecting resources to complete reconstruction after the earthquake.

Sources: Infobae Colombia; El Tiempo; El Espectador; La República; Blu Radio; Ministerio de Hacienda y Crédito Público; DIAN; Cámara de Representantes.

World.title: Fonatur Nayarit Resort Is Mexico’s First in Twenty Years
World.content:
Mexico · TOURISM

Key Facts — What happened Fonatur has started work on its first new resort in twenty years, in Nayarit.

— How big The first phase covers 542 hectares and costs 7,134.7 million pesos (US$422 million).

— The real story The agency is returning to its classic role of building destinations from scratch.

— The catch No completion date or hotel count has been announced; only the first phase is underway.

— On the map Centro Turístico Sustentable Compostela sits in Compostela, Nayarit, on Mexico’s Pacific coast.

— What comes next Later phases remain undefined, with the focus now on Boca de Chila and Chacala-Las Cuevas.

The new Pacific coast project marks a return to Fonatur’s classic role as a state developer. Meanwhile, the agency’s focus shifts toward the Tren Maya.

Empty coastline in Nayarit on Mexico’s Pacific shore, the kind of shore Fonatur has spent fifty years turning into resort towns.

The Fonatur Nayarit resort is Mexico’s first new state tourism development in twenty years. The federal agency, Fonatur, has begun work on the Centro Turístico Sustentable Compostela in the Pacific state of Nayarit.

A New Beginning for Fonatur

However, Mexico’s state tourism developer is building a new destination for the first time in two decades. According to El Economista, the project is the Centro Turístico Sustentable (CTS) Compostela, in the municipality of Compostela, Nayarit.

Work has already started this year. The first phase covers 542.32 hectares, about 1,340 acres, and requires an investment of 7,134.7 million pesos (US$422 million).

The project marks a return to Fonatur’s traditional role. After two decades, the agency is again building a destination from scratch.

The project is located in Nayarit, a Pacific coast state north of Puerto Vallarta. However, this marks a significant shift for the agency, which has focused on other duties.

What Is Fonatur?

Fonatur is the Fondo Nacional de Fomento al Turismo, or National Tourism Promotion Fund. Moreover, it is a federal agency that assembles land and lays down roads, water, and power.

The agency sits under the tourism ministry. In fact, according to the Diario Oficial de la Federación, Fonatur is a parastatal body assigned to the Secretariat of Tourism.

Fonatur develops land for tourism, then sells or leases it to developers. This model has produced major resort cities across Mexico.

Fonatur’s model involves assembling land and providing infrastructure, then attracting private investment. As a result, it has created major destinations like Cancún and Los Cabos.

The New Project’s Components

The site brings together two sustainable tourism projects. El Economista reported that CTS Compostela will integrate Boca de Chila and Chacala-Las Cuevas.

These are part of the first phase, which has already begun. The investment figure is 7,134.7 million pesos, which at the Banxico FIX rate of 16.90 pesos per dollar is about US$422 million.

The first phase covers 542.32 hectares, or about 1,340 acres. This area includes two sustainable tourism projects, Boca de Chila and Chacala-Las Cuevas.

Boca de Chila and Chacala-Las Cuevas are the two sub-projects within the first phase. Meanwhile, the investment of 7,134.7 million pesos (US$422 million) will fund this initial development.

Fonatur’s Past Creations

Fonatur has a long history of building resort cities from scratch. Its own list names five Centros Integralmente Planeados, meaning resort cities planned from scratch: Cancún, Ixtapa, Huatulco, Los Cabos and Loreto.

In short, these are large, planned destinations with airports, hotel zones and road grids. Cancún is the most famous example.

These planned centres are designed from scratch on empty coastline. Each includes its own airport, hotel zone, and residential areas.

These five centres are known as Centros Integralmente Planeados, or CIPs. In addition, they represent the agency’s most ambitious projects, each with its own airport and infrastructure.

Smaller Projects in the Mix

In addition, Fonatur lists three Proyectos Turísticos Integrales, or Integral Tourism Projects. These are Marina Cozumel, Litibú and Playa Espíritu, and they are smaller than the CIPs.

The new Nayarit project is a different category, a sustainable tourism centre. Still, it follows the same model of state-led development.

These smaller projects are part of Fonatur’s portfolio. They are less extensive than the five major centres.

These Proyectos Turísticos Integrales are smaller than the CIPs but still significant. However, the new CTS Compostela is a different category, focusing on sustainability.

A Nearby Precedent

The nearest precedent is in the same municipality. Fonatur’s Proyecto Turístico Integral Costa Canuva sits in Riviera Nayarit, in Compostela.

According to a Fonatur communiqué, Costa Canuva has capacity for 7,208 lodging units, of which about 3,200 will be hotel rooms. Meanwhile, that project involves a US$1.8 billion investment across 250 hectares, with a Ritz-Carlton Reserve as the first hotel.

Costa Canuva is a larger project in the same region. However, the new CTS Compostela is a different category, focusing on sustainability.

Costa Canuva is a larger project, with a US$1.8 billion investment across 250 hectares. In contrast, the new project’s first phase covers 542.32 hectares, though its full scope is unknown.

How Fonatur Works

What Is the Mexico Diesel Subsidy?

The Mexico diesel subsidy is a fiscal stimulus, not a direct payment. It waives part of the IEPS, the special tax on production and services, charged on every litre of fuel.

The finance ministry, known as SHCP, decides each week how much of the per-litre tax to forgo. Because the tax is part of the pump price, waiving it holds retail costs down.

— How big 91.7% of households are in debt, with 20.9 million people owing money to banks or digital wallets.

— The catch The 15.5% arrears rate includes digital wallets, which official bank statistics often miss.

— Who it hits Families in Buenos Aires province, where 60% borrowed for essentials like rent and utility bills.

— What comes next President Milei rejects state intervention, leaving borrowers to negotiate privately with lenders.

Argentine household debt is not about buying luxuries; it is about putting food on the table. According to the country’s main small-business federation, families are borrowing because their wages no longer stretch to cover basic needs.

The Real Reason Behind Argentine Household Debt

Argentine household debt is rising, but not because people are splurging. In fact, Salvador Femenía of CAME says borrowing is driven by a fall in purchasing power.

In an interview with Diario El Esquiú, Femenía explained that households are forced to finance basic products such as food and medicine. He stressed that loans do not go on entertainment goods but barely cover spending on food, drink, and the chemist.

CAME is the Argentine Confederation of Medium-Sized Enterprises, the country’s main small-business federation. However, its spokesman’s remarks were made in a press interview, not in a published report.

Femenía’s remarks were made in a press interview, not in a published CAME report. However, they echo a broader concern about falling purchasing power, known as poder adquisitivo.

What Households Actually Spend On

The numbers back up this picture. Financial daily El Cronista reported that 64% of households that take on financing do so to buy food and medicine.

Another survey found that 63.8% of households used their credit or loan to cover spending on food and health, above all medicines. In short, borrowing is a survival tool, not a lifestyle choice.

In addition, the provincial ombudsman’s office in Buenos Aires province found the same pattern. Its report stated that 60% of households had to borrow for food or essential costs.

The ombudsman’s office, an independent public body, confirmed the same trend. In addition, it listed rent and utility bills as key triggers for borrowing.

A Widespread Problem Across the Country

The issue is not confined to one region. As a result, a report found 60% of households in Buenos Aires province had to borrow for food or essential costs.

The same report listed the main triggers: food, rent, medicines, and utility bills. Meanwhile, a third-edition study from March 2026 found that 91.7% of Argentine households are in debt.

In addition, there was a sharp rise in those carrying more than three debts. Meanwhile, the study from March 2026 found 91.7% of households in debt, with many carrying multiple debts.

As a result, the quality of borrowing has deteriorated, making the situation more fragile. The provincial ombudsman’s report, titled “Hablemos de deudas,” highlighted inequalities and gender issues.

Meanwhile, the national study showed a sharp rise in households with multiple debts.

The Scale of Arrears

The Centro de Economía Política Argentina (CEPA), a Buenos Aires think tank, tracks household debt through its CENDEU database. It puts real household arrears, counting digital wallets as well as banks, at 15.5%, affecting 5.91 million people.

A separate measure counts 20.9 million debtors across banks and digital wallets, of whom 5.8 million are behind on payments. These figures are higher than bank-only measures because digital wallets, known as billeteras virtuales, are mobile payment apps that also lend.

CEPA’s CENDEU database counts digital wallets, which official bank statistics often miss. Therefore, the arrears rate of 15.5% is higher than a bank-only measure.

The 15.5% arrears rate, or morosidad, includes digital wallets. However, the 5.91 million and 5.8 million figures are separate measures and must not be merged.

Government Response: A Private Matter

President Javier Milei has taken a different view. Still, in early August, he rejected the idea that the state should take on the difficulties of people who took out credit.

Moreover, his government’s approach is that falling inflation and interest rates should let banks and debtors find solutions through private refinancing. Therefore, no official relief or refinancing scheme has been announced.

Perfil reported that Milei defined the situation as a problem between private parties. In addition, his approach relies on falling inflation and interest rates to encourage private refinancing.

Milei’s government has resisted intervening in private credit disputes. As a result, no official relief or refinancing scheme has been announced.

Why This Matters for the Economy

The reliance on credit for basics signals a deeper economic strain. When families borrow to eat, they have less room to spend on other goods, which can slow retail sales and consumption.

CAME, which represents small and medium businesses, regularly publishes readings on retail sales and consumption. Its spokesman’s remarks highlight how household debt is a symptom of a broader purchasing power problem.

When families borrow for basics, they have less to spend on other goods, slowing retail sales. However, CAME’s spokesman argues that this borrowing is not discretionary but forced by falling purchasing power.

The Role of Digital Wallets

Digital wallets have become a major source of credit, but official bank statistics miss much of this lending. That is why the CEPA reading is higher than a bank-only measure.

In fact, the inclusion of digital wallets in the data reveals a larger pool of debtors and arrears. Therefore, it paints a more complete picture.

Digital wallets, known as billeteras virtuales, are mobile payment apps that also lend. Including them in the data reveals a larger pool of debtors and arrears, offering a more complete picture.

A Regional Pattern

The pattern is consistent across the country. In Buenos Aires province, the ombudsman’s report highlighted that borrowing for essentials is widespread, not just in urban centers.

Meanwhile, the national study from March 2026 showed a deterioration in the quality of borrowing, with more households carrying multiple debts. This suggests that Argentine household debt is becoming both more common and more fragile.

The ombudsman’s report from Buenos Aires province listed food, rent, medicines, and utility bills as main triggers. Meanwhile, the national study from March 2026 showed a sharp rise in households with more than three debts.

Looking Ahead

As long as purchasing power remains under pressure, households will likely continue to rely on credit for basics. The government’s hands-off approach means the burden falls on private negotiations between lenders and borrowers.

In short, the data make clear that Argentine household debt is a daily reality for millions, not a distant statistic. The question is whether falling inflation will ease the strain, but that remains to be seen.

As long as purchasing power remains under pressure, households will likely continue to rely on credit for basics. However, the government has declined to intervene, leaving the burden on private negotiations.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Argentine household debt?

Argentine household debt refers to the money that families owe to banks, digital wallets, and other lenders. According to recent studies, a large share of this borrowing is used to buy food and medicine, not luxuries.

How much debt do Argentine households have?

The exact total is not known, but CEPA data shows that 20.9 million people are debtors, with 5.91 million in arrears. Another measure counts 5.8 million behind on payments, and 91.7% of households are in debt overall.

Why are Argentine families borrowing?

The main reason is a fall in purchasing power, or poder adquisitivo. This forces families to finance basic products like food and medicine.

What is the government doing about household debt?

President Javier Milei has said the state should not take on the difficulties of borrowers, calling it a private matter. The government expects falling inflation and interest rates to allow private refinancing, without a specific state policy.

Sources: Diario El Esquiú; CEPA and CENDEU; El Cronista; Defensoría del Pueblo de la Provincia de Buenos Aires; Perfil.

— How big The deal covers about 560 km of National Routes 22 and 151.

— The real story Roads stay federal, but Río Negro gains decision-making power for 20 years.

— The catch The US$60 million loan for repaving is under discussion, not part of the deal.

— Who it hits Governor Alberto Weretilneck signs with cabinet chief Diego Santilli and economy minister Luis Caputo.

The deal hands Río Negro control over two national highways and a passenger railway, but the roads stay federal property.

Argentina signs the Río Negro highway transfer on Monday 24 August 2026. The province takes over two national routes and a passenger railway.

Cabinet chief Diego Santilli and economy minister Luis Caputo will sign the agreement with governor Alberto Weretilneck at 1pm. The signing will take place at the presidential palace, Casa Rosada.

What the Río Negro Highway Transfer Includes

The Río Negro highway transfer covers National Route 22 and National Route 151, together about 560 kilometres of key corridors. Route 22 connects Río Colorado to Cipolletti, while Route 151 links Cipolletti to the La Pampa border.

In addition, the agreement includes the Tren del Valle, a passenger service running between Plottier and Cipolletti. The province will take over operation after a six-month transition period, according to Ámbito Financiero.

The signing is set for Monday 24 August 2026 at 1pm at the presidential palace. Cabinet chief Diego Santilli and economy minister Luis Caputo will formalize the agreement with governor Alberto Weretilneck.

The signing will take place at Casa Rosada, the presidential palace in Buenos Aires. Cabinet chief Diego Santilli and economy minister Luis Caputo will join governor Alberto Weretilneck.

Ownership Stays National

This is not a transfer of ownership, as regional outlet ANRoca explained. The roads remain national.

However, the power to decide what is done with them passes to the provincial government in Viedma. Therefore, the province can carry out works and sign contracts without permission from Buenos Aires.

It assumes full responsibility for the national roads, including technical design and dealing with companies. As a result, the roads remain national, but the province gains decision-making power.

This arrangement was described by ANRoca in April. The roads will remain national routes, owned by the federal government.

However, the province gains the power to decide what is done with them, as ANRoca explained.

Twenty-Year Term Confirmed

The cession runs for 20 years, the same term agreed with other provinces, reported Ámbito Financiero. Río Negro had initially asked for 30 years, but the signing reflects the shorter period.

Meanwhile, the railway piece has its own timeline. A six-month transition period was set before the province assumes operation of the Tren del Valle, according to the same report.

However, the term is 20 years, not the 30 years originally requested. This matches the period agreed with other provinces, though none are named.

The 20-year term matches what other provinces have agreed, although none are named. Río Negro had initially asked for 30 years, but the signing reflects the shorter period.

Province Takes on Maintenance and Works

The federal government framed the deal as transferring operation and maintenance of the national roads, without losing their national status. Mejor Informado reported that a decree would define this arrangement.

As a result, Río Negro will handle daily upkeep and future projects. Investments, according to the April description, would be financed through peaje, or tolls, rather than federal transfers.

In addition, the province will handle technical design and manage contracts with companies. Investments will be financed through peaje, or tolls, as described in April.

The province will handle daily upkeep and future projects, with investments financed through peaje, or tolls. This arrangement was described in April and remains the basis for the deal.

Railway Transfer to Provincial Company

Governor Weretilneck said the national government’s decision is to transfer the Tren del Valle. Therefore, the Plottier–Cipolletti service goes to Tren Patagónico.

This was reported by Diario Río Negro in April. After the six-month transition, the province will run the service.

No changes to the service itself were documented in the research. Meanwhile, the Tren del Valle service will transfer to Tren Patagónico, the provincial railway company.

The six-month transition period allows for a smooth handover. The Tren del Valle service will transfer to Tren Patagónico, the provincial railway company.

The six-month transition period allows for a smooth handover, as reported by Diario Río Negro.

Funding Dispute Before the Signing

Río Negro had held out for money before signing. NoticiasNet reported on 12 August that the province demanded legal conditions and the release of financing before moving ahead.

Provincial public works minister Alejandro Echarren said Río Negro had offered to take charge of routes 22 and 151. However, the nation refused the funds, according to the same report.

Still, the province demanded legal conditions and financing before moving ahead. The nation refused the funds, but the signing proceeded.

Río Negro demanded legal conditions and financing before moving ahead, but the nation refused the funds. However, the signing proceeded on Monday, according to NoticiasNet.

Separate Loan for Repaving

Separately, NoticiasNet reported a US$60 million loan to begin repaving once the transfer takes place. This loan is under discussion and is not part of the agreement signed on Monday.

It is not compensation from the federal government. The loan would fund initial road works, but no budget figures or start dates were confirmed.

However, the loan is under discussion and not part of the agreement. It would fund initial repaving, but no start dates were confirmed.

The US$60 million loan is under discussion and not part of the agreement. It would fund initial repaving, but no start dates were confirmed.

Wider Policy Context

The 20-year term matches what other provinces have agreed, according to Ámbito Financiero. However, the report does not say how many provinces have signed or name them.

Still, this deal fits a broader pattern of the federal government shifting road responsibilities to provinces. Río Negro is one province that has offered to take charge of its national routes.

In addition, this deal reflects a broader trend of transferring road responsibilities to provinces. Río Negro is one province that has offered to take charge of its routes.

What Happens Next

After the signing, the province will begin the six-month transition for the railway and prepare to take over road operations. In short, the Río Negro highway transfer shifts decision-making to Viedma while keeping the roads federal.

The railway will follow a similar path, with the province taking control of the Tren del Valle. After the signing, the province will begin the six-month transition for the railway.

Meanwhile, it will prepare to take over road operations, though specific powers of Vialidad Nacional remain unspecified.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Río Negro highway transfer?

It is an agreement signed on 24 August 2026. It transfers the running and upkeep of National Routes 22 and 151 to Río Negro province.

How long does the transfer last?

The term is 20 years, according to Ámbito Financiero, the same period agreed with other provinces. Río Negro had initially asked for 30 years.

Does the railway transfer to the province?

Yes, the Tren del Valle service between Plottier and Cipolletti will transfer to Tren Patagónico, the provincial railway company. A six-month transition period is set before the province takes over operation.

Will drivers pay tolls on these roads?

According to the April description, investments in the roads would be financed through peaje, or tolls. However, no toll rates or booth locations were confirmed in the research.

Argentina · TRADE

Key Facts — What happened Argentina’s trade surplus reached US$2.1 billion in July, with exports up 14.1% and imports down 1.7%.

— How big July’s US$2,115 million surplus came in under June’s US$2,194 million, while total trade rose 6.7 per cent.

— The real story Energy trade, driven by Vaca Muerta shale, ran a first-half surplus of US$5,076 million, up 61.7 per cent.

— The catch June’s monthly energy surplus fell to US$468 million from US$623 million a year earlier, despite export gains.

— What comes next A Mercosur-Singapore trade deal awaits a Chamber of Deputies vote, after a favorable committee report on August 12.

— Why it matters The deal, signed in December 2023, could open Southeast Asian markets, but its tariff details remain unpublished.

Exports rose while imports slipped, and a separate trade deal with Singapore moved a step closer in Congress.

Argentina trade surplus reached US$2.1 billion in July, according to the national statistics office. Exports climbed while imports fell, keeping the country in positive territory for another month.

July Trade Figures Released

The Argentina trade surplus stood at US$2,115 million in July 2026, as reported by INDEC, the national statistics institute. Exports reached US$8,854 million, up 14.1% from a year earlier.

Imports, meanwhile, totaled US$6,739 million, a decline of 1.7% compared with July 2025. This combination of rising exports and falling imports widened the trade balance.

The surplus was reported in INDEC’s monthly Intercambio Comercial Argentino report. This official data, published on August 20, 2026, covers all goods trade.

The surplus of US$2,115 million was reported in INDEC’s monthly report, which covers all goods trade. Meanwhile, the report also noted that total trade reached US$15,593 million.

Argentina Trade Surplus Narrows Slightly

Total trade, which is exports plus imports, reached US$15,593 million in July, up 6.7% year on year. This shows that despite the import dip, overall commercial activity remains robust.

In fact, the monthly figures reflect a steady flow of goods across Argentina’s borders. The surplus, however, was slightly smaller than June’s.

However, the July surplus came in under June’s US$2,194 million. This slight dip followed a stronger June.

The July surplus was slightly smaller than June’s, which stood at US$2,194 million. However, the year-on-year growth in exports remained strong at 14.1%.

June Surplus Was Larger

In June 2026, the surplus came to US$2,194 million, with exports at US$9,055 million and imports at US$6,861 million. That month’s total trade was US$15,916 million, up 16.4% year on year.

INDEC described June’s total trade as the highest since August 2022. Therefore, July’s figures, while strong, did not match that peak.

Meanwhile, June’s total trade of US$15,916 million was the highest since August 2022. That peak, however, was not matched in July.

June’s surplus of US$2,194 million was larger than July’s, but the gap was modest. In addition, June’s total trade was the highest since August 2022, a peak July did not match.

Energy Sector Drives Surplus

Energy has been a key engine behind the Argentina trade surplus. In the first half of 2026, the fuels and energy balance posted a surplus of US$5,076 million.

That is a jump of 61.7% from US$3,139 million in the same period of 2025. This growth is largely due to Vaca Muerta, the shale formation in Neuquén province.

Sector exports surged 42.5% to US$6,594 million, while imports held steady at US$1,518 million. In addition, the fuels and energy surplus in the first half of 2026 jumped 61.7%.

This growth was driven by Vaca Muerta’s shale output. Energy exports in the first half of 2026 rose 42.5% to US$6,594 million, while imports held steady.

As a result, the fuels and energy surplus jumped 61.7% from a year earlier.

Monthly Energy Picture Differs

By contrast, the monthly energy surplus in June was smaller than a year earlier. It stood at US$468 million, down from US$623 million in June 2025, even though chapter 27 exports rose 28.5%.

Chapter 27, which covers crude oil and refined fuels, saw exports of US$1,234 million in June. Crude petroleum oils led at US$918 million.

Still, the overall balance narrowed. Although June’s energy exports rose 28.5%, the surplus fell from a year earlier.

This was because imports also increased in that month. In June, energy exports rose 28.5%, but the surplus fell to US$468 million from US$623 million a year earlier.

This was because imports also grew, offsetting the export gains.

Mercosur-Singapore Deal Advances

Separately, a free trade agreement between Mercosur and Singapore moved forward in Argentina’s Congress. A joint committee of the Chamber of Deputies issued a favorable report on August 12, 2026.

The Senate has already given its media sanción, meaning one-chamber approval. The bill now awaits a floor vote in the Deputies, though no date has been set.

The favorable dictamen came after the bill entered the lower house on April 6. Since then, it has moved through committee review.

The favorable committee report came after the bill entered the lower house on April 6. However, the Chamber of Deputies has not yet voted on the agreement.

Deal Brings Bloc Closer to Asia

The agreement, signed in Brazil on December 7, 2023, aims to bring Mercosur closer to the Southeast Asian market. It entered the lower house on April 6 and was referred to two committees.

Imprensa Mercosul said the deal brings the bloc closer to the Southeast Asian market. It also reflects Argentina’s push to widen its trade partners.

The agreement was signed in Brazil on December 7, 2023. However, its full details remain unpublished, including tariff schedules.

The agreement was signed in Brazil on December 7, 2023, and aims to bring Mercosur closer to the Southeast Asian market. Meanwhile, its full details, including tariff schedules, remain unpublished.

Legislative Path Explained

In Argentina, a bill needs approval from both chambers of Congress to become law. The Senate’s media sanción is just the first step, and the Deputies have yet to vote.

The favorable dictamen, or committee report, clears the bill for a floor vote but does not guarantee passage. Therefore, the deal’s fate remains in the hands of the lower house.

After the committee report, the bill is now ready for a floor vote. Still, no date has been set for that vote.

The Senate’s media sanción is just the first step in Argentina’s legislative process. After the committee’s favorable dictamen, the bill now awaits a floor vote in the Deputies.

Trade Outlook Remains Positive

Overall, the Argentina trade surplus shows resilience, driven by energy exports and steady demand. While July’s surplus dipped slightly from June, the trend remains upward.

Meanwhile, the Singapore deal could open new markets for Argentine goods. As a result, the coming months may bring further trade gains.

The July surplus, while slightly smaller than June’s, still reflects a healthy trade balance. Meanwhile, the Singapore deal could open new markets for Argentine goods, boosting future trade.

What is the Argentina trade surplus for July 2026?

The Argentina trade surplus was US$2,115 million in July 2026. Exports rose 14.1% to US$8,854 million, while imports fell 1.7% to US$6,739 million.

How does July’s surplus compare with June’s?

July’s surplus was slightly smaller than June’s, which stood at US$2,194 million. June also saw higher total trade, which INDEC called the highest since August 2022.

What role does energy play in the surplus?

Energy is a major driver, with a first-half surplus of US$5,076 million, up 61.7% from a year earlier. However, the monthly energy surplus in June fell to US$468 million from US$623 million.

The Senate has given its media sanción, and a Deputies committee issued a favorable report on August 12. The Chamber of Deputies has not yet voted on the bill.

World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Mexico · Markets & Economy

Mexican Stocks Post Their Best Day Since June

Key Facts — The session. The S&P/BMV IPC closed Friday at 65,729.18, up 2.14%, its biggest one-day gain since 11 June. The FTSE BIVA rose 2.17%.

— The peso. The Banxico FIX in force today is 16.9018 pesos to the dollar. The analyst consensus is that it weakens to 17.68 by year end, not that it strengthens.

— The diesel. Fuel duty relief on diesel reached 82.59% for 22–28 August, worth 6.08 pesos a litre. That is the highest of 2026, above April’s 81.20%.

— The underspend. The government spent 499,000 million pesos, about US$29.5 billion, less than programmed in the first half. Pemex accounted for 45,297 million of it.

— The energy cut. Ramo 21, the energy budget branch, lost 61.7% of its approved first-half budget as transfers to Pemex were cut by 164,000 million pesos.

— The bond. FONDO, one of the four public agricultural trusts run by the central bank, raised 4,500 million pesos, about US$266 million, in three tranches on the Mexican exchange.

A strong Friday on the exchange, the year’s largest diesel tax break, and half a trillion pesos the government did not spend.

Paseo de la Reforma at dusk. (Photo: Ricardo Esquivel, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

A good Friday, after a bad week

The S&P/BMV IPC closed on Friday at 65,729.18, up 2.14%. That is its largest single-day gain since 11 June, a gap of just over ten weeks, and it came three days after the index touched its 2026 low of 63,933.69. The FTSE BIVA, the rival exchange’s benchmark, rose 2.17% in step.

Grupo México led, up 4.17%, with GCC up 5.05%, Pinfra 3.16% and Cemex 2.40%. Walmex fell 1.55%, and the consumer names generally lagged — which fits the retail data. Sales were down 0.2% month on month in June, against expectations of a small rise.

One correction worth making plainly, because the number is circulating. There is no analyst forecast of 16.50 pesos to the dollar. The Citi survey published on 20 August, covering 37 institutions, has a year-end consensus of 17.68, with the most optimistic house at 17.00 and the most pessimistic at 19.03. The currency is near 16.90 now, so the consensus view is mild weakening, not strengthening.

The state is paying most of the diesel tax for you

The finance ministry publishes a fuel duty waiver every Friday in the official gazette. For the week of 22 to 28 August it set the diesel stimulus at 82.59%, worth 6.0813 pesos a litre and leaving drivers paying 1.2821 pesos of the duty.

That is the highest diesel relief of 2026. The previous peak was 81.20% in early April, and the year’s low was 14.63% in late June. Petrol relief is far smaller: 22.44% on regular, and 4.03% on premium.

The reason is upstream. Brent rose more than 6% in the week to 21 August and WTI more than 5%, on Iran sanctions and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Because the Mexican fuel excise is a fixed peso amount per litre rather than a percentage, it does not fall automatically when crude climbs — so the government waives it instead, and takes the hit on tax collection.

The bigger fiscal story is what was not spent

The finance ministry’s second-quarter report, presented on 30 July, records net spending of 4.856 trillion pesos in the first half — 499,000 million pesos below what was programmed. Finance Secretary Edgar Amador Zamora said the pace of spending “will have to normalise”.

Energy took the deepest cut of any branch. Ramo 21, the budget line through which federal transfers to Pemex flow, lost 61.7% of its approved first-half budget, as the government withdrew 164,000 million pesos in subsidies to the oil company. Pemex’s own underspend was 45,297 million pesos, a 16.1% real contraction against its calendared budget, concentrated in physical investment, pensions and plant maintenance.

This is not an accounting curiosity. Pemex’s second-quarter profit fell 69.7% year on year, and fuel theft cost it 9,180 million pesos in operating losses between April and June, the worst since 2018. Deferred maintenance at a company in that condition is a liability being carried forward, not a saving.

Money for the countryside

On Friday FONDO placed 4,500 million pesos of long-term certificates on the Mexican exchange, about US$266 million. It came in three tranches: 1,337.5 million at a floating rate over 18 months, 2,234.25 million fixed at 9.11% over five and a half years, and a 928.25 million social bond at 8.84% over four and a half.

FONDO is one of four public trusts run by the Bank of Mexico under the FIRA umbrella. They are a second-tier development bank: they do not lend to farmers, they fund and guarantee the commercial banks that do, and they raise the money in the bond market. The paper carries top national-scale ratings from all three agencies that rated it. This was FONDO’s first long-term issue, though its sister trust FEFA placed 8,000 million pesos in July.

One story we are not running

A claim circulating on Monday held that the state tourism fund Fonatur will build its first new resort development in twenty years, in Nayarit, for 1,734 million pesos. We could not verify any element of it, and we are not publishing it.

Fonatur has announced no such project, in Nayarit or elsewhere; its August news was a sale of existing lots in Huatulco, Ixtapa, Loreto and Los Cabos. The agency’s own published strategy explicitly abandons the resort-building model. There is a large new development in Nayarit — Costa Nayarit, in Compostela, presented in April — but it is private, led by Grupo Prodi and partners, and worth more than 20 billion pesos, twelve times the figure quoted.

Why this matters if you are invested here

Two numbers frame Mexico this week. The policy rate is 6.50% and most analysts expect it to stay there through next year, which is what has been holding the peso up alongside remittances and nearshoring flows. Growth consensus for 2026 is 1.2%.

Against that, the state is forgoing fuel tax revenue at the highest rate of the year while running 499,000 million pesos behind its own spending plan, and the company at the centre of both is losing money faster than it is being recapitalised. Friday’s rally was real. The fiscal arithmetic behind it has not changed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Mexican peso expected to strengthen to 16.50?

No. The most recent Citi survey of 37 analysts, published on 20 August, puts the year-end 2026 consensus at 17.68 pesos to the dollar. The most bullish house in the survey is Barclays at 17.00. With the currency near 16.90 today, the consensus expects it to weaken from here, not strengthen.

What is the IEPS diesel stimulus and who pays for it?

IEPS is Mexico’s federal fuel excise, charged as a fixed number of pesos per litre rather than as a percentage of the price. When crude rises, the tax does not rise with it, so the government’s lever is to waive part of the duty each week. An 82.59% stimulus means the state forgoes 82.59% of the charge. It shows up as weaker tax collection rather than as spending.

Why did the energy ministry underspend so heavily?

Because federal transfers to Pemex flow through it. The finance ministry attributes the shortfall to “lower resources allocated to the financial strengthening of Pemex”. Ramo 21 lost 61.7% of its approved first-half budget while the state oil company’s own underspend concentrated in physical investment, pensions and maintenance.

What is FIRA, and what did it sell?

FIRA is a group of four public trusts administered by the Bank of Mexico that function as a second-tier agricultural development bank. They do not lend to farmers directly; they fund and guarantee the banks that do. FONDO, the oldest of the four, placed 4,500 million pesos in its first long-term issue, including a social bond at 8.84%.
