World.title: Billions at stake in NATO’s new pledge: how much of the defence spend stays in Hungary?
World.content:
NATO’s new 5% defence commitment could become one of Europe’s most important fiscal and economic-policy questions over the next decade. For Hungary, the sums involved could run into several billion euros a year, but the economic impact will depend heavily on how much of that additional spending is retained in the domestic economy. Halftermayer & Partners’ latest defence-industrial and macroeconomic study is authored by Dr. Ferenc Antal, a defence industry and critical infrastructure expert. The analysis finds that the same headline level of defence expenditure can produce very different growth outcomes depending on whether it is spent on imported equipment or on production, services and technology that create domestic value added.

Author: Dr Ferenc Antal

At the 2025 Hague Summit, NATO Allies agreed a new Defence Investment Pledge. By 2035, Allies aim to devote at least 3.5% of GDP to core defence requirements and up to a further 1.5% to broader defence- and security-related expenditure (NATO, 2025; NATO, 2026).

This represents a significant step up from the previous 2% benchmark and moves the debate well beyond defence policy alone. Higher military and security spending can affect budget deficits, public debt, industrial output, imports, investment and employment at the same time. The economic-policy question is therefore not only whether European countries can meet the commitment, but also how the money is spent and what economic structure develops around it.

Not every euro of defence spending has the same GDP effect

One of the central findings of the study is that policymakers need to distinguish between the location of procurement and the domestic value added actually created. A company operating in Hungary may still rely heavily on imported inputs, while a foreign-owned plant producing in Hungary can generate substantial local value added through wages, taxes, engineering work and supplier contracts.

From an economic perspective, the relevant question is therefore not simply the nationality of the contractor, but how much of total public expenditure ultimately becomes domestic production and income. If a major military platform is imported as a finished product, its direct domestic GDP contribution is limited because higher public demand is accompanied by higher imports. Domestic manufacturing, maintenance, infrastructure, engineering services, R&D and supplier activity, by contrast, generate activity inside the economy.

European value capture is not the same as Hungarian domestic value added. EU defence-industrial policy increasingly seeks to retain a larger share of defence expenditure within the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base (EDTIB). This can strengthen Europe’s collective industrial capacity, but procurement from another EU Member State may still generate only limited direct value added in Hungary (European Commission, 2024, 2025; Council of the European Union, 2025).

There is no single ‘defence multiplier’

International research does not support the simple proposition that every increase in defence spending raises GDP by the same amount. Studies by the IMF, OECD, Bank of Finland and others produce a wide range of estimates. The outcome depends on what governments buy, the foreign value-added content of procurement, how expenditure is financed and whether sufficient productive capacity is available (Bank of Finland, 2025; Furceri et al., 2026; OECD, 2026).

Investment- and technology-intensive spending can generate stronger economic feedback than consumption-like expenditure. However, if domestic industry cannot absorb rapidly rising demand, part of the additional spending may show up in higher prices, longer delivery times or further imports rather than higher real output. This is particularly relevant for Europe as countries simultaneously seek to increase defence demand and expand manufacturing capacity.

If you missed it: Deterrence needs a balance sheet: The rise of Europe’s defence finance ecosystem

For Hungary, the scale could be EUR 6–7 billion a year

Hungary has already reached defence expenditure of around 2% of GDP. Antal’s study asks what the order of magnitude would be if, purely as an illustrative exercise, the full move to 5% were treated as three additional percentage points of GDP in new expenditure.

On Hungary’s 2025 GDP base, that would correspond to roughly EUR 6.5 billion per year; on the study’s 2026 modelling base, about EUR 6.8 billion. This should not be interpreted as the expected net fiscal cost of the NATO pledge. Up to 1.5% of GDP may include broader resilience, infrastructure, cyber and security spending, some of which could already exist elsewhere in the public budget.

Even so, the order of magnitude illustrates the policy challenge. A permanent multi-billion-euro annual increase can materially affect fiscal and debt dynamics, particularly in an economy with limited fiscal space. According to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office, public debt stood at 74.6% of GDP at the end of 2025 (KSH, 2026).

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

The scenarios show how wide the economic gap can become

The study therefore uses two illustrative cases within a five-year gradual spending path. The low case assumes 10% domestic value added and represents import-dependent procurement. The higher case assumes 40% and represents substantial industrial deepening and greater domestic value capture. The 40% figure is not an estimate of Hungary’s current defence-industrial structure, but an illustrative deep-localisation case.

Illustrative case Domestic value added First-year GDP effect Cumulative additional output 2026–2030 Import-intensive 10% +0.18 pp EUR 6.8bn Deep localisation 40% +0.57 pp EUR 20.9bn

The associated impact multipliers are 0.30 and 0.95. These pairings are modelling choices informed by the international literature rather than an empirically estimated causal relationship between domestic value added and the multiplier. Under the five-year ramp-up, the first-year GDP effect is approximately 0.18 percentage points in the low case and 0.57 percentage points in the higher-DVA case; cumulative additional output over 2026–2030 is approximately EUR 6.8 billion and EUR 20.9 billion, respectively. These are mechanical scenario outputs, not forecasts.

Higher domestic value added must be built, not assumed

A sustained domestic value-added share around 40% across a broader procurement portfolio would require deeper qualified Tier 1–3 SME supplier networks, greater local engineering and systems-integration capability, stronger defence-related R&D and intellectual-property creation, expanded MRO and lifecycle capacity, higher-value processing and component manufacturing, and integration into export markets. These capabilities should not be assumed to arise automatically from higher procurement volumes or local-content clauses; they would have to be built progressively alongside the spending ramp-up.

This does not mean that every military system or component should be produced in Hungary. The relevant question is where genuinely competitive domestic capability can be developed and sustained. Artificially maintaining uneconomic local production can be as costly as forgoing strategically valuable capabilities altogether. International evidence also suggests that defence industries tend to pay above-average wages and operate with relatively high R&D intensity, creating the possibility of longer-term technology spillovers (AIA, 2026; ISED Canada/CADSI, 2026).

The composition of spending matters as much as its size

Europe’s debate over the next few years is likely to focus less exclusively on what percentage of GDP each country spends on defence. A more consequential distinction will be which countries can translate larger defence budgets into competitive industrial capacity, technology, supplier networks and export capability.

For Hungary, the 5% NATO commitment is therefore also a question of industrial capacity and competitiveness. If higher spending largely turns into an import bill, the fiscal burden remains while domestic economic feedback is limited. If procurement is linked to competitive domestic production, services, technology and know-how, the same security expenditure can create substantially more economic value at home.

The question is therefore not only how much Hungary spends on defence, but how much value ultimately stays in the Hungarian economy.

World.title: “Where did public money disappear?”: Investigation into alleged abuses at Hungary’s central bank to begin this week
World.content:
The parliamentary committee investigating alleged abuses related to the operations of the Hungarian National Bank (MNB) will hold its first meeting at 1 PM on Wednesday, the TISZA parliamentary group told MTI on Sunday evening.

Attila Csőszi, chairman of the investigative committee, said in a video posted on Facebook that hundreds of billions of forints in public money had been transferred to foundations established by the Hungarian National Bank. He said the investigation would, among other things, seek to establish what happened to those funds.

According to the politician, the committee will examine “who was responsible and where the public money disappeared”, who benefited the most from it and what it was spent on. The committee began its work at the initiative of the TISZA parliamentary group.

As an example, Csőszi cited the case of Kecskemét, where the Neumann János University and Tudásváros received HUF 144 billion. However, he claimed that a significant portion of the money – HUF 127.5 billion – was “gambled away on the stock market”.

He also referred to a property in Balatonakarattya, saying that HUF 20 billion had been spent on its renovation before it was subsequently put up for sale for HUF 9 billion. Regarding the MNB’s headquarters, Csőszi raised the issue of its construction costs, saying the original budget of HUF 55 billion eventually rose to HUF 105 billion.

The chairman of the investigative committee said its aim was to establish who was responsible for what happened. He added that the ultimate goal was to ensure that similar cases could not occur in the future.

World.title: Sunshine, storms and then scorching heat: Hungary braces for a sweltering end to August
World.content:
The final week of August will begin with moderately warm, pleasant summer weather, with daytime temperatures around 30°C and refreshing mornings. However, the heatwave will return in the second half of the week. Showers and thunderstorms may occur in several parts of Hungary on Tuesday, but most of the week is expected to be sunny and dry, according to a forecast from HungaroMet Zrt. sent to MTI on Sunday.

The beginning of the week

On Monday, cloudier areas will gradually clear and become more broken, followed by plenty of sunshine alongside high and developing cumulus clouds. The northern parts of the country may remain cloudier at times, with a chance of light rain or showers. Northerly winds may occasionally produce stronger gusts. Daytime temperatures will generally range from 26 to 32°C.

On Tuesday, cloud cover will increase significantly from the south-west and west. Showers and thunderstorms may occur in several parts of Transdanubia, with rain potentially spreading further east from the evening onwards. Southerly and south-easterly winds will occasionally strengthen in Transdanubia, while easterly and north-easterly winds will pick up elsewhere. Temperatures will rise from 9–19°C in the early morning to 26–33°C in the afternoon.

Wednesday and Thursday

By Wednesday morning, patches of fog and low cloud may form in western and south-western Hungary. Once these clear, sunny weather is expected across the country, with only a few cumulus and high clouds. A few showers may still occur in the morning, but no further rainfall is expected later in the day. Winds will generally remain moderate. Morning temperatures will range from 11 to 21°C, while afternoon highs will reach 27–32°C.

Thursday will be mostly clear and sunny, with only a few high and cumulus clouds and no rainfall expected. Winds will turn south-easterly and southerly and strengthen. Overnight lows will range from 9 to 19°C, while afternoon temperatures will reach 29–34°C.

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

The weekend

Friday is expected to be sunny with only a few clouds. No rain is expected during the day, although showers and thunderstorms may develop overnight in northern and north-western areas. South-westerly and southerly winds will strengthen across much of the country. Temperatures will range from 14–22°C in the morning to a scorching 32–38°C in the afternoon.

On Saturday, cloud cover will temporarily increase significantly, with scattered showers and thunderstorms likely. Winds will turn north-westerly and may become strong across large parts of the country. Early morning temperatures will range from 18 to 24°C, while afternoon highs will generally reach 28–34°C.

Sunday is expected to be mostly sunny, with no significant rainfall. North-westerly winds may bring occasional stronger gusts. Temperatures will range from 11–19°C in the morning to 25–30°C in the afternoon, according to HungaroMet (met.hu).

World.title: Former House Speaker Kövér accused of refusing handshake from Tisza deputy speaker at memorial ceremony
World.content:
A dispute has erupted over an alleged handshake snub involving former parliamentary speaker László Kövér and Krisztián Kőszegi, a Tisza Party MP and deputy speaker, at a memorial ceremony in Báta on Sunday.

Kőszegi said Kövér refused to shake his hand during the event commemorating the 500th anniversary of the national assembly held in Báta before the Battle of Mohács. He shared a photograph appearing to show himself extending his hand while Kövér keeps his hands in his lap.

The photograph does not establish whether Kövér ultimately refused the handshake or whether the two politicians shook hands at another point during the ceremony.

‘We would expect more dignity from a former speaker’

Kőszegi criticised the alleged gesture, saying: “We would expect more dignity from a former speaker.” He argued that the history of the Battle of Mohács should serve as a reminder of the consequences of division replacing cooperation in a country.

The Tisza politician said Kövér’s “deliberate turning away” only deepened the social divisions he believes Fidesz had deliberately created over the past 16 years. Kövér served as Speaker of the Hungarian Parliament from 2010 until 2026, when Fidesz lost power following the parliamentary election.

Current Speaker: ‘It is simply inhumane’

Ágnes Forsthoffer, the current Speaker of Parliament, also reacted to the incident in a Facebook post, describing the photograph as “shocking”. “There is no way to sugar-coat it, this is simply inhumane to me. Humiliating,” Forsthoffer wrote.

She said a handshake should not be treated as an ideological issue, but as a basic human gesture. “A handshake is not about party affiliation, but about seeing the person in the other person first,” she wrote.

Forsthoffer also claimed that Kövér left the parliamentary office without meeting her. According to her account, he did not consider it important to say a few words of appreciation to the office staff he had worked with for 16 years.

She said Kövér came to Parliament to say goodbye to the staff while she was still undergoing her preparation for the role of Speaker, and that she had been advised to leave the building during his visit. Forsthoffer thanked Kőszegi for representing Parliament at the memorial ceremony and added: “Thank you for extending your hand on my behalf as well.”

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

Fidesz does not deny the alleged snub

Fidesz communications director Bertalan Havasi was asked by Telex whether Kövér had indeed refused Kőszegi’s handshake and, if so, why. Havasi did not confirm the incident, but neither did he deny it. “I don’t know, I wasn’t there, and for that reason I wouldn’t disturb our party’s national council chairman on Sunday evening,” he said.

However, he went on to argue that, if the incident had happened, Kőszegi was a representative of the Tisza Party, which Fidesz accuses of undermining the democratic rule of law.

Havasi referred to Fidesz’s July “Declaration of Resistance”, in which the party declared its total opposition to what it described as Tisza’s “anti-democratic system”. He said Fidesz members and all Hungarians had the right to freely express their opposition to the Tisza Party and its representatives.

The exchange highlights the increasingly bitter political divide between Fidesz and Tisza, which has been in government since winning the April 2026 parliamentary election.

World.title: Hungary’s Kossuth Radio to relaunch on Monday with new ‘everyone’s radio’ slogan
World.content:
Hungary’s Kossuth Radio is set to relaunch on Monday with a completely revamped programme structure, new presenters and a new slogan promising that the public broadcaster will once again be “everyone’s”.

The renewed station will officially return on 24 August, with the Rákóczi March marking the start of its new public-service programming at 4.30 AM. The station’s new slogan will be “Kossuth Radio – everyone’s again”, according to a statement from Hungary’s public media operator, MTVA.

The broadcaster said the station had spent the past month and a half broadcasting radio plays and “timeless, emblematic” interviews around the clock while its new programming was being prepared. Channel director György Kerényi said the station would preserve what was worth keeping while saying goodbye to programmes and formats that had become tired.

News and current affairs to be revamped

News programmes and several key time slots will undergo major changes. The station says its new approach will focus on reliable reporting, credible stories and knowledgeable guests, promising that its “news will be true, our stories will be authentic and our guests will be knowledgeable.”

Several new programmes will also be available as podcasts, while the station says some of its content will even be broadcast through traditional Sokol radios. Zsolt Bogár and Péter Magyari will serve as the station’s two deputy editors-in-chief.

Magyari, who previously worked for Válasz Online, will launch Nyílt titok (Open Secret) on Saturday mornings. The programme will examine controversial cases from Hungary’s past 16 years – and, according to the station, the past 36 years – with investigative reporters Róbert Báthory and Áron Kovács.

Magyari will also host Világrend (World Order), a foreign affairs analysis programme due to launch on 29 August.

The morning news and information programme Felkelő, the Krónikák news bulletins and daily current affairs programmes will be presented by Rita Benyó, Erika Hatvani Tóth, Tímea Tatár and Nóra Teszári.

György Farkas, László Illisz, István Dániel Király and Gábor Kiss will work as editors, while Dávid Dercsényi, Mátyás Fórizs, Anna Kovács, Roland Papp and Ildikó Sipos will work on the news programmes. Pálma Fazekas will head the news department.

If you missed it: Hungary’s revamped public broadcaster launches new flagship news bulletin with a surprising shift

New programmes focus on different perspectives

The revamped station will also introduce programmes covering current affairs from different perspectives. Necces, an afternoon live programme hosted by Csilla Orosz and Zsófia Sashegyi, will examine public affairs through a female perspective.

Sunday mornings will feature two new programmes focusing on Hungarians living beyond the country’s borders and religious affairs.

Anyanyelve még mindig magyar (Hungarian Is Still Their Mother Tongue) will air from 7 AM and will be hosted by Vince Rácz, a journalist at Pátria Radio, the Slovak public broadcaster’s Hungarian-language service in Bratislava.

Hetedik nap (Seventh Day) will focus on religious and church-related issues and will be hosted by journalist Dóra Laborczi. The station also plans to significantly expand its cultural programming and radio plays.

Anita Bödő will head the revamped cultural department, while new daily programmes will include Doktor Kossuth, focusing on health, and A Föld marad (The Earth Remains), dedicated to sustainability and environmental issues.

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

Kossuth Radio seeks a new identity

The relaunch comes after years in which Kossuth Radio and Hungary’s wider public media system were heavily criticised by opposition figures and independent media for serving as a vehicle for the former Fidesz government’s political messaging.

Former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was a regular guest on the station’s Friday morning Jó reggelt, Magyarország! programme, where his appearances were frequently described as interviews despite rarely involving challenging follow-up questions.

The public media system itself underwent a turbulent transition earlier this summer. On 7 July, Hungary’s public media broadcasts were temporarily interrupted as an interim management team took over, with the M1 television channel displaying an apology message for an extended period.

World.title: Rare ‘water devil’ filmed on the Danube in Hungary – video
World.content:
A remarkable weather phenomenon was captured on video near Ráckeve after a swirling dust devil moved from the riverbank over the Danube and briefly transformed into a spectacular ‘water devil’.

The unusual scene was filmed by Péter Tóth, a member of the Pilis Park Forest team, who had originally gone to the Danube to document the river’s exceptionally low water level. Instead, he ended up recording a rare and striking atmospheric phenomenon.

Dust devil turns into water vortex

Tóth was working in the Ráckeve area when he noticed a small swirling column of air and dust on the riverbank. At first, he was unsure whether the phenomenon was worth filming. But when he realised that the rotating vortex was moving directly towards the Danube, he reached for his phone.

As the vortex reached the water, it began lifting droplets from the river, creating a spectacular swirling column above the surface. Tóth later described the sound of the falling water droplets as resembling a fountain operating in the middle of the river.

Although the phenomenon itself was relatively small and disappeared within a short time, it left behind a clearly visible disturbance on the Danube. According to Tóth, the vortex created waves similar to those produced by a small boat passing through the water.

What is a water devil?

The term “water devil” is commonly used to describe a short-lived rotating column of air over a body of water. However, such phenomena should not automatically be confused with a tornado or a classic waterspout.

Small vortices can form close to the surface when local heating, rising air and particular wind conditions combine. A dust devil developing over land can also move over water, as appears to have happened near Ráckeve.

Humidity, air movement, surface temperatures and local wind conditions can all influence the development of these vortices. Their appearance can be spectacular despite their typically short lifespan.

Can a water devil be dangerous?

According to Kemma, a small, short-lived water vortex is generally much weaker than a conventional tornado, but it can still pose a risk to people nearby. For small boats and kayaks in particular, sudden rotating winds, waves and disturbed water can create dangerous conditions.

The precise meteorological classification of the phenomenon filmed near Ráckeve cannot be established from the footage alone. What is clear, however, is that the vortex was strong enough to lift water from the Danube and create noticeable waves that remained visible even after the swirling column disappeared.

The extraordinary footage also provided an unexpected glimpse of nature at work during a period when the Danube has been making headlines for a very different reason: its exceptionally low water level.

World.title: Romanian Air Force to open Bucharest International Air Show 2026
World.content:
The Romanian Air Force will open the flight program at the Bucharest International Air Show (BIAS) 2026 on Saturday, August 29. The displays will begin at 10 a.m. at the Băneasa International Airport.

The aerial program will include aerobatics, tactical demonstrations, and formation flights featuring F-16 Fighting Falcon jets, C-27J Spartan and C-130 Hercules transport aircraft, and IAR-330 helicopters, according to the Ministry of Defense.

Military aircraft from Spain, Germany, France, Italy, Turkey, and Slovenia will also perform at this year’s event at the invitation of the Romanian Air Force.

The static exhibition will feature an F-16 Fighting Falcon, a C-27J Spartan, IAR-330 and IAR-316B Alouette helicopters, and an IAK-52 training aircraft. Visitors will also be able to see a replica of the Vlaicu II aircraft, a full-scale model of the IAR-80, an IAR-317 Airfox helicopter, and a TPS-79R radar.

The exhibition will further include HAWK and M903/PATRIOT systems, flight and infantry weapons simulators, and an explosive ordnance disposal vehicle.

World.title: Uber analysis reveals different mobility patterns across 39 Romanian cities
World.content:
Cities across Romania show distinct ride patterns depending on the day of the week, local demand, and popular destinations, according to an Uber analysis covering 39 urban areas. The data, based on rides ordered through the app in the first half of 2026, also found that 10 p.m. was the busiest evening hour in almost every city analyzed.

One of the clearest differences was between weekday and weekend activity. Smaller cities generally recorded more visible shifts, while demand in Bucharest remained almost unchanged throughout the week.

As such, Bistrița registered the largest weekend increase, with ride activity approximately 22% higher than on weekdays. It was followed by Târgu Mureș, where activity rose by around 20%, and Buzău, with an increase of approximately 10%.

On the other hand, in Bucharest, the difference between weekend and weekday activity was only 0.4%.

According to the same report, while 10 p.m. was the most active evening hour across nearly all cities, the number of rides varied significantly. Bucharest recorded more than 701,000 trips during the peak time slot over the six months analyzed. Timișoara followed with more than 150,000 rides, while Iași recorded approximately 84,600 and Cluj-Napoca more than 66,300.

Restaurants were the most common category of destination in all 39 cities. Schools, hospitals, railway stations, and other transport hubs also frequently appeared among popular destinations, alongside shops and hotels.

Uber said mobility patterns were influenced by factors including city size, local infrastructure, working schedules, social habits, public transport networks, and access to local services.

“The data show that users turn to the app for both leisure activities and essential trips to schools, hospitals, railway stations, and airports. There is no single mobility pattern for Romania, and the services we provide must reflect this diversity,” said Iwona Kruk, Uber’s communications lead for Central and Eastern Europe.

Uber has been authorized in Romania as an alternative transport digital platform operator since 2020 and works exclusively with authorized partners. The app is currently available in 39 Romanian cities, and operates in more than 10,000 cities across over 70 countries worldwide.

World.title: Romania’s central bank ups inflation forecasts for end-year 2026 to 2028
World.content:
According to the new forecasts issued by the National Bank of Romania (BNR), the annual inflation rate in the country will stand at 6.1% in December, compared with the previously estimated level of 5.5%, and will decrease to 3.4% in December 2027 and to 2.8% in June 2028, compared to 2.9% and 2.7%, respectively, forecast in May for the end of 2027 and March 2028.

BNR officials part of the monetary policy meeting said that the inflation rate will undergo a substantial downward correction in Q3 2026, amid the exhaustion of the direct effects of the removal of the electricity price cap and the increase in VAT rates and excise duties.

"The annual inflation rate will fluctuate slightly in Q4 2026 and will then resume its decline on a trajectory higher than that shown in the May 2026 forecast, re-entering the target range at the end of 2027, two quarters later than in the previous projection," the same source said, cited by News.ro.

Data published earlier this month showed that the annual inflation rate in Romania fell by 2.2% for the first time in the last twelve months to 8.2% in July.

The annual inflation rate began to decline in June, as anticipated, falling to 10.42%, from 10.85% in May, but remained visibly above the level recorded in the last month of Q1, of 9.87%, given the significant increases in the dynamics recorded during this period in energy and fuel prices and regulated prices.

Board members noted the prospect of a gradual decline in the annual inflation rate starting in Q1 2027, as well as the relatively higher level at which it is expected to stand, particularly in the middle segment of the forecast horizon.

It was also noted that the action of these factors takes on a strongly disinflationary character in Q3 2026, including as a result of lower vegetable and fruit prices. However, until then, higher telecommunications and RCA insurance tariffs, as well as high natural gas and fuel prices, will keep inflation high before coming down again.

Short-term upside risks for the trajectory of Romania’s inflation rate were the evolution of electricity and food prices, amid this year's severe drought, as well as the trajectory of crude oil and other commodity prices, as the war in Iran drags on.

Mild disinflationary pressures were expected from fundamental factors in the near future, BNR board members said, referring to the considerable size reached by the aggregate demand deficit in Q1 2026 and the prospect of its continued deepening over the following two quarters.

The disinflationary pressures from fundamental factors will, however, be felt increasingly strongly over a somewhat longer horizon, BNR officials argued, noting that the aggregate demand deficit is expected to deepen through Q3 2026, thus falling to lower values than previously anticipated.

BNR data also pointed to a sharper decline in private consumption in 2026 than previously forecast, implying a further improvement in the structure of aggregate demand in the current year, in favor of the contribution of investment, with implications also for the evolution of potential GDP over the longer term.

"The annual dynamics of core inflation will, however, continue to be affected in the short term by the indirect effects of higher fuel and natural gas prices for non-household consumers, and will feel the impact of higher telecommunications tariffs and RCA insurance policy prices, as well as the removal of the cap on the commercial markup for basic food products, board members noted," the document stated.

In addition, the dynamics of import prices will probably continue to increase until around the middle of next year, generating, together with the evolution of the leu/euro exchange rate, additional inflationary effects domestically.

Disinflationary pressures will come primarily in 2027 from the base effects associated with the price increases caused this year by the global energy shock.

World.title: AgriStart launches in Romania to support early-stage agrifood startups
World.content:
Romanian founders developing solutions for agriculture and the food industry can apply until September 7 for AgriStart, a new support program for early-stage agrifood startups. Ten selected teams will receive mentoring and workshops, while two will advance to a second stage offering commercialization assistance and specialized services worth up to EUR 2,000 per startup.

AgriStart is organized by Impact Hub Bucharest, acting as EIT Food’s representative in Romania, with support from EIT Food and Bayer. EIT Food is supported by the European Institute of Innovation and Technology, an EU body.

The first stage will run from September to October and cover business model validation, customer needs, market-entry strategies, and pitching. Each team will also receive four individual mentoring sessions with entrepreneurs and industry specialists.

Two of the ten startups will be selected for a second stage running from October to November. They will receive additional commercialization support, access to an advisory board of industry experts, and specialized services valued at up to EUR 2,000 each.

The program is open to early-stage entrepreneurs and startups, researchers seeking to turn their work into products, university staff, corporate or NGO innovators, EIT Food Challenge Labs alumni, and multidisciplinary teams.

Eligible projects may be at the validated idea, prototype, minimum viable product, or initial market-testing stage. Areas covered include agricultural and food technology, precision and digital agriculture, smart farming, sustainable food, circular economy, food waste, packaging, and supply chains. Participants must have established a legal entity in 2026 or commit to creating one by the end of the program’s first stage.

Applications are open through September 7, with the selection scheduled for September 8-9. The chosen teams will be announced on September 10, and the program will begin with an online meeting on September 15.

World.title: Western Romania: Railway traffic temporarily halted after “electrical installations” discovered on tracks
World.content:
Romania’s national railway operator CFR announced on Sunday, August 23, that railway traffic was temporarily halted on the Simeria–Orăștie section, in western Romania, after personnel identified “improvised electrical installations, placed by unknown persons” in the Turdaș railway tunnel.

According to a press release, the competent authorities went to the site and conducted investigations to establish the circumstances in which the installations were placed in the tunnel and to identify the persons responsible.

At the same time, CFR personnel carried out checks on the railway infrastructure and assisted the authorities during the investigation.

The railway operator drew attention to “the seriousness of any unauthorized intervention on the railway infrastructure or in its safety area,” as such actions can pose major risks to train traffic, passengers and railway personnel.

Railway traffic resumed at 16:41 on the same day on both tracks of the Simeria–Orăștie section, main line 200, after the completion of checks carried out in the area of the Turdaș railway tunnel, the National Railway Company CFR said in a statement. According to the cited source, no elements were identified that would require maintaining the traffic stoppage measure. The temporary stoppage did not cause delays or other implications for train traffic, the statement said.

It is not the first time that objects were intentionally placed on railway tracks. There have been four other cases in which railway workers detected obstacles on the railway line. The first incident occurred on June 18 at Constanța railway station. A piece of concrete (a safety marker) was intentionally placed on the railway, which could have led to a train derailment.

This was followed by a railway sabotage attempt in Suceava, eastern Romania, another one between Constanța Technical Group and the entrance to Constanța Railway Station, and one in Petroșani, on the other side of the country, according to Club Feroviar.

Earlier this month, CFR announced that it found three objects on the Constanța-Mangalia railway line, between Constanța and Agigea. Branches and concrete objects were intentionally placed within the railway clearance gauge and were removed. The Railway Transport Police was notified and began conducting investigations.

World.title: Romanian firefighters, Black Hawk helicopter deploy to Serbia to fight wildfires
World.content:
A total of 69 Romanian firefighters deployed to Serbia over the weekend of August 22 to 23 to protect communities affected by fires, according to an announcement made by Romanian foreign minister Oana Toiu. The detachment included 15 technical vehicles and a Black Hawk helicopter.

The Romanian firefighting module supported Serbian colleagues in the localities of Kajtasovo and Grebenac, amid vegetation and forest fires occurring in the area, according to the Department of Emergency Situations, or DSU.

Operational activity began with personnel traveling to the two localities, and two intervention sectors were established to carry out the operation, one in each locality, with the Romanian firefighters' main objective being to limit the spread of the fires and protect the communities. The intervention involved finding and extinguishing hotspots as well as monitoring affected areas to prevent re-ignition and spread.

During the two-day intervention, the Black Hawk 277 helicopter, operated by IGAv within the European RescEU mechanism, carried out 37 water drops using the Bambi Bucket system in areas affected by fires in Serbia. The helicopter dropped 92.5 tons of water on the hotspots, mainly on Sunday, August 23, according to the DSU.

Serbian foreign minister Marko Djuric thanked Romania for its assistance in fighting the fires in a social media post.

“Deeply grateful to Romania, to foreign minister Oana Toiu, and to the courageous DSU Romania firefighters for standing with Serbia at this difficult moment. Your swift and substantial assistance embodies the finest spirit of friendship, good-neighbourliness and European solidarity. Serbia will not forget it,” the official said on X.

On Friday, August 21, a thick layer of smoke covered the western Romanian city of Timişoara for the second consecutive day, following recent out-of-control wildfires in Serbia. In response, authorities recommended that residents stay indoors.

radu@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: DSU on Facebook)

World.title: New Romanian Urban Planning Code requires green roofs on large buildings, eco-friendly parking
World.content:
Romania’s new Urban Planning Code introduces mandatory green roofs for certain large buildings and sustainability requirements for outdoor parking areas, the Development Ministry announced. The legislation, approved by Parliament at the government’s proposal, enters into force this week.

According to the Ministry of Development, the local authorities will have 12 months to designate zero- or low-emission areas pending updates to their urban planning documents.

Starting January 1, 2027, permits for office, commercial, industrial, and storage buildings, as well as covered parking facilities with surfaces exceeding 1,000 square meters, will require green roofs covering at least 50% of their area, subject to the conditions established by law.

At the same time, outdoor parking areas larger than 500 square meters will need to provide permeable surfaces and sustainable rainwater drainage. Trees or shading systems must also cover at least 30% of their surface. The requirement can include solutions that generate renewable energy.

“We are introducing clear climate adaptation measures,” interim development minister Cseke Attila said. “New developments must reduce the surfaces that cause cities to overheat, manage rainwater more effectively, and contribute to clean energy production.”

The measures are intended to improve air quality, increase climate resilience and reduce the urban heat island effect.

The new Code also provides exceptions where the requirements would affect built heritage or where their implementation is not technically or economically feasible.

The Territorial Planning, Urbanism and Construction Code was drafted by the Development Ministry and adopted by Parliament following a government proposal.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Yuriy Nedopekin/Dreamstime.com, AI generated)

World.title: Rompetrol Rafinare to build solar power plant and energy storage system at Vega refinery in Romania
World.content:
Rompetrol Rafinare plans to develop a 4.8 MW photovoltaic power plant and an energy storage system of approximately 9 MWh at its Vega refinery in Ploiești. The investment is valued at nearly RON 27 million and is scheduled for completion by December 31, 2028.

According to the announcement, around RON 7 million of the project’s cost will be financed through the Modernisation Fund, while Rompetrol Rafinare will contribute approximately RON 20 million.

The photovoltaic plant is expected to generate more than 6,200 MWh of renewable electricity annually, all of which will be used by the refinery. The estimated output is equivalent to around two-thirds of Vega’s annual electricity consumption, based on its budgeted 2025 level.

The planned storage system will allow the refinery to manage the electricity generated according to its consumption profile and operational needs.

“By implementing the project, Rompetrol Rafinare estimates an annual reduction in greenhouse gas emissions of over 3,800 tons of CO2, contributing to improving the energy and environmental performance of the industrial platform,” reads the company statement.

The company also reported a reduction in the refinery’s specific energy consumption, from 2.65 GJ per tonne in 2017 to 2.42 GJ per tonne in 2025, representing a decline of approximately 9%.

Vega stopped processing crude oil in 2004 and now focuses on specialized petroleum products. It is Romania’s only producer of bitumen and supplies approximately 20% of domestic demand, with its entire output sold on the Romanian market.

The refinery also produces polymer-modified bitumen, n-hexane, solvents, chemical gasolines, and heating fuels.

During the first half of 2026, Vega processed 163,550 tonnes of raw materials and produced more than 48,000 tonnes of bitumen, up by 40.5% from the same period last year.

Rompetrol Rafinare’s major shareholders are KMG International, with a direct and indirect stake of 54.63%, and the Romanian state, which owns 44.7% through the Energy Ministry.

World.title: Translation Cutbacks Limit International Access to North Macedonia’s Literature
World.content:
For a small country of just under two million people, with a small language and an even smaller literary market, getting books translated and published abroad can be crucial to keeping its literature visible beyond its borders.

But for the past two years, Macedonian authors and publishers have had one fewer tool to help them do that. A government programme that provided grants to foreign publishers willing to translate and publish Macedonian books has been suspended since 2024.

The good news is that the Culture Ministry told BIRN there is a “real possibility” it will relaunch a redesigned translation programme later this year. But the bad news is how many excellent books have been denied a wider readership over the last two years.

The Ministry says it typically allocated between one to four million denars [16,000- 65,000 euros] a year for the programme. In 2024, around 84,000 euros was distributed through 31 contracts with foreign publishers. Foreign publishers interested in Macedonian literature could apply to North Macedonia’s Culture Ministry for funding to cover translation costs, reducing the financial risk of publishing authors who are largely unknown in their markets.

Without that incentive, publishers say, some potentially valuable translations simply do not happen. “Our success at international book fairs, such as Frankfurt, is diminished,” says Bojan Sazdov, editor-in-chief of the publishing house TRI and president of the Macedonian Association of Publishers.

“When there is interest in translating a Macedonian book, we can no longer point publishers to the programme as a way of obtaining funding for the translation.”

World.title: Hanging Out: Serbia’s Ruling Party Funfair is About Suppressing Voter Turnout
World.content:
Without Novi Sad’s EXIT Festival, this year’s summer entertainment in Serbia was provided by the ruling Progressive Party funfair.

After a long day visiting factories, inspecting schools, roadworks and parks, government ministers, advisers, and local authorities hung out with people under white tents.

The show included music, dancing, feasting, and live television broadcasts.

Just in the first 18 days of August, President Aleksandar Vucic made 64 live appearances on Serbian TV, according to the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability, CRTA.

Not quite a formal election campaign, if you ask Vucic. Something between a ‘presidential tour’ and a prequel to the actual election campaign that everyone expects in the autumn.

Such media domination is familiar to those who follow populism; party leaders skip formal institutions and speak directly to the people.

When this media takeover combines with the atmosphere of a village fair, people tend to ask private questions publicly. Here’s where the media literacy classes provided by Serbia’s tabloids begin paying off.

World.title: Seven Days: Ukrainian Recalls Captivity at Hands of Bosnian Serb
World.content:
Mykola said he spent most of his captivity in a forest pit between the villages of Shybene and Krasny Rih. He said his hands were tied and there were rats in the pit. When he killed one after it bit him, he said a soldier hit him in the head with a rifle butt. The soldier told him: “Kill another one and I’ll shoot you.”

Mykola said he saw other captives being tortured.

According to the Ukrainian Media Initiative for Human Rights, MIHR, which inspected the site, the pits were some 90 centimetres deep; those inside had to sit in water; they lost feeling in their legs; and they had to urinate and defecate in the same spot.

Lidiia Tarash, a journalist and head of the documentation department of MIHR, said the researchers were led to the site by Mykola. A dead body was found in one of the pits, as well as the remains of Russian military rations, fortifications and ammunition boxes.

MIHR identified five locations in the area where civilians were held and documented the capture of 43 individuals. Its findings helped lead to the indictment of Savicic. Multiple interlocutors said Serbs were among the Russian forces. Everyone named Savicic as being in charge, Tarash said.

In late May last year, the X account of Milorad Dodik, then the president of Bosnia’s predominantly Serb-populated Republika Srpska entity, published a photo of himself visiting the representative office of the Serbian Orthodox Church in Russia. Savicic was in the photo.

Britain imposed sanctions on him in November 2024.

Mykola said Savicic and his unit are the reason he still has trouble sleeping at night. His back was damaged during his captivity and he said he is haunted by the word ‘liberation’, which he heard over and over again from his captors.

“They kept saying: ‘We came to liberate you.’ But liberate me from what? From a normal life?”

Savicic’s trial is a matter of justice and responsibility, he said.

“None of them can say: ‘I was just following orders’ and to think they aren’t responsible for it,” Mykola told BIRN. “Someone gave you an order, but it was still your choice whether to execute it.”

World.title: Saudi Dissident, Held by Bulgaria Since 2021, is Freed
World.content:
A photo of Abdulrahman al-Khalid that was distributed at a demonstration calling for his release in March in Sofia.

Saudi dissident and human rights activist Abdulrahman al-Khalidi was freed on Friday, having spent almost five years in administrative detention in Bulgaria after he was designated as a threat to public security.

“Abdulrahman has just been freed following a modification of the control measure,” activist and publisher Victor Lilov. who has long campaigned for al-Khalidi’s release, confirmed to BIRN.

The Bulgarian Helsinki Committee NGO, which also confirmed al-Khalidi’s release, described his four years and ten months of custody as “one of the most prolonged cases of detention of an asylum seeker in Bulgaria”.

Al-Khalidi has been kept in detention centres in Bulgaria since October 2021 and has reportedly been subjected to beatings by police, suffered from dire living conditions and a lack of transparency over the reasons for his detention.

For most of this time, he was held in the Butmantsi Detention Centre on the outskirts of the Bulgarian capital Sofia. In January 2026 he was transferred to a temporary accommodation centre for foreigners in Lyubimets, near the border with Turkey.

“After almost five years of detention, this is an extremely important moment … Thank you for standing with me throughout all these years,” al-Khalidi wrote to supporters on Facebook as he was being transferred from Lyubimets to Sofia’s Migration Directorate.

Al-Khalidi’s lawyer, Diana Radoslavova from the Voice in Bulgaria Centre for Legal Aid, explained to BIRN that his release happened because he was about to compete the maximum term for which people can be held in migration detention, 18 months. He had previously been held in asylum detention.

Radoslavova was with al-Khalidi after he was released. She said the first thing he did was speak with his wife and children.

“He’s doing extremely surprisingly well, for me. He’s psychologically a very strong person because this is not an easy transition for him,” she said.

Al-Khalidi became politically active in Saudi Arabia around the time of the Arab Spring protests. Interviewed by BIRN in 2024, he explained that political arrests, often followed by death sentences, were frequent in late 2012 to early 2013. That is why he decided to leave the country in 2013.

He continued his activism abroad, also working as a journalist writing articles critical of the Saudi government. According to Human Rights Watch, he was part of late Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi’s movement, called the Bees Army, which sought to counter pro-Saudi government propaganda.

After leaving Saudi Arabia, he lived in exile in Qatar, Egypt and Turkey, where his wife, son and daughter still live.

In 2021 his Saudi documents were about to expire. The only way to renew them would have been to enter the Saudi embassy in Istanbul, the same embassy where Khashoggi was killed in 2018. To avoid Saudi officials, he decided to apply for asylum at the Bulgarian border. That is when Bulgarian authorities first placed him in detention in response to information passed on by the State Agency for National Security that the applicant posed a national security threat.

In April 2024, despite the Supreme Administrative Court in Sofia’s decision that he was eligible to receive asylum, the State Refugee Agency and the State Agency for National Security continued to keep him detained on the grounds that he was a threat to public security.

His case has been taken to the European Court of Human Rights, where a verdict is still awaited. In March 2026, 18 MEPs wrote an official letter to the Bulgarian government expressing concerns regarding his detention conditions and calling on Bulgaria to comply with legal decisions.

In recent years, multiple instances of Bulgaria denying asylum or deporting people under questionable conditions have come to light, as well as cases of police brutality, such as recent allegations of widespread violence against migrants being held in a detention centre in Pastrogor.

World.title: Week in Review: Momentous Moves and Dubious Intentions
World.content:
Last week Turkey adopted a momentous law on the disarmament of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). Many see the law as a major step towards ending the decades-long conflict with the Kurdish militants. In return for disarmament, the law foresees supervised release and postponed sentencing for many of those convicted of being involved in the PKK.

While the end of the conflict with the PKK would be welcome news for Turkey, many still wonder what motives are driving the ruling party and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to pursue such a deal. For many ordinary Kurds, there is still trepidation over whether they will truly see an improvement in their rights and freedoms.

World.title: EU Questions Serbia’s Turn to Russia for Help in Battling Wildfires
World.content:
After Russia sent an aircraft to assist with wildfire fighting in Serbia, the European Commission said late Thursday that it is also ready to provide assistance, but EU candidate state Serbia hasn’t yet activated the bloc’s Civil Protection mechanism.

“Should Serbia activate in the upcoming hours/days in response to wildfires, we will immediately coordinate with European partners to mobilise assistance in line with actual needs and the situation on the ground,” a European Commission spokesperson told BIRN.

There are 20 active wildfires in Serbia, Luka Causic, head of the Interior Ministry’s Department for Emergency Situations, said on Thursday. The situation is most dire in the Deliblato Sands nature reserve, which has been battling wildfires since late July.

Following a request from Serbia, the European Commission provided satellite imagery to support the response of local firefighters.

However, Serbia turned to Russia for air support. A Russian Emercom Il-76 aircraft arrived in Serbia on Wednesday evening, said Serbian Interior Minister Ivica Dacic.

“The aircraft can drop up to 42 tonnes of water in a single pass, making it one of the most powerful operational firefighting aircrafts, given that there are currently no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the EU Civil Protection Mechanism,” Dacic wrote on Instagram on Wednesday.

The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote on X on Wednesday evening that “the Serbian side appealed to Russia for assistance amid a critical wildfire situation and growing threats to populated areas”.

“Russia consistently supports the brotherly Serbian people,” it added.

However, the European Commission spokesperson declared that “relations with Russia and Putin’s regime cannot be ‘business as usual’”.

“When it comes to the support received from Russia, let us reiterate that the EU wants to count on Serbia as a reliable partner,” the spokesperson said.

On Sunday, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said that both the EU and Russia had offered to help with wildfires in Serbia, but that help was not needed at the moment.

“I would like to thank Ursula von der Leyen for the fact that she has included us on the map of countries at risk, and for ensuring that European mechanisms are monitoring the events here, meaning that we can expect assistance at any moment,” he said.

“The Russians have also offered us support and assistance, but it is not necessary at this point. We have sufficient forces, expertise and helicopters to deal with this situation ourselves,” Vucic added.

Serbia has been part of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism since 2015. Participating countries can request assistance via the mechanism when the scale of an emergency overwhelms the response capabilities of a country.

World.title: Thaci Expects Acquittal as Hague Court’s War Crimes Verdict Nears
World.content:
Hashim Thaci with co-defendant Rexhep Selimi (R) in court in The Hague, April 2023. Photo: EPA/Koen van Weel/Pool.

Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci said in an interview broadcast on Thursday evening that he anticipated being acquitted of all charges in the war crimes and crimes against humanity case against him and three other former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA leaders at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague.

The verdict in the case against Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi is expected on September 16.

“I expect to be acquitted of every charge. I have nothing to add to the arguments of the defence team or to my final statement in the courtroom,” Thaci said in the written interview with the Pristina-based broadcaster RTV Dukagjini.

The four men are accused of individual and command responsibility for crimes committed against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and in neighbouring Albania, including 102 murders. The crimes were allegedly committed during and just after the Kosovo War in 1998 and 1999.

All four defendants have pleaded not guilty.

Thaci said he did not regret supporting the creation of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers when he was in office, but said he had not expected the decision by Kosovo’s elected representatives to be “misused so brutally”.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA. It is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo.

In the interview, Thaci spoke about a 2010 report by former Swiss Council of Europe rapporteur Dick Marty, which alleged serious crimes including organ-trafficking by KLA-linked figures. The report ultimately led to the establishment of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers. Thaci claimed that its allegations were developed with the involvement of officials at the Council of Europe from Serbia and Russia – both of which oppose Kosovo’s independence.

“The freedom and the construction of Kosovo’s independence were unswallowable for Serbia and Russia. After failing to delegitimise it at the International Court of Justice [which ruled that Kosovo’s independence declaration did not violate international law], they turned to the Council of Europe. The aim was clear: to discredit the state of Kosovo,” he said.

Thaci also criticised the prosecution’s treatment of defence witnesses and evidence in his trial.

He accused prosecutors of giving greater weight to what he described as “fabricated testimony” originating from the time when Slobodan Milosevic was in power in Belgrade, and dismissing testimony from senior Western and international officials who were “the eyes and ears” in Kosovo.

“The prosecution is elevating evidence fabricated during the era of the Milosevic regime, and ignoring the testimony of senior officials from the US, NATO, Britain, the UN, the OSCE and other international institutions,” he said.

Thaci noted that the appearance of such international figures as defence witnesses demonstrated their concern about the proceedings.

“It is not easy for these personalities to sit in such a courtroom. I understood that they were seeing that something wrong was happening in this process. They felt a moral obligation to tell the truth,” he said.

Thaci declined to comment on the current Kosovo government’s approach to the Specialist Chambers.

Asked whether his rights had been violated during the proceedings, he replied that he considered the “process as a whole” to have involved violations.

He also criticised the decision not to release him on bail, saying that the arguments used against his release were based on “prejudices and hypotheses”. Thaci said several NATO member states had offered guarantees on his behalf and that he remained grateful to them.

During the trial, the prosecution attempted to prove that, as members of the KLA General Staff, they were responsible for lower-ranking fighters who committed crimes. The defence argued that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have real authority over lower-ranking KLA fighters.

Thaci resigned as Kosovo’s president in November 2020 to face the charges and together with the other three men was sent to detention in The Hague, where they have been ever since. The trial started in April 2023.

During the trial, KLA veterans and their supporters have staged protests in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague, accusing the Specialist Chambers of bias.

In 2024, Thaci was also charged with obstruction of justice, alongside four others, including former Kosovo Justice Minister Hajredin Kuci. The trial for this case started in February, days after proceedings in the war crimes and crimes against humanity trial ended. Thaci and the four others accused of obstruction of justice – Kuci, Isni Kilaj, Bashkim Smakaj and Fadil Fazliu – have denied wrongdoing.

World.title: Zadar Was the Most Expensive Croatian City in July
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – Zadar was the most expensive Croatian city of all in July, with strong economic growth very much being a double edged sword for the area.

Buying basic groceries has long been a negotiation with one’s own wallet for people in Croatia, but in July, the toughest conditions spilled over onto the area of Zadar County. The basic consumer basket for a four-member family here reached a record 498 euros, reports HRT. Morski writes that a basic daily trip to the shop or the market has become a source of stress for many, and citizens openly complain about the constant quiet price rises:

a previously bustling market sits almost empty

“Vegetables have become very expensive, they get used up quickly, you need a lot of them. Fruit is also very expensive and it seems to me that meat has gone up, fish has also gone up a lot,” says Zadar resident Katja. For pensioners, the situation is even more alarming. Every single purchase requires calculation and a search for discounts: “I really don’t go to the shops much. You buy where you can according to your wallet and that’s it, and yes it’s expensive, it’s definitely expensive, this isn’t for us pensioners, it’s abnormal,” is the honest assessment of Zorica, who lives on the Zagreb–Zadar route.

That consumer habits are changing and that people are buying significantly less than in previous years was confirmed to us by the sellers themselves. Zadar’s market, which in July should be bustling with local and foreign visitors, at times looks unusually empty.

Seller Rada briefly summarises the problem: “Everything is expensive, the shops too.” Her colleague Ilonka points out that even regular customers have thinned out their visits: “There are no customers. I normally have my own customers, but look, two people are walking through the market.”

the price of rapid expansion

How did it come about that Zadar took the top spot for the most expensive groceries? Experts explain that the answer lies in a specific economic effect of the rapid expansion of the regional economy.

Assoc. Prof. Dr. Jurica Bosna, Head of the Department of Economics at the University of Zadar, clarifies the background to this trend: “Nobody wants to have the most expensive basket of goods, but it still shows that the county is developing strongly, and this is an effect known in economics, when we grow faster than we perhaps should according to some optimal economic rates, then it’s unfortunately inevitable that inflation will develop and that the result will be like this,” he stated.

While macroeconomic indicators record the growth and development of the whole of Zadar County, for the general public, that statistic brings no comfort whatsoever. The vicious circle in which the economy advances strongly while prices rise in an unbridled way leaves the deepest mark on household budgets. Since wages and pensions do not come close to keeping pace, the consumer baskets of Zadar residents remain ever emptier.

World.title: Meet the Croatian Road Often Compared to the Legendary Route 66
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – There’s an incredibly scenic Croatian road frequently compared to the legendary Route 66 across the pond in the USA – and a drive along it is nothing less than breathtaking.

When someone mentions Route 66, most people immediately think of the endless American highway, old motels, neon signs and kilometres of asphalt running through some of the most famous landscapes of the United States. Few realise that Croatia has its own very interesting road with the same number in Croatia as well. It goes without saying that Croatia’s D66 doesn’t have thousands of kilometres or hold the status of an American icon, but because of the designation it carries and the landscapes it passes through, it resembles the US legend in many ways.

Putni kofer writes that it has been referred to many times as the Istrian version of Route 66 and presented it as a road that evokes old, nostalgic Istria. Today, the impressive D66 connects Pula, Labin and Vozilići with Opatija, and according to the official decision on the classification of public roads it is about 90 kilometres long. Still, if the goal is to find its most spectacular part, one should head towards the eastern coast of Istria, that is, towards Plomin.

the most impressive section begins at plomin

Plomin is an excellent place to start this short road trip. The old fortified little town sits on a hill above Plomin Bay, and right by the D66 there is also a rest area with a viewpoint. A few kilometres further on there is another spot from which the view opens towards the Kvarner Bay, Cres and Lošinj.

After that begins the stretch that makes it worth driving this road slowly. The asphalt winds under the slopes of Učka, the sea is almost constantly somewhere in sight, and on the other side of the Kvarner Cres appears. In certain places the road runs high enough above the coast that the view feels almost like from a large natural balcony. The greatest advantage of state road D66 is precisely that, over a relatively short distance, viewpoints, medieval places, steep coastline and well-known Kvarner resorts alternate.

the stunning Brseč, a town from 1102 towering above at 157 metres above the sea

SONY DSC

One of the places worth turning off the road for is Brseč. D66 reaches it after driving along the slopes of Učka, and the old part of the settlement is situated on a cliff 157 metres high above the expanse of Kvarner. The first written records of Brseč date back to 1102, although the area was inhabited much earlier. It is particularly interesting that the history of Brseč is also directly linked to the road that passes this way. The Tourist Board of Mošćenička Draga notes that the economic development of the place in the 19th century was spurred by the new road from Pula towards Plomin, then Brseč and Mošćenice and further towards Rijeka.

Today the medieval character of Brseč can still be felt in the narrow streets and passages of the old town core. From the cliff by the little church of St Magdalene one of the most beautiful views in the area opens up, while from the western entrance to the place Cres can be seen. Beneath the high rocks a completely different world is hidden. Between Brseč and Mošćenička Draga lie the beaches of Uboka and Jelenšćica, which can be reached on foot via paths that descend from the main road. The coastline in this area is extremely indented, with steep cliffs, tiny coves and stone fishermen’s cottages by the sea.

from ancient towns to well-known resorts

After Brseč the scenery changes again. D66 continues towards Mošćenička Draga, one of the best-known places at the foot of Učka. The road approaches the sea, and the high rocks gradually give way to beaches and a more built-up coastline. Mošćenička Draga developed from a fishing harbour, and today it is especially known for the long pebble beach of Sipar. Its pebbles were formed by the action of the stream that descends from the slopes of Učka and the sea that has shaped them over the years.

Just a few kilometres further on lies Medveja, another place along the D66 with a long pebble beach. After it comes Lovran, where the whole drive takes on a more elegant appearance. Instead of the almost wild coast around Brseč, old villas, gardens and houses appear along the road that recall the time when this part of the Kvarner became one of the favourite resorts of Central Europe.

just over 90 kilometres from pula to opatija

The entire D66 from Pula to Opatija is a little over 90 kilometres long, but for a panoramic outing the stretch from Plomin to Opatija is especially interesting. According to the kilometres listed on the EuroVelo 8 route, from the Plomin area to Opatija it is roughly thirty kilometres of driving.

That may not sound like much, but that is precisely the charm of this road. In a short drive one passes Plomin Bay, open views towards Cres and Lošinj, medieval Brseč, the steep slopes of Učka, Mošćenička Draga, Medveja, Lovran and finally Opatija. Although it forms part of the Croatian cycling route EuroVelo 8, this road should not be imagined as a lonely carriageway without cars. On the official route website traffic on certain sections is marked as moderate, and from Medveja towards Rijeka as heavy, so if you decide to cover it on four wheels, extra caution is recommended for cyclists.

World.title: Drniš Bypass Construction to Benefit Šibenik Port
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – The future Drniš bypass will greatly benefit the local economy, as well as Šibenik Port directly.

The construction of the second and third phases of the complex Drniš bypass project has begun, with the client being Hrvatske ceste (Croatian roads), and the contractor being the consortium of Texo Molior from Cavtat and CGP Slovenia.

Transport Minister Butković pointed out that after securing the financial structure and signing the contract, work on the project is now starting. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that he also noted that it is a technically complex intervention with a route that includes two overpasses, two viaducts and a bridge over the Čikola River. Speaking about the continuation of activities on the future Šibenik–Drniš–Knin expressway, Minister Butković highlighted that the preparation of project documentation for the section from Drniš towards the Oklaj interchange is in an advanced stage.

a 34 million euro investment

After the design of that phase is completed, a tender is planned to be issued, so the project is being gradually prepared for phased implementation. He also referred to the reconstruction of state roads DC56 and DC33, which connect the Drniš area with Split and Knin respectively, and whose total reconstruction value is around 34 million euros. After the design of that phase is completed, a tender is planned to be issued, gradually preparing the project for implementation.

“A tender has already been issued for one, the other is in preparation, so there will be a great deal of investment in road infrastructure here in the area of the town of Drniš and Šibenik-Knin County,” added Minister Butković. Šibenik-Knin County Prefect Paško Rakić stressed that the Drniš bypass is of great importance for the entire county, especially for the traffic connection of its hinterland, and that residents of the wider Drniš and Knin areas will use it.

“The Šibenik–Drniš–Knin expressway, as well as this bypass, is the backbone of Šibenik-Knin County in terms of traffic, and it is as important to us as the Pelješac Bridge,” emphasised Prefect Rakić. “This is historic for us,” emphasised Drniš Mayor Tomislav Dželalija, noting that generations of Drniš residents have waited decades for this project.

a massive development boost for the area

Expressing satisfaction that the works were ceremonially started today, he pointed out that the removal of transit traffic, along with increased traffic safety, will create additional preconditions for the expansion of the economic zone and the further development of the town. He added that the Government of the Republic of Croatia, through strong investments including road and railway infrastructure, is giving impetus to the town’s development, and thanked them for the projects being implemented in the Drniš area.

President of the Management Board of Hrvatske ceste Ivica Budimir emphasised that the project has a broader economic significance for Drniš, especially because of the direct connection of the industrial zone with the Šibenik port.

“After this road is constructed, the industrial zone in the entire Drniš area will develop significantly faster, better and to a higher quality, and become much more competitive,” emphasised Budimir. Speaking about the technical demands of the project, he added that almost ten percent of the route consists of viaducts, while the most significant structure is the large bridge over the Čikola River canyon, with a span of 220 metres, along with a series of other structures along the route.

World.title: Baćina Lakes – Meet Croatia’s Freshwater Phenomenon
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – Baćina Lakes are Croatia’s freshwater phenomenon, with water warmer than that in the sea and the ability to swim year-round.

If you’ve ever driven from Makarska down toward Dubrovnik, you’ll have passed by them. You probably glanced left for a second, spotted a blue patch amid the greenery, and continued on toward the sea. Yet there, just a few kilometres from Ploče, lies something no other Croatian town has: seven lakes within the boundaries of a single town. They are called the Baćina Lakes and bear names that sound like a list from an old book: Oćuša, Crniševo, Podgora, Sladinac, Šipak, Plitko Lake, and Vrbnik.

Putni kofer writes that six of them are interconnected by narrow passages, so you can paddle or boat from one into another, while Vrbnik, which is also the smallest, is completely separate from the rest. Together they cover about 138 hectares.

they’re warmer than the sea

The Baćina Lakes form a cryptodepression, meaning their surface is only slightly above sea level, while their bottoms lie deep below it. Although they are just a step from the sea and surrounded by permeable limestone, the lakes are freshwater. Some springs are nevertheless directly connected to the sea, so salt water appears in the deeper layers. In the Klokun area near Plitko Lake there is a spring that supplies drinking water to the town of Ploče and the surrounding area.

During the scorching summer, the water in the lakes is noticeably warmer than the sea, with tourist sources citing a difference of roughly three degrees. Because of this, the swimming season here starts earlier and ends later than on the coast. The best-known bathing spots are those near the Mindel spring, and the hidden coves and small beaches are reached by kayak, paddleboard, or traditional Neretva boat.

links with queen teuta

Legend has it that the Illyrian Queen Teuta adored this area, and the lakes are still called Teuta’s pearls. Historians, however, have their own evidence and explanations. Near Sladinac Lake the remains of the Roman settlement of Praetoria have been found, along with the remains of an early Christian basilica from the 6th century and a necropolis of stećci tombstones.

Around the lakes a walking and cycling path about 15 kilometres long has been arranged, with benches, springs, and information boards. In 2020 the Public Institution for Protected Natural Areas of Dubrovnik-Neretva County installed 19 educational boards about dragonflies, amphibians, reptiles, and birds. Near the Oćuša spring there is a bird-watching hide, and the lakes also contain three small islets, one of which is named the Island of Love. The entire area forms part of the Natura 2000 ecological network, within two zones of the Neretva Delta, as a habitat for strictly protected and endemic species.

a worthwhile stop off on a long drive south…

A visit to the Baćina Lakes is truly an experience you will remember for a lifetime. Walking the paths that wind right beside the lakes will reveal scenes covered in water lilies, the reflection of clouds mirrored on the still water, and the song of rare birds that creates an almost meditative atmosphere.

Here you can also swim in crystal-clear water that provides refreshment during the great heat, and a special experience comes when the sun sets and the whole landscape is immersed in golden and pink tones. Then the lakes take on an almost fairy-tale appearance. It is a perfect moment for a photograph, but also for simply enjoying the silence of nature.

In the heart of the summer season, a parking space at the viewpoint along the main road is almost impossible to find. Down by the lakes themselves, however, there are usually no crowds. Most travellers photograph the view and drive on, while those who go down to the water, sit in a boat, or cycle a loop are completely enchanted and, like us, probably think: “How is this place not far better known?”
